FROM DAY TO DAY_ IN AMERICA. A BRIGHT PICTURE. - BY JOSEPH ELLIiiON. "Well, well, I never met with such kindness in all my life! Here's a man walking along with his team on Main-street giving pears to the people free. See what a fine one he placed in my hand as I passed him." Such was the address I made to my fellow clerk as I entered the store on return from dinner to-day, and because it forcibly touched the jovial part of me, I want to tell it you. It is however an apt illustration, in a simple way, of the exceeding kindness bestowed upon me freely by the people of Worcester, ever since I thoroughly made myself known to them. On every side of this many-sided life I meet with flowers and perfumes; and,although thorns of discontent are sometimes felt through lost ideals, or hope deferred, the way is bright. Does it not seem quite a time since many in my native town heard anything about me? Gracious how can it be the 17th of September ? How time flies and how life wears away! And yet I have never written you one account, Mr. Editor, of its running wheels de die in diem ! Censure ? Yes, myself ; yet excuse—here's the bustle of city life, and there the store where bread is earned ; whilst on the charm- ing Sabbath are souls waiting for the bread of heaven. For many a long day I have wanted to exonerate an anxious mind by pushing this letter between these crowding engagements. Indeed seven or eight weeks have come and gone since writ- ing a quarter column that lies before me; and it has grieved, me often when I have looked at it, and thought of it, and could not run the pen along. I have been often gratified when told by private friends of the inquiries of the boys I left behind me in Warrington. To know that they consider me worth inquiry or remembrance is no small pleasure, you know. During this exodus they have .not allowed .my' name nor interests to sink in absolute forgetfulness, but from lines direct and indirect have gleaned some knowledge of their neighbour's doings. With your permission, I make this public acknowledgement of their kindness, at the same time asking them to accept of this short account of my activities in return. THE WAY IS BRIGHT, I say, with hops; but my firmament has its clouds —it has had them right along from the 15th April, when I said farewell to those at home. And when a village boy is enveloped in mists, and blind with mental cobwebs in a foreign country, it is rather awkward. That's just how I felt when first realis- ing a changed social condition, wherein are found ideas,expressions, and customs peculiarly American. Climatic change, dietary, hours of loneliness, (the loneliness arising from knowing and speaking to no one) added to the weakening La Grippe, were amongst my earlier troubles. I suffered and waited patiently until all were past, took each day's light or shade just as it came; and now I feel strong and well again. " He's all r'ght." "'Who's all right? Jo Ellison "! You want to know ABOUT WORCESTER? Well, that's wherei live. It's 45 miles from Boston, situate amongst the hills of Massachusetts. Oh! how I wish Warrington was as beautifully set,with hills that rise like bulwarks on every side covered with nature's summer attire ! How I wish her authorities would allow mother nature to adorn her sfireets*ith all the shades of green! Worcester martes 4escribed as being in a valley on a hill. The valley is the business part of the city, and on the eastern and western slopes are the homes of many of her 95,000 inhabitants. Every street has its trees. Whenever a new street is made,two rows of trees some twelve yards apart are planted; and, when these are grown, beautifully shaded streets are the result. Walking in some portions of Elm, Chestnut, May, or Main Streets.one is ready to ask," Where are the houses ?" and standing on a distant prominence, "Where are the factories ? " Trees you can see anywhere. Like Warrington, Worcester manufactures large quanti- ties of wire of almost every description ; to which are added corsets, pistols, organs, machinery, car- pets, tools, envelopes, boots, shoes, and slippers. There are seven or eight shoe factories, but most of their goods go west. Yet the visitor must go to the street to learn of their existence. If he takes half- an-hour's ride from City Hall,he won't realise there is a city anywhere near the everlasting hills around him. Free from the smoke and bustle, he may lie by the peaceful lake with fostered thoughts of bliss. Why did I come to Worcester? What led me here? Well, God led me, that's all. Dispute it if you like. Oh, incredulous, it is true just the same. Of all the cities on this continent Worcester was the last I purposed visiting, but somehow I saw an advertisement in a Boston paper for a reporter on the "Worcester Telegram." I answered and ob- tained a place on the staff. A flattering offer came along from Chicago, but I let it go for the "Tele- gram,' where I worked three weeks—only three long, idle, monotonous weeks; then I quit. Going to work at 1.30 p.m. was too had, as the freshness had gone by that time. Then working to midnight, and Sunday as well was even worse. So after toss- ing about a week or two I struck a job in a shoe store. However even this is not my sphere, al- though I have continued for quite a while; and possibly the employer won't like me leaving him next month, when I purpose mounting the car for Chicago, Council Bluffs, Denver, and San Francisco. Then I shall get my wish gratified. During my stay here I have ASSOCIATED WITH THE BAPTIST CHURCH on Lincoln Square, where I found the friends and friendships so true, and strong and staunch for the doing of many a deed. To these people I preached my first sermon in America on the morning of June 21st, in their meeting-house,with gallery round and organ to tlke right. Pastor Miller conducted devo- tional exercises,and I preached on "Salvation to the uttermost." When the service closed, the people thronged me with smiling faces,kind commendations, and hand-shaking. "I am surprised, Mr. Ellison; I did not know you were a minister. Why didn't you tell me !" In the afternoon Bro. Weston drove me to their mission at Greendale 3miles out,where I preached on "Laying down one's life." Actually the people there were drawn towards me too, for I have preached to them. every Sabbath since, con- ducted their week evening service, and had charge of the whole work. They call me their pastor, and indeed ere long I may be in another sense of the word. After the first Sunday's efforts, the pastor asked me to take charge of the pulpit at Greendale, for three or four weeks. When these were over,his deacons decided to have me continue until the be- ginning of October, when other arrangements were pending; informing me at the same time that they were wanting a man to devote Ins whole time and effort for the spiritual interests of the people. Now the probation is almost complete. The deacons have met their pastor in conference on the work and the the worker, and from an indirect source I learn that everything is in my favour. Friends have gathered round on every side, much kindness and interest is shown, smiles and God-speeds are frequent, and altogether I feel that to leave them now would be using the knife or touching the iron in the soul. Did I not say God led me here? Do you doubt it?

CALIFORNIA? now AND wrung ? Well is is just like this; I thought it would not be amiss for me to ask for four weeks before enter- ing on the work permatiently,to allow time for the trip, and a good stay there with the friends I love so much. That is just how matters stand with me at present—bright and promising as I said before. There is nc need for me to supplement the descrip- tions of American life given by Mr. J. S. Green on his return home. Your paper is Anglo-American enough, but, if only for the sake of my friends, you might print this letter, and when further develop- ments have come and gone I may write to them again. Only they must not look for logic, politics, or labour disputes, as my mind tends en familia at prelent. All hail to your Free Library, and your Free Education! Oh my native land, why so far be- hind this little State? Why so slow to move with aese educated working people? I regret to say you are far behind.

At the fourth annuall-rneeli—ng of the Scottish Rome Rule Association at Aberdeen, on Tuesday, a letter was read from Mr. Gladstone, written from Fasgue,Laurence- kirk, in which the right hon. gentleman said :—" Since I spoke at Aberdeen in 1870 the wants and convictions of Ireland have been made known to us in a manner at once most constitonal.and most emphatic by the voice of the representatives given in overwhelming propor- tion. With respect to Scotland I continue to think the present arrangements and practice under them most un- satisfactory, and that she suffers by them both in com- mon with England and on her own account. I also think the Scottish people are as well entitled as the Irish to form and express their judgment as to the best mode of mending them, and I have the firrnest conviction that, both as to the time of making their demands, and as to the form and character of those demands they will proceed -with all the aids that reflection and experience can supply, and with that wise combination of firmness and circumspection for which they have commonly been distinguished in the management of public affairs."

div.head: _ THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 3, 1891. IN CALIFORNIA. A DARING IMPOSTOR.
div.p: _ THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 3, 1891. IN CALIFORNIA. A DARING IMPOSTOR.
A DARK PICTURE. BY MR. H. WHITHAM.

It is possible that readers of the "Examiner" may feel somewhat tired of the American question. They have had, for quite a time now, descriptive articles of almost all and everything pertaining to life on this great continent, so that it would seem super- fluous on my part to attempt giving any further useful, or interesting information. Well, at the risk of being termed a bore, I have determined to use up a little more ink We all know the story of the shield. How easy it is for two men, ah. or a dozen men, to look at the same article, and differ in their reports as to what the article is like. bo do we differ, who attempt to describe life, scenery, or the climate of this great country. This is not to be wondered at, when we consider its size, and the nature of the immigration constantly going on. Place California in Europe, and it would extend from London, across France and well into Spain. Lay Texas on the face of Europe, and this giant, with his head resting on the mountains of Norway, with one palm covering London, the other Warsaw, would stretch himself down across the kingdom of Denmark, across the empires of Germany and Aus- tria, across Northern Italy, and lave his feet in Vle Mediterranean. There may be A LITTLE SPREAD EAGLEISM _ _ _

in this big talk; but what then? It will give the general reader a better idea of the size of this country. It is said that this golden West has up- wards of 200,000 square miles of coal measure,thirty eight times the area of all the coal fields of Great Britain. From where I write to New York is 3,500 miles, and the travelling is of such a description as to appal any one who sat down to think of it. Take up any morning paper almost, and you find illus- trated descriptive accounts of trestle bridges being either washed out, burnt out, or of the lines being so warped by the sun's heat that whole trains are precipitated to destruction. Yes, my readers, this is a great country, and its very gieatness has affected and will continue to affect, the minds of its people to such an extent that they do and must despise the men and " the day of small things." One of your correspondents recently said that, if he didn't live in Oregon he would want to. I can only say that " If I didn't live in California, I should be glad ; and if I did not live in this free (?) country at all I would be mighty pleased." And yet, the tale must not be half told. I am often told Cali- fornia is not America, as I have it constantly dinned into my ears that above all things San Francisco is neither California nor yet any part of America. This as to the ways of her people, of which more anon. IS CALIFORINA A BEAUTIFUL STATE? IS it a fine country for 3ne to come to? Well, let us look at the shield from the same point of view, and then we shall understand one another. Cali- forina is a mighty state, mighty in size, and awfully grand in its scenic effects. To travel is costl3 ,and has, so far, been entirely beyond my reach. My , little trips have so far been confined to short rides from the city, of not more than 200 miles. This at home would mean setting your house in order as if you were going to do,and to dare,a desperate thing. I see it frequently said that cost of travelling is much lower here than with you. It need be; with stations scores of miles apart, it would takes pretty f, Jod pile for one to get a move on if the cost was much higher. And yet it has not been entirely beyond my hopes to see the Red Wood and the Big Tree of California ; I have wandered some little amongst them. The Big Tree grows in graves of which there are about nine, scattered through various counties in the State, and is partial to the

lower parts of the Sierra. A grove may cover a belt of 3,200 feet long by 700 feet broad. In the Calaveras grove there are between 90 and 100 trees, one of which has had the bark stripped from it up to the height of 115 ft. above the ground. One large tree measures 57ft. in circumference, at three feet from the ground. A stump, so burned that only one halt remained, was 23ft. in diameter inside the bark at 3ft. from the ground. Another tree, which had fallen, and had been burned hollow, was large enough for three horsemen to ride abreast into the cavity for a distance of 30ft., its height and width being about lift. The trunk of this tree was bored through at 120 ft. from the ground, and at that point had a diameter,. exelusive of the bark, of 13f 5., and at 169 ft. from its base the tree was 91t.in diameter. Accompanied by a friend who is now leaving for Warrington, and will most likely be Ithere as soon as this letter, a few of my family ' arranged :A PICNIC INTO THE MOUNTAINS. It was carried out and thoroughly enjoyed during the past summer. A more interesting ride can scarcely be imagined than the one into the moun- tains. Starting from the city, the bay has first to be crossed, and a very short distance suffices to leave the level grcund behind. Through miles after miles of orchards, of peaches, apricots, and pears ; past cottages almost lost to view, enshrined in moss; past lanes whose hedges seem to be made up of rose trees, and the beautiful everlasting flower; on we go up into the mountains, where from or- chards we have changed to vineyards. New is the time to see the grapes growing; Within half an hour's ride of our own door we can see the moun- tain sides covered with vines. Celiforniaie going to be a great country for wine making. But let us get done with the picnic. When we arrived at our destination we were among.the-Big Trees. But they seem to be disappearing fast, which is. a great pity. It is fine to look at them, to think that on the stump of a tree a very few feet from. the ground a score of couples may dance to the sound of a band of music perched on another stump a few- feet away. Fire plays an important part in. these for- ests. It will make a road right through atree-, or will hollow one out cave-like to form. a home for those who fancy camping out. Our party struck out from the car track, thinking to have a good time in walking over the mountains-where- all this grand scenery is. It pretty nearly turned out serious' for us; we got lost. Fancy being lost in these I mountains; what a sensatiomit would: have been to have come across Mr. Bruin roaming about in search of some lone morsel walking about on, two, legs. We had an idea that if we went far enough, we should strike the car track. Of one thing we were sure, if we didn't strike the, track pretty soon., a. right in the mountains was before.useand that was no joke. It was all very well to admire Big Trees., and wonder at the big stumps surrounded by tall suckers, but we didn't want to, pitch, our seat amongst their damp and dripping boughs. We halted and held council hnrriedly. ' • we could find our way back, we thought iso back we startech It was. down hill, that was one good job,. so oft we. started, a general stampede, hailing joyfully every sign that ensured us that we were on the right track. We came out all right and were soon seated. in the cars tired and thankful that " that ends well." Yes, it'e a fine eountry this, flowers and fruits to satiety, but one can- not live altogether on these things. now. If it were so, I should say—" Come, come," for there- islfruit and flowers in abundance here in California.. More than this, I are quite sure that men with a little capital, say, from .EaX) to £B,lo.may„with a first outlay of a part of these sums become.. in, at least five years tittl2, owner of their own fruit growing farms, and able to take life easy, while sitting beneath their own fig trees. Unfortunately the great majority of us are not pcesessed of wren the smallest of these suns ewe come over here generally in the poorest fire In debt maybe, as in ray case; then the struggle is a pretty stift one: If they happen to meet employers,. as I have done, without heart or conscience, woe be to them, for they will find themselvesenot only left, but so far away from the rest of the-world, that, if they are not careful they:will find .the downgrade made easy for their weary limbs. I have, during the-past few weeks, come across vite a heap of workmen, who have but one tale to tall, that is the in difference of enaployeraand managerato their work- men's welfareand responsibilities. The following sketch of the employer whom I trusted when I came out, may, I am afraid, be taken as a sample of the majority in this city. I have PRECIMIS BIT OBpp , besides me which reads as follows: " San,Fiancleco, ilkugust 19th, 1.591. H. Whitham Esq.

• Dear Sir, We have decided to lay off some of our hands,. and you are included among the number. Therefore your services will not be required after the present date.. Yours truly, G. R. CLAPP." Am I not right in calling;this a precious document? I My dear friend Mr. Clapp, who is foreman of Cali- fornia Wire Works, addresses me in the most courteous language. He not only dubs me "Esquire,' but says I am a "Dear Sir." Truly I am honoured by such condescension on his part. This is the land of liberty, and surely a foreman can discharge a " hand " without consulting anyone. What matters it that the " hand " had depending upon him a family of six, nay eight as will appear further on.

I was one of the oldest "hands " in the mill, several have tome and been "broken in" since I came. Most of the men are single; my family is nearly as largo as the whole of the men's families combined. I am selected as the first man; so far I am the only man. Everyone will naturally ask—Why what is he discharged for? Did not Mr. Hallidie engage him in Liverpool? Was he not promised three dollars a day? Yes, I answer to all this. Not only is this so, but Mr. Hallidie paid my own fare from Liverpool to San Francisco. Then what is it all about? More than this, no hint was given me that the mill did not run more than half the time. Since

I have been here, now nearly four years, I do not think I have earned on the average more than a dollar and a half a day. This, with fifteen shillings a week out for rent, will leave me at this writing almost a millionaire. I waited, of course, upon Mr. Hallidie after getting the notice. He could give me no answer, no explanation. He listened to all I had to say, but could give me no satisfaction beyond saying that he would write me out as good a character as I could desire, and a little pecuniary help was also suggested. It was hinted that I could not get along with the foreman. This I thought strange. The foreman that was here when I came was twice discharged. The first time because of the harsh character of his dealings with others in authority. He took a dislike to me because a certain woman from Warrington,one who should have been a friend instead of an enemy, cir- culated the report that I had come to take his place as manager. He twice had me in his office to answer this very grave charge. To injure me he circulated the statement, a very damaging one here, that I was a trade agitator, a dissatisfied trade unionist, and a socialist. I think he has since met his reward. The next foreman was, after about a month's trial, was also sent away. But my dis- charge cannot be, or should not be, much of a loss. The works stopped last May for a month '- we , played all through June. When we commenced it was with a double turn of men to work one shift. ' This went on for quite a time, when several of us ' asked the fore:rim how long it was going to con- tinue, and suggested that the single and newer hands should make room for those who had families and were older workmen. In a few days the result ' came as I have shown above. But I have got " a character," and here it is : " California Wire Works, Sept. 10, 1891. ' Mr. Henry Whitham has been in the employ of the California Wire Works for some years. Slackness of work has thrown him out of employ- ment.
I can recommend him to any one needing the services of an intelligent, trustworthy, and con- scientious man.
A. S. HALLIDIE,"
Sinee then

I HATE WALKED TUB STREETS., ray daughter also, seeking work.. A more heartless piece of business I never knew, If the consciences of those engaged in it are at rest, why, I have no need to grumble. Nuone but those engaged in it know what it is to go tramping clay after clayr a weary distance into the city seeking work. I have met scores, who, lite myself, have walked the shoes off their feet in tba dreary task of seeking work. There are scores of employment offices,whose chief occupation seems to be the getting of dollars out of the pockets of tha poor. There are some offices honest enough, I think, but you, must first post a dollar, and afterwards pay ape centage on your first month's earning.- Our Hama has paid as much as 7 Ms. out of a month'-earning,. although the position was only temporary. I got &job offerect me during one of my searchiw.rounds,and accepted it. It was to go into the mountains to, labour at a trestle bridge which had been burnt out. I started off at noon on a.- hundred miles ride, and got in late at night. If I had not felt so.miserable about the whole thing, I ahould have enjoyed' the ride. It was through a beautiful country. All along the roads were to be seen the

CAMPING GROUNDS of parties who had rushed far away from the. mad: ding crowd of the-city. This camping out is-fine.- tents are to be seen pitched in the valleys all along the line, and as the train stopped at the various places appointed it`was quite a• sight to • see the pleasure seekers, young and old,..inale and female, come running up to the train, anxious for- letters from friends, or more supplies for the inner- man. When we arrived at our destination, we found it to be a small hamlet suvrounded by farm and forest, a sleepy sort of place, but having qxtite enough-so' the depot about it to fancy it was leading ahusr life. :Fire had cleared the hill sides, and there and there could be seen standing just a brick,chimney and tire place, the wooden shanty itself barnt away,. The railway bridge whi3h had spanned a valley sometfew hundred yards wide, and near ninety feet high, was entirely cleared out. It was a grand sight. end the amateur photograplwrsoon found it out. I was set to work with a lot of Chinamen carrying lumber for the carpenters. Oh ! the disgui•st I felt all that day, hauling and carrying lumber with half-a-dozen pigtails up and down the mountainsides. Tiithink that it was for this that I had lea old England! When night came I w,uld scarcely .walk to the-saloon where I had to sleep, but if I could'ut walk, .Peould make my mind up. NO TRESTLE :WALKING KATE. SO I inquired the pay. Two dollars a day ; and bow- much for board and lodging? One dollarr. This, when carefully reckoned up, leaves one dollar for enying the company of the almond-eyed celestial for ten hours. I soisght the boss, and 'asked him if' he-would grant me• a pass back to the city---it was a 1%. ride—and pay me off.- Ile was kind enough to do this; that is ilia gave me thepass,and took the-. 1 cheque to the saloon keeper tellinghim to cash tho-1 cheque and pay himself. I receilied just one quar- ter, Is. for my day'), work. Wheal told :Cif* other- nay-vies, wasn't theresome sweet, ifinguage all expected at least two and a tall dollars-a day:. Lots of them cleared out of the .sakoon and !sought, quarters in the railway carriagesor elsewhere. They,- wouldn't pay half', what they earned for • bed and • board, and they all wished they c:ank-1 get atpass and so clear out of the sob. When I tisk for a ,pick and shovel job, they look at me.. "'No,' they answer; "- we have lots of' men who are used to setch worls:"' , Some of my readers may say wrrNur LOOKIEfiNB:ER ?? Well I have done that, ,with the result-of finding,' that market atao glutted. It is no -usedooking4to the country. If a rumour reaches the. city that- there is a scarcity of labour on -the fruit ranches,- hundreds of applications a day reach the State Board of Trade for a, chance of work._ Ilhave-been to the. railways to-day, and am told they,•are over-handed. ara now melting enquiry a.s to another place„ and, if successful :401 soon leave-San; Francisco a Ming,: way behind me; I don't see-bow, We can all altar. out. My daughter's husband was taken sick some eighteen mouths ago- I thought it was parals-of the lower limbs; the doctor says it is a spineicona. .plaint. Anyway he cannot leave-his bed, and my , wife divides her time betwixt the two houses, Happy me,. nay, happy us, we seem to be spoiled favourites-of fortune. I saw. recently in an Araeri- can letter publisheatin the ‘4 Examiner" whare the writer salift "loan get a man for u, dtdlar a clity„aed I can ears, 31 ; so youiseeit does not pay- me 'to do all the hard work:" What- pleasant readang this! Verily the ways of Frovidenae are insarntauble. I wonder it I &m-, one of the, dollar-a-day-men. Perhapa I am; perhaps not ;:we sball see. September WI, 1891, 814 Bay-street,. San Francisco.

div.head: THEI STORY OF AN INNOCENT CONVICT.
div.p: THEI STORY OF AN INNOCENT CONVICT.
BY ALFRED R. CALHOUN.
CHAPTER NM. THE END OF A THRILLING SCENE
" A felon!"

This was the exclamation that burst from tire tips of those assembled, as they glanced from Mott Rey bold to his victim. "I repeat it; that man's true narue is Allen Ike:. He is an ex-convict, and last summer he returned from Sing Sing, where he served a long term for forgery; for a forgery, mark you, whish he tried to fasten on a member of this family. Speak, sir, and say if I have not told the truth." Mott Reybold had nerved himself for the occasion, and now, with his right hand clenched and raised be towered above Allen, as if he were going to strike him.
At this a look of henor came into the faces of the people. 31r. Lefferts tried in vnin to speak. _ _

Irene's lips were parted, her -face white, and her hands clasped in agony over her heart. For an instant Allen; who saw that all eyes were riveted on him, felt stunned by the sud- denness of the blow that had been so cruelly dealt him.

"What say you to this charge?" asked Dr. Put- man, addresming himself to,Allen when the silence had become painful. "He says it is a hideout, lie, coloured with at. little dangerous truth!" cried Florence, coming over and throwing her arxns. about her brother's; neck.

The sound of her brave voine; and the touch of her gentle hands stirred Allen into life. He rose to his feet, and looking steadily into Reybold's eyes, faced him without a tremor. His lithe, erect form, intellectual face and all the exterior indications of a noble manhood, contrasted strongly with the bearing =1 expression of his accuser.

"it is just to my friends that I shonld explain Reybold's charges here and now,. but before I do so, let me ask him if he has anything more to say." " Is your name Allen Gilbert t"' sneered Reybold„ making as if he would retire. "I shall answer to that with th*other &large." "Will you deny that you were a -felon r "Before replying, let me ask you)if a felom is not one guilty of a crime against the law. 7" " I will accept that definition, M. Lee," said Rey- bold, with a smile of triumph. "Then I am not a felon 1" "Were you not tried f3c forgery r
"1 was:"
"And found guilty r
"And sentenced to Sing Sing
id served your timer
"1 did?

" That is all I care for you to confty3s-attliii-tihre unless, indeed, you acknowledge that 3-.ou have used your talents, since your return, to- delude good people into your schemes for money getting.without Labour. I came here to say this muchs.nowl shall go and leave you to explain; said Reybold, as, he, turned to the door.

He evidently meant tO go ont, but before ho coul take a step, Allen sprang before him,Jseized'him-by the shoulder, and exclaimed: "You have made your chalre." IsTowy, sir; Tent must listen to my defence." "Your- &fence !" Reybold rcanged to say, a.s he i staggered back; "the place to make yonr defence was before the judge and jury who. tried 'and victed you." "Yet you shall hear me," said Allen, novionder-- tiny cool, and resolute. "Yea," joined in the doctay- "as -con., have made your accusations here, you ',should listen to what M. Gilbert has to say in his own de— fence."

Reybold again, sat down, and Allen ~first excusing himself far the length of the story he was to. tell; went onto, give an account a his father and mother, and his own early life. He told of hia father's failure in business; .and of his- own efforts, to support the family from his salary in the bank. lia those days he hoped to be a bankerlimself bef ore he reached:middle age, and, with &little money he had 'saved'Oi° had' fr:.lwantlY discounted good notes for-small sums, charging a legal interest for the. sew commodation,,and making his collections 'through the bank with whicla he was connected.'
Ih this way he met Mott Reybold, and several times•got hi, accommodations, for he knew he was the son of a rich,. man and the Lica. of Frank Lefferts.

One day Reybeld and a friend came to Allan with] a note for fifteen hundred dollars, made payable to I tile order of himself and signed by ap well-known. gentleman of the city. Allen got him the money, , and put the note in the bank for collection. When that note came due, and was, presented to the gentleman whose signature it bore as maker, he declared it was a forgery. It was then taken to Mott Reybold, and he denied ever having indorsed.; it; or. ever having had any business transactions , with rao,' continued Allen, his eyes riveted on Rey- hold's faoe. "'she-result was that r was -arrested,. and, on,the trial, that man Reybold,whohadrobbed, ' me of all my money, swore that he hadneversigned4 nor sold that note: "I, shall not dwell on that triab. I could, nob- employ able lawyers. I was nearly.Talone- in the: world and defenceless. For the sake of: the dear. ones dependent on me, I made the best fight I:' could, but the very intelligence and deterrninatiom with which I fought my own caseonly servekin, the opinion ofthe jury, to confirm my guilti "But I shall-net dwell on what followed -J Lwas4 convicted, on the testimony of a.robber and a per- jurer, and torn avray from my family. Por nearly five years I; .as- innocent as the unborn, wore the uniform of crime and consorted witheriminals. "-Often I prayed for death, and .I: would have sought it, but. for the feelinc, of love and duty that ever kept my parents and sister before my, eyes: "At length-came a day when the prison garb-was tahen off, my threadbare clothes, removed so long before, were handed me, and I was toldWcould go ' into the wend- a free man.

"I wandered, to New York, Qucl, tried\ to find, my and.at the same time to get work; L could not find ray, furaily, and among,those who knew me a: old I Gould' not get work. The name Lee; as-eon- nected with,myself, was disgraced in the eyes of a prejudicelworld. So, in my de.iporatiou, L took my mother's name,. Gilbert. "The memory of the pask':and' the trials of the present were driving me to madness, when one day I read in.,,the papers that Mott Reybold—tAe per- jured wretch, who had blasted my liie—was-ltading the young men of spirit anclfashion at Long Branch. Desperate and revengeful„ for lift had become a burden,, I spent my last coin fora.ticket, and went down the coast to find this saan,wadi lay him dead at my feet. "Asa stood looking crat•at.the sea+ anei wishing I were. at rest under the waves; I' heard the cry that stirred me to the rescue of a, drowning woman. 1 "You know the rest; but all of you do not know that AIL Lefferts sent me fifty dollars through that Reybokl,, which my necessities forced me to accept,. With that money, I again searched for my family,, and at length found them hi a hovel, which I reached in time to reoeive thohlessizg of my dyin%

father. "Of the kindness of Mita Lefferts and Dr. F"atnarn I shall not speak save to say that the hands they extended have lifted rue and mine from the depths of despondency to the heights of hope. "Often I have wanted to tell my friends all about my past, bat, dreading to think of it myself, I feared that a confession would result in their enstrangement, and—and, in my being cast adrift again. "That is mF stbry," said Allen, as in coaclusion he raised his. face heavenward, "and the Great 3ndge, who needs no jury to confirm his opinion, knows I have told only the truth." There was not a person ip the room who was not ieeply moved while Allen was speaking. geybold's face became livid, and several tunes no made an effort to interrupt, but the words stuck in his swollen throat. He broke the silence that followed Allen's defence by rising to his feet, and saying: "My name is unstained. It is for you to say if this fellow Lee's word is to be taken as against mine. I have done what I believe to be laay duty in warning you. Good night." He bowed, and tottered out ef the room, as if the scene which be had just witnessed had had an in- toxicating effect on him. As soon as Reybold had gone Mr. Lefferts left the parlour without a word, but it was evident to all that he was much excited. Irene looked as if she were goint to faint, and during the verbal encounter between the young men her eyes wandered from one to the other as if she were measuring them, and weighing what they said.
Of all the veule rresent Florence ajoiao ap- . _ _

Earl Spencer addressing a Liberal meeting‘at Buxton on Thesday ni;ht, saidthey might expect a. dissolution of Parliament next year, and the Liberals were anxious to submit their views to the country. Referring to foreign affairs he advocated the withdrawal of British troops from Egypt as soon as was consistent' with the. safety of bovernment. If- they did not complain of lord Salisbury's foreign policy, it was because the Con- servatives, had adopted the policy proclaimed by tie , Liberals, which was that of non-intervention. On mat- ters of home policy harnaintained that the Government had not the confidence of the constituencies. The religt- ous difficulty in Wales, for instance,. would be settled not by a Government Tithes Bill, but by a Liberal GOAN ernmeat on linessimilar to those appßed to the Irish Churches. The, Liberal party intended to put Horne Rule for Ireland to the fore-front of the coming battle. He denied that any measure would satisfy Ireland ex- cept that of lion3e Rule.

Her eyes blazed, her cheeks flushed, and her delicate nostrils quivered with scorn as she tried to catch Reybold's eye; and when Allen had con- cluded his thrilling explanation she kissed him, and looked up at him with an expression of confidence and pride that intensified and glorified the beauty of her face.

Dr. Putnam, though ordinarily a man of great self-command, was so upset by Reybold's interrup- tion that it was some time before he could speak with his customary deliberation. "I do not think," he said at length, "that what we have heard from Mr. Reybold should at all Influence us in ou.v purpose. We are here not to benefit ourselves, save as we are benefited by doing good, but to assist the poor and needy children of the city, so far as lies in our power. Mr. Gilbert read his sister, through their unselfish efforts, have called our attention to this matter, and it is for us to carry out the work, and not to inquire into the history of the workers." "I quite agree with Dr. Putnam," said; the Rev. Paul Enfield, a young clergyman of great prudence. "Still' I think it would be wiser to let Mr Gilbert stand in the background tor the present. Mark you, lam eager to believe that our friend all he claims, but as Mr. Reybold will, without doubt, give publicity to what he told us here, we must not do anything that will loot like defying public opinion." Mr. Enfield was quite right in this, thouglithe doctor thought him somewhat heartless. An innocent or reformed convict, engaged in a pod work, and co,operating with goo&people, was some- thing the world would be very slow to believe. Allen relieved' all present by not only resigning his position, 'Jut also by severing, for the present his connectiorz with the society. "The Humming To," and there are •threeleading characters in it, each one of the great- • est interest.; Them are St. Peter, his most noble excellency, Count Geirfollig„and the crippled child- -of a day labourer. Ah ! you are ints.rested, now. So was St. Peter, as - ,• you will see when you reach the story. It begins with • ,the count, who hasjnet died. . Peter angrily._ "All that is charge& fast enough,. not to your credit, but:. against you, because it wasdone for ranbition and.. selfishness, and ostentation and hypoczisy." "My life's best work," continued the•count, still more proudly ".how L made my fatherland great.: and glorious beyond all lands on earth,. I do not need to mention, for II presume my fame has long; ago ascended here." "Your • fame, retorted St. Peter with increasing: indignation. "has not reached us, ,but groans of, dying youths have risen to us from your battle- fields-and desolate homes, the despair of mothers. and bsides:.and I, tell you, wretch,. it you have-no- thing better-than this to urge you are a lost man."" -- A visitor who was fishing off Deal pier 18. st week brought up a gold watch and chain on his hook. It is supposed to be one lost off the pier by a resident en last Bank Holiday, but the fortunate fisher has not been seen since his lucky find.

Mr 'Gladstone has an article on " kncient Beliefs in a Future State" in the October number of "The Nineteenth Century," thus demonstrating afresh to Mr. Dicey and others his renewed good health, vigour, and elasticity of mind.

Princess Christian, who hastened her return from Germany in compliance with a summons from the Queen, has gone to Balmoral, end she will stay there with her Majesty until Princess Beatrice is conva- lescent after her acetuchement, which is daily ex- pected to take place.

Lord Methuen knew 'he was dying. lie was an ardent Freemason, and tuntil four months ago was Provincial Grand Master of Wiltshire. His retire- ment was taken to indicate that he knew recovery was hopeless, as he was proud of his osition as the oldest P.G.M. in England, with the single exception of Lord Leigh in Warwickshire.

The announcement of Lord Alinzton's.engagement to Miss Eva Leigh, daughter of the late Mr. Blundell Leigh, will be a surprise to those who know the dis- parity.in age taween the couple. Lord Alington is the 'father of several handsome grown-up daughters, one of 'whom has lately taken to driving ponies four4n-hand, while the other exbribitsn more serious turn of mind, and devotes therself to good works 'under the auspices of the RomanCstholic Church.

This iss, pretty little disclosure about the bully- ing on board the training ship Britannia. Fancy the-senior-cadets (isn't there a syllable too much there?) appropriating all the pocket money of the juniors during their first two terms? And this is the education by which we produce "an officer and a gentleman." No wonder it 'fares rather badly -sometimes with the inhabitants of out-of-the-way parts of the globe when a British naval officer is let` loose upon them.

'A beautiful little memorial of the late Mr. W. H. iffladetone has just been publis)qed at Chester. It -contains a sermon preached the Sunday after the 'funeral by the Rev. E. C. 'Wickham, and other -notices, with a preface by 'Lady Frederick Caven- dish. The gem of the book is its dedication to thel -widow, and the reference -it .contains to the Right Ifon. W. E. Gladstone. The dedication is as fol- lows To the brave and tender mourner who • counts; for her own one of the jewels of the Lord." 14. correspondent wishes to invite the attention of, .our readers to the Society ' for the Protection Birds, which has the Duchess of Portland for its president. The society numbers 10,060 members, and has forty branch secretaries. Two of the rules ti the society are :—/. That members shall dis- courage the wanton destruction of birds, and interest themselves generally in their protection. 2. That lady members shall -refrain from wearing the feath- ers of any bird not killdd for food, the ostrich only •-accepted.

• Among the inmates of the Metropolitan Asylum at Catherham is an old' man named Samuel Gibson. -11 e is, I am told, a hundred and one years of age,and in fairly good health. He served with the 27th • Inniskillings in the Teninsula and at Waterloo, and his story has just been substantiated by the regi- •,mental authorities. There is no Waterloo man now •in Chelsea Hospital. The last survivor of the battle -on the records of that institution was John WlCay, who died there a few years ago. He served with the Black Watch.

Lord Randolph Churchill is not one of those pro- phets who are honoured everywhere but in their - own country. On the-contrary, he seems to be get- ting himself disliked wherever he goes. The Boers have just been amusing themselves by burning him - in effigy at Pretoria, with the usual honors. 'This is a very appropriate return for the roasting that Lord ' Randolph has given the Boers. But it shows what a lot of mischief this/ noble lord has done by his offensive and superficial criticism of people of whom ' he knows nothing. 'They say in South Africa that - the hostility between'fßoer and Briton is fiereernow than it has been for years.

The news that although severely injured Seymour Lucas wax not killed in the disastrous railway collision in Spain has been received with a feeling of relief. But Art has suffered enough in the accident, for Mr. Maurice Long, who is -slain, was the son of a great artist of that name. Mr. Seymour Lucas is comparatively a young man. He • was born in 1849, theyear that witnessed the ad- • vent into this world of Lord Randolph Churchill ..*nd a few other remarkable men. His special line is pictures of antiquarian or historical interest, or "costume pictures,' ,as they are sometimes ,satiri- , cally called by peopletwho cannot do them. He is pcobably the best living authority on costume.

An interesting disetision is now in progress upon the question whether an operatic libretto should be • written in prose or verse. M. Gounod is known SOMO years ago to have determined to set a prose 'play to music. Verdi has not entered the discussion, 'but it is understood he prefers verse. M. Massenet :And M. Reyer think prose suitable, so long as the . style is elevated. MM. Ambroise Thomas and Sal- •vayre prefer verse, M.Ts.ladilhe is indifferent, while M. Benjamin Godard sagaciously remarks that a ;great deal deuends upon the inspiration of the musi- A:llan. The Spanish composer, Senor Thomas Breton, -,suggests a compromise, the recitatives (or 'those -portions which in modern opera stand for reeittrtives) lobe in prose, and the songs in verse.

Dr. Robert Spence Watson, L.L.D., who,. in his .donble capacity of President of the National Liberal Federation and Chairman of the Newcastle Liberal ,Council, took the chair at the great Liberal meet- ingant Newcastle-on-Tynegis one of the best known politicians in the North cif England. Dr. Watson is solicitor in practice at 'Newcastle, and lives at Bensham Grove, on the other side of the river. His connection with politics has lasted as long as his 'professional career, and he has taken part in all the greatfLiberal movements a the last thirty years. Hetoilk the chair at the meeting called by Mr. Joseph Chamberlain in -1,677 to inaugurate the National Liberal Federation, and was also among the original founders of the National Liberal Club.

Sitjames Fergusson stated on Monday night, in anewerto a question, that he was "in favour of gratrtingto Ireland the same Term of Government as to England," and hoped that next session would see a Local Government Bill for Ireland. If Sir James meant that he would give the Irish county councils the same powers as the English county councils enjoy, he was promising what he knows his party will not perform. Mr. Balfour's attentu- ated measure of Irish local government, giving Irish coanty,councils only the powers of the grand juries in England is condemned by the leading party organs, and has not the support of any leading Tory. The Irish electors in North-East Manchester will not be deceived by Sir JamesTergusson's plau- sible promises.

Mr. Henry IrV.ing has of late been giving us in- teresting reminiscences of his first introduction to the boards. His tutorin those distant days was a certain William Hoskins, a member of the company that Samuel Phelps gathered round him at Sadler's Wells. Hoskins emigrated to Australia, became an ektor-tnanager on the gold fields, made and lost for- tunes in quick succession, and eventually settled divevn in Melbourne. He was the finest Sh akes- perean actor of his time on the colonial stage. Soon after his death, about five years ago, there was a crowded meeting of tke profession in the Mel- bourne Princesse's Theatre to erect a memorial in his honour. A cable message from London was handed to the Chairman. it was a request to be put down for IWO, and was signed "Henry Irving."

Lard Alington, who is a young bid man, is best known as the Prince of Wales's crony and a member of the Jockey Club. The peerage is modern, but the family acres in Dorsetskire are old, and when the Prince and his family visited Crichel last De- cember, the Duke of Clarence occupied the room and couch which had borne the gross weight of George IV. seventy years ago. Crichel is not a show place, but the gardens are famous for their violet bed, and people go from far aid near to see the Lady Aling- ton's White Parra, where no beast or bird is pet- mitted to be used or reared that is not pure white.

MR. T. D. SULLIVAN, M.P., AT WARRINGTON, On Tuesday evening a very largely 'attended and enthuz,l43tic meeting was held in theo-opera- live Sankey-street, under the auspices of the Warrington branch of the Irish National League. The speakers of the evening was Mr. T. 1). Sullivan, M.P. Mr. F. Loughlin presided, and amongst those present were Councillors Fleming, H.. Roberts, and Dixon's; Messrs. T. Morris, T. Birchall, Kiernan, M. Lyon, J. Albinson, Holford, Donnellan, &c. The CIAIRMAN said that most of them were aware that the general election was now withea a measurable distance, and they in Warrington had a great work to do. That work was no other than the changing, or the attempt to change, their representation in Parliament. He believed that, for a considerable time, they had been very dissatisfied with the manner in which they had been represented, and they were determined to change the representation at the first opportunity. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Sullivan was there that night to give them a helping hand in that work. (Applause.) From his (the chair- man's) observations he thought their prospects were very hopeful. In the first place he believed the register upon which in all probability the general election would be fought was very favourable to the Liberal party in this town ; and another reason that led him to hope that they would be victorious was that there was a perfect under- standing and agreement between the Irish electors and the Liberal party in the town on the one all-important question. (Hear, hear.) When the recent unfortunate crisis occurred in the ranks of the Irish party, it found them in Warrington practically unanimous and decided I to go on in future as they had crone on in the past, with- out any change whatever. They preferred to goon with lelr.Parnell, but if that were impossible they would go on profiting by the lessons he had given them, and advoca- ting the policy he had taught them in the past. (Hear, hear.) He -was pleased to say that, when the day of battle came, whoever might be the Liberal candidate he did not stand to lose the vote of a single Irishman in Warringtm. (Applause.) A reason why they might be hopeful in Warrington was that they would not be troubled very muctewith two classes of men. He did not think they would be troubled with any dissentient Nationalists, and he did not think they would be troubled with any dissentient Liberals—(hear, hear, and laughter)—and when they were absent he theught they might say that it would be a fair stand-up fight between Liberals and Tories. That being the case, he had very little doubt as to what would be the result of the contest. (Applause.) There was one slight draw- back, and that was that they had not a candidate, but bethought he could promise them, with out a breach of confidence, or revealing any secret whatever, that in a very short time—much shorter than many of them thought—a gentleman would be brought before them, who would,no doubt,be heartily accepted by the Liberal party.. One thing he might be expected to do, and that was to advocate the strongest and most Liberal measure of Home Rule for Ireland. (Applause.) As Mr. Glad- stone had said; "Ireland blocks the way" and they would ' endeavour to send from Warrington a representativewho would help to remove that block. (Loud applause.) Mr. KIERNAN moved the following resolution :—" That we renew our vote of confidence in the ;Irish Parliamen- taryparty, approved of by the voice of 'lreland; and that we deeply sympathise with our brave countrymen the-evicted tenants, and pledge ourselves to have a share in sustaining them until, despite treason and tyranny, the cause for which they suffer is crowned with lasting victory and success." (Applause.) Councillor H. ROBERTS seeonded the resolution. He said hecordially agreed with every word in the resolu- tion, and he expressed the hope that the alliance which had now existed so long between the Irish party in War- rington and the English Liberal party would be main- tained for many years to come, because their sympathies were in common upon all subjects and general politics. (Hear, hear, and applause.) 'Mr. T. D. SULLIVAN met with an enthusiastic recep- tion. He remarked that one reason why he felt very much at home that night was that he saw he had before him a mass of honest working-men. Without desiring to 'flatter them he said what he believed to be true, that the working class was the most honest, the most unsel- fish, and the best class in this country—the best for the nation, and the best for the future interests, honour, well-being, and the glory of these countries. There was ...virtue, and honesty, and talent in every class in the community, but he looked to and relied upon the working classes above all other people for the achievement of great reforms. (Hear, hear). The time was come when they could at last exercise in the affairs of these countries the influence and power which should of right belong to the industrial classes of the community, the men who made the wealth and constituted the strength of England and Ireland. (Applause.) There were, however, still restrictions and obstacles put in the way of the exercise of their political power, but all these would be swept away when they put the true friends of reform and advancement into a posi- tion that would enable them to do so. The first Liberal administration they had in England would make it one ,Of their first duties to ensure that every qualified and capable citizen should not only have his vote without delay or trouble or expense on his part but also that he should carry it with him wherever he went. (Applause.) He advised them to vote at the bye-elections and at the general election, for that party who had, during the long history of England, been friends-of liberty and of justice, and the helpers of the working people of the country. What party that was they would know. Surely it was not the Tory party. (Laughter and applause.) He had never been able to understand, and could not understand now, how a working-man could vote for a Tory represen- tative. (Hear, hear.) He hoped•the alilance between theeknglish and the Irish Home Rulers would never be broken up. (Applause.) They had given proof of their , good faith to their English friends. They had gone through a time of great anxiety and much sorrow. They had-endured a dreadful disappointment. An honoured I and a trusted man had failed them:: he had turned his backeipon his past, and had departed from the ways of ' righteousness, of honour, and of -virtue. He had fals- ified his record, and lost his high and his glorious position. He,,efter doing many good things and saying many wise things, after advisingand promoting a friendly alli- ' ancebetween the democracies of elreland and England, had departed from that way. He had broken his pro- mises and his faith, and had insulted the man whom he complimented and praised in other times, and he had asked the Irish people tc. follow 'his lead in the matter and to obey his directions. (Cries Of" Never.") They had refused emphatically to do anything of the sort. (Loud applause.) Let him also say on the part of Irish- men that they gladly recognised the fact that the Eng- lish Liberals had stood true and unchanging by their side in their trouble. Both the 'English and the Irish Home 'Rulers had come through the trial both stronger and better than they were before. Their alliance was unbroken and more closely knit and,solidified than be- fore, and they would go forward hopefully and confi- dently to the great battle that was coming and at which they would reverse the verdict of the last general election (Loud and continued applause.) The resolution was then carried unanimously and enthusiaeically. A vote of thanks was afterwards passed to Mr. Sulli- van on the proposal of Councillor FLEMPIG, seconded by Mr. Dencenieeex. A similar vote to the Chairman brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: MURDER IN GLASGOW.
div.p: MURDER IN GLASGOW.

Samuel'Jcanes Nicholson, 25, salesman, living in Glas- gow, was returning home from his shop early on Sunday morning, when he was attacked by four men and a woman. His wife heard his shouts for help. Assistance was obtained. an Nicholson was removed to his house in an unconscious state. It was then found that he had ,been fearfully injured, and he died on Monday morning. The police have arrested a man with whom the deceased recently quarrelled.
StSPECTED MURDER AND SUICIDE,

Gri Saturday William Forster, farmer, of Brow Knowe, Nichol Forest, on the borders of Cumberland, was found lying dead in a field near his home, shot through the body, and with a battered skull. James Armstrong, labourer, living near, was suspected, but when the con- stables attempted to arrest him he threatened to shoot them. The officers withdrew for assistance, and Arm- strong was subsequently found in his cottage with his throat cut. He died shortly afterwards. It appears that Armstrong was a poacher, and that Forster was attracted to the fatal spot on Saturday by the firing of a shot from a gun. Forster's dog was also shot, and ap- parently met its death while attacking Armstrong.

div.head: REVISION COURTS.
div.p: REVISION COURTS.
EDDISBURY DIVISION.

On Tuesday Mr. E. Burke Wood,, barrister, com- menced the revision of the lists of voters for the Parliamentary Division of Eddisbury. He held his first .court at Dunham o'-th'-ilill. The Liberal party were represented by Mr. W. Handley, of Runcorn (assisted by Mr. B. Kniveton), and the Conserva- tives by Mr. R. N. Owen, of Chester. The Conser- vatives had objected to 21 navvies who had been placed on the list by the overseers, and they were struck off on it being shown that they had not oc- cupied the qualifying period. FRODSHAM.
On the same morning-i;.—WOOd revised the list of voters of the Frodsham Polling District and of others in the surrounding neighbourhood, at the Bear's Paw Hotel.

_ THE VALIIII OF LODGINGS. John Francis Wright claimed a vote as a lodger in respect of the use of a sitting-room and sole use of a bed- room at the house of his uncle, John W. Rothwell,Church- st., Frodsham ; a tradesman by whom he was employed. In reply to the Barrister he said the accommodation was worth 10s. a week.—Mr. Handley: That is higher than in any other part of the division.—Mr. Owen: Why the navvies at the huts below pay ss. 6d. per week for a little bit of a truck bed.—Mr. Handley: But for a regular lodger 10s. per week is more than the average price.— The Barrister: I should say that the 10s. would bear whittling down a little. But still at the same time it will leave more than necessary. He had a letter from the uncle stating that he considered the board and lodging wlrth £1 a week and that he paid him a certain sum of money besides as wages.—The claim was allowed.
LANDLORD V. OTERSERRS.

The Conservatives claimed for Geo. Forster, of Ship- st., in respect of the occupation of a field on Frodsham Marsh.—Mr. Handley: This man lives with his mother and it was proved last year that he was not in ' occupa- tion.—Mr. Owen produced a letter from Mr. Ralph Bate, who said the claimant had held the land at a tent of £l6 a year since March 1890.—Mr. Handley: Where is the rent book. There was no answer to this query.— The Assistant Overseer (Mr. Jones) said the claimant adly came in possession of the land last February.—Mr. Handley: Does his name appear on the rate book.— The Assistant Overseer. It does not.—The Barrister: But the letter from the landlord is very definite.—Mr. Tiley : I have seen the rent book and it is all right. Overseers are not to be depended upon in these mat- ters. Mr. Jones would admit that himself.—The Bar- rister allowed the vote.—Mr. Handley: You have de- cided to admit this case without production of the rent book.—The Barrister: I have.—Mr. Handley: Quite right. It will be the same for one as another. TEE CITRATE'S TOTE. _ . .

The Rev. F. D. R-In-g;i-se, -C-u-rate-,--a Overton Parisk Church, claimed through the Conservatives for a vote under the lodger franchise in respect of rooms occupied at the Vicarage. On the rev, gentleman stating that he had occupied the rooms nearly two years the vete was at once allowed. • FORMER RUNCORN CHEMICAL MANUFACTURER CLAIMS.

Mr. John Alcock Johnson, of Westcliffe-road, Birkdale, claimed to be placed on the ownership list in respect of a freehold farm in Frodsham Lordship. The Liberals had objected.—The Assistant Overseer said Mr. Johnson's name did not appear on the rate book.—Mr. Handley : By repute the property belongs not to Mr. Johnson but ti his sister.—Mr. Owen: You must prove that by evi- dence.—Mr. Handley: I have nothing to do but to ask Mr. Johnson to come and prove his right to vote.—Mr. Owen: That is an absurdity.—Mr. Handley: I am not used to talking absurdities on registration law.—Mr. Owen : There is not the slightest evidence of this being anyone else's property.—The Barrister: Except that his sister's name is on the rate book.—Assistant Overseer: The entry is "Miss Johnson's representatives."— Mr. Handley: Mr. Johnson is trustee for his sister I know him personally and I know perhaps sornethine about this property.—The Barrister: I must call upon you now Mr. Owen.—Mr. Owen: I shall have to ask for an adjournment, but Mr. Johnson would have a good claim for costs against Mr. Handley.—Mr. Handley re- torted that no ground of objection was required to a new claim. The claimant must put himself in court.—Mr. Owen: But the objector must give evidence of repute. —Mr. Handley: Not at all. No man is entitled to go on the ownership list until he has proved his title thereto. —The Barrister (to Mr. Owen) : You have got to prove your claim.—Mr. Owen: Not before evidence is given. —The Barrister: Yes, if objection is taken.—Mr. Owen said if Mr. Johnson proved his title he would claim costs.—Mr. Handley said costs could not arise on a new claim except under exceptional circumstances.—The Barrister said he could grant costs if he thought it was a fair case, but the fact that the sister's name appeared on the rate book was a fair objection to take.—The Bar- rister agreed to adjourn the case to Chester.—Mr. Hand- ley said if Mr. Johnson would send the deed, and his aunt's will that would be sufficient. The Conservatives had put in a claim for Joseph Grice, farmer and innkeeper of Kingsley, and Mr. Owen stated that although Mr. Grice was one of the principal inhabit- ants of the place he had been persistently left off during the past two years by the overseers.—The Assistant Overseer: It has been an entire oversight. We worked on last year's list. Mr. Owen had maintained that the name had been left off purposely.—Mr. Owen: Mr. Grice is one of the principal tenants of the parish.—Mr. Hand- Icy: The name has been inadvertently left off.—Mr. Owen: We know what inadvertent is. But this is the second year.—The Assistant Overseer said he had told Mr. Grice he did not know about the matter until he had made a claim, and he was glad he had made a claim.— The Barrister: We will drop the matter now, please.— Mr. Grice: I want my expenses.—The Barrister.—l cannot give them to you.—Mr. Grice (nolding up a form, What does this printed paper say.—The Barrister : It doesn't say we are going to give you anything—Mr. Grice: What is a printed form for ?—Mr. Owen: You ought to be particularly grateful to your assistant over- seer.—Mr. Grice said he bore no animosity, and the mat- ter dropped.

div.head: THREE MEN DROWNED.
div.p: THREE MEN DROWNED.
At Hull, on Tuesday, five men were engaged at the Alexandra dock, in bringing ashore in a boat the end of a dredger chain cable, when the boat capsized, and three were drowned.

div.head: FASTEST SAIL FROM AMERICA.
div.p: THE FASTEST SAIL FROM AMERICA.

On Tuesday morning the agents of the White Star Steamship Company at Queenstown received a telegram from the Fastnet, stating that their steamer Tsutonic from New York passed at 10.45 a.m., making the passage in 5 days 17 hours, which is the fastest voyage on record across the Atlantic. She left New York at 5-30 last Wednesday.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

Under the title of " English Writers," Professor henry Morley is issuing,volume-by volume, what is called, "An attempt towards a History of English Literature." We have previously had to speak in the highest terms of this exhaustive work, which is published by Messrs. Cassell and Co. The volume to hand, No. 7, covers the period from Caxton to Coverdale. Referring to the close of the 15th cen- tury, Professor Morley says :—" Meanwhile the people had their songs and stories by the fireside,on the green, and at the Whitsun ales. Descendants in this office of the scop and gleeman, using the rustic crowd or fiddle for a glee beam, preserved the memory of Chevy phase, and multiplied the tales of Robin Hood. Incidentally some account is given of" The Greeks in Italy ;" "Discovery of America and the literature of the Reformation, while chap- ters 5 and 9 are devoted to writers north of the Tweed. There is a description of Morality Plays, of More's Utopia, the writings of Erasmus, and the controversy between Luther and Henry Bth ; and of Tyndal's translation of the 'Scriptures. The last chapter is devoted to Coverdale's translation of the Bible, and to the work of Cranmer, Thomas Crom- well, Sir Thomas Wyatt, and Riginald Pole. The 'bibliography which is furnished with each volume is indicative of -enormous research by the author, while the index is, as usual, of the fullest kind. The next volume will carry the reader on from Surrey to Spenser. A secand edition has just been published of Slater 's Directory of Warrington, St. Helens, Widnes and Earles- town. It is much more complete than the first issue, each town now having a separate alphabetical, classified trades, and street directory. This, as is obvious, makes the work of reference an easy matter. Great pains have been taken to ensure accuracy, and the work is on the whole thoroughly reliable. Historical and other valu- able information is given in connection with each town, and there is a list of bankers of the United Kingdom, and of members of Parliament. The price of the work to non-subscribers is 10s. It should have a large sale amongst business men. "Education and Heredity" is a study in sociology by J. M. Guyau. The volume to hand is published by Mr. Walter Scott, of London, in his Contemporary Science Series; and it is a translation from the second edition by W. J. Greenstreet, M.A. There is an interesting intro- duction by Mr. G. F. Stout, M.A., which gives a brief sketch of the short life of Guyau, who was born in 1854, and died at the age of 33. He made his mark in France as philosopher and poet; and "Education and Heredity" furnishes ample testimony of his thought, skill, and learning. He is evidently familiar with all the great writers on education, and has distinct views of his own, which are well worth considering in these days of edu- cational activities. He believes in man being educated as asocial being, and insists on the development of the physique in youth with a view to the adult being strong morally, intellectually, and socially. In the "Canterbury Poets" we have for current issue "Scottish minor Poets," from the age of Ramsay to that of David Gray. The selection has been made and edited, with an introduction and notes, by Sir George Douglass, Bart. Although this is a volume of minor poets, the reader will find many old favourites, and many new poems which are delightful reading. Lady Nairne, for instance, is the writer of "The land of the leal," "Caller herrin'," and "The lass o' Gowrie." Amongst the selec- tions from David Gray is his epitaph, which is as follows . Below lies one whose name was traced in sand ; He died not knowing what it was to live, Died while the first sweet consciousness of manhood To maiden joy electrified his soul, Faint beating in the calix of the rose; Bewildered reader I pass without a sigh, In a proud sorrow ; there is life with God, In other kingdom of a sweeter air; In Eden every flower is blown.

Amen. The volume, which is published at is., includes a glossary and biographical notes of the various writers. Mr. Walter Scott has also issued, price 3d.," A popu- lar account ot Parliamentary procedure." It is a reprint of papers which appeared in the " Newcastle Daily Chronicle," and gives a satisfactory account of the way in which business is done in the House of Commons._

" Comsat's Column: A story of the 20th century," is an outcome, in a sense, of" Looking Backward," and is published in a style uniform with it by Messrs. F. Warne and Co., the author being Edmund Boisgilbert, M.D. (Ignatius Donnelly). Without distinctly controverting Bellamy's theories, it takes a view of the tendency of society at the present day which is wholly different from that portrayed in " Looking Backward," and de- picts a scene of horror which is imagined as resulting, when the millions of hard-ground poor at length turn upon and rend the luxurious rich of the next century. The story as a story is admirably told, the interest,apart from the doctrines propounded, being sustained from beginning to end. " The Tourist's Guide to the Continent." published under the authority of the Great Eastern Railway Co., is a capital sixpennyworth. It is edited by Mr. Percy Lindley, and is furnished with a useful map and numer- ous illustrations. ." Walks in the Ardennes'. is also edited by Mr. Percy Lindley, and is illustrated with a number of pen and ink sketches by J. F. Weedon. It gives in small compass a large amount of information suitable for persons who ; either walk, drive, cycle, or boat, besides supplying fish- jug and shooting notes. The price is 6d. The October number of the "Magazine of Art" com- mences a new volume, and contains an extra sheet, including title and contents of volume 14. The frontis- piece is a fine etching of Julien Dupre's charming picture of "The White Cow." An article on Daniel Murray, A.R.A., is adorned with striking illustrations of his works, and a portrait, and is from the pen of Mr. Walter Armstrong. There is a similar illustrated article on Charles Chaplin, by Mr. M. H. Dixon. Other illustrated articles are "The sculpture of the year ;" " Illustrated Journalism" and " Knole " (the seat of Lord Sackville) by T. G. Stephens. The current issue of " The Cabinet Portrait Gallery," is the first part of the new volume, and leads off with a most artistic and highly finished photograph of the Queen. Other cabinet portraits are of Mr. H. A. Jones, dramatist. and Professor Henry Morley. The portraits are in each case accompanied with a brief biographical sketch. Amongst miscellaneous illustrated papers in the October number of " Cassell's Magizine " may be mentioned "Among the Scillies ;" "When George the Second was King ;" "Uncle John's Prize Chrysan- themums," and "The brightening of three dreary Back Rooms." There are besides two serial stories and four complete stories. The" Quiver" has three serial stories running at the present time, namely, " For Erica's sake; " " On stronger wings ;" " The Oyster and Ow Oyster shell; " Amongst the principal contents may be named " Happy hours for poor children ; " " The two gardens; ""Rough Rides in China ; " " Quite a character ; " " Silvern speech and golden silence ; " ":Little Folks" has for a frontispiece a very pretty chromo with the title of "Dolly's Lecture." The con- wh tinned tales are "Four on an Island" and "To school and away." iTllhuesretraitsend which , lack of i osshotortssatoy rtiheas tatnhdesketelies a publica- tion is as bright as ever, and maintains its high level. The fine art edition of "Robinson Cruse" gains rather than loses as it proceeds in beauty and strength of its illustrations. Cassell S "Storehouse of General In- formation " has for frontispiece, in the current part, a coloured map of Europe. The work promises when com- plete to be a modern and valuable cyclopoedia. div.head: COLLINS GREEN.
div.p: COLLINS GREEN.
TERRIBLE COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT

t "TWO MEN KILLED. A shocking accident occurred at the Collins Green Colliery, near Earlestown, on Tuesday night, by which two men were killed. The colliery is owned by the Collins Green Colliery Company and for some weeks past a tunnel connecting the Potato Delph Mine and the four-foot seam of No. 2 pit has been under repair. On Tuesday afternoon, two men named Joseph Rigby and Richard Booth, descended the shaft in order to continue the work of timbering the roof of the roadway. They commenced opera- tions at a spot about 200 yards from the bottom of the shaft, after all the colliers had left work. About five o'clock the underground fireman, named James Taylor, was on his round of inspection, and found that a tremendous quantity of stones and dirt had fallen from the roof, crushing down the bars and props and entirely blocking up the road. He at once called out for the two men, but received no answer, and fear- ing that they were beneath the debris, he gave an alarm The fall had occurred exactly at the spot where the men were working, and Mr. A. Jackson, the certificated manager of the mine, was immediately summoned. Mr. Jackson at once descended the shaft, and on inspecting the scene of the disaster made arrangements for re- covering the bodies of the missing men. The news of the accident quickly spread, and there were plenty of willing volunteers. A gang of about twenty men was set to work to remove the stones and dirt, which were estimated to weigh over 150 tons. These men worked , eagerly from both ends of the debris, and tons upon tons of the rubbish were cleared away. In about a couple of hours the workers came upon a lamp of one of the wen, but the bodies of the men were not found until three hours later. The colliery officials from, the first entertained no doubt at all that the men had been killed. At the earliest possible moment they made the usual " knocking " signals, and called out to the men, but no answer was received. The unfortunate man Rigby was married, and resided at Mercer's Cottages, or what is known as Ashbury-terrace. Burtonwood, and the other man Booth, who was isot married, resided in the same neighbourhood. The fall of the roof is stated to be th most serious that ever occurred in the district. Both men were experienced in road making and "timbering," Rigby was also an occasional contractor for colliery road making. At night a large crowd of colliers and their riends gathered on the bank anxiously awaiting news of the discovery of the remains.

div.head: FURTHER DETAILS.
div.p: FURTHER DETAILS.

The shocking accident at Collins Green Colliery has occasioned a general feeling of sorrow throughout the neighbourhood. Falls of stones and dirt from the roofs of colliery workings are of frequent occurrence' but it is seldom that one of such dimensions •%s that at Collins Green is reported from a mine in full working order. The tunnel in which the accident occurred was originally made by Joseph Rigby, one of the men killed. As soon as the accident was discovered the colliery doctors, Drs. Gaskell and Jackson, of St. Helens, were informed by telephone, but as the colliery officials saw how hopeless was the prospect of saving life, and that several hours must elapse before the bodies of the two men could be reached, another message was sent intimating that their services would not be required. The clearing operations were conducted by a gang of willing workers under the orders of Mr. Andrew Jackson, the certificated manager, and Mr. C. G. Duncan, the mining engineer. After five hours incessant labour a leg of one of the men was found protruding from the mass of stones and dirt, , but so difficult was the work of removal that another hour elapsed before the crushed and mangled body could be carried to the bottom of the pit shaft. It proved to be that of Rigby, though, as one of the workers informed a press representative, his features were so cut and crushed that he personally did not recognise them. The body was found in a crouched position, lying on its side. Ten minutes later the body of Booth was discovered. Booth was found leaning over a tub or waggon, in which were placed the new props and bars for use by the men in repairing the roof. The stones and dirt had completely covered the waggon and the man, and the opinion was that death in the case of both Booth and Rigby was in- stantaneous. Both of Rigby's legs were badly smashed, and it was supposed that Booth's neck or back was broken. The bodies were taken up the pit shaft, and were removed to Mercer's Cottages, Burtonwood. Rigby was a married man, and leaves a widow and an adopted child. He was 41 years of age. Booth was a single man, 30 years of age, and lodged at the house of a col- lier named Dowd. They had been employed at the col- liery for some years, and were considered to be careful and steady men. Rigby was a kindly, cheerful fellow, and was a member of the Committee of the Collins Green and Burtonwood Village Club. piThe inquest will be held at the Pear Tree Inn, Collins , Green, on Saturday forenoon.

div.head: NARROW ESCAPE OF THE SCOTCH MAIL
div.p: NARROW ESCAPE OF THE SCOTCH MAIL

An exciting accident occurred early on Thursday morning at Penrith, by which the West Coast mail train had a terriktly narrow escape. The mail leaves Carlisle at midnight,andcovers 90 miles to Preston without stop - ping, passing through Penrith with two engines at a high speed, After the mail had been signalled clear to Plumpton, the signalman at Keswick Junction box noticed something wrong with a goods tram on the main down line, and immediately afterwards saw that four wagons were off the metals, and on the up line. He stopped the goods train,and telephoned to the station and as a result of his instructions a man ran along the up line with a red light. The mail driver saw the signal, and managed te pull up within a very short distance of the obstruction. But for the promptness of the signal- man, the catastrophe must have been fearful. Both lines were blocked for six hours, all trains being stopped as far away as Shap.

div.head: EMPEROR FRANCIS JOSEPH IN
div.p: THE EMPEROR FRANCIS JOSEPH IN
BOHEMIA.
SUPPOSED ATTEMPT TO WRECK THE IMPERIAL
TRAIN.

REICIIENBERG, TRURSDAY.—The Emperor Francis Joseph arrived here at nine o'clock this morning. His Majesty's journey from Prague to this place was a perfect triumphal procession, incessant cheers being rajsed by the dense crowds assembled along the route. The Em- peror specially directed the coachman to drive slowly, in order that he might be able to acknowledge the en- thusiastic popular acclamations. Last night, some time before the Imperial train passed over:a railway bridge near Rosenthal, two small bombs which had been placed against the abutments exploded, making two openings, a yard wide and about two feet in depth. The report of the explosion immediately brought the railway officials to the scene, and the damage was repaired without delay, so that the Imperial train was to-day able to pass over without hindrance. The authors of the outrage have not been discovered. The affair is regarded as a dastardly attempt to wreck the bridge and possibly destroy human life ; but in view of the fact the the ex- plosion preceded the arrival of the Emperor by some hours, it appears open to doubt whether a deliberate at- tempt on the life of the Emperor was intended.
