div.head: TEE SKIP CANAL.
div.p: TEE SKIP CANAL.

OPENING OF THE WEAVER SECTION. ELEVEN MILES OF WATERWAY. The Ship Canal was on Tuesday opened for traffic between Eastham and the Weaver estuary,a distance of 11 miles. Although the completion of a third, or all but a third,of the entire wateway is an event of conspicuous importance, it was celebrated only in a minor way. In a drenching rain the Directors of the Company and some of the chief officials left the Liverpool Landing stage in the little steamer Fanny at half-past ten, !entered the canal through the gates at Eastham, and a little more than an hour passed through the locks at Weston Marsh in- to the Weaver Canal. Afterwards the salt boats from Northwich and Winsford took the course of the Ship Canal to Liverpool and more distant ports. Some little demonstration was made by tug boats which were passed by the Fanny. Bunting was dis- played on their meagre yards, and their whistles sounded in unmusical triumph. At Ellesmere Port some huge cranes hid their black heads in colour, while at the Weston Marsh lock there was a roughly framed inscription oncanvas wishing success to the undertaking. In this simple way a big stage of pro- gress, accomplished after four years of heavy work was marked. A description was recently given in these columns of the two sections included in the 11 miles of completed waterway, so that it is not now necessary to enter into details. It may be said, however, that the canal makers have got through the most difficult part of their task. There are some heavy pieces of work, it is true, on the higher sections, but the digging of the trench itself is proving an easy matter in comparison with the struggle which has had to be maintained below the Weaver. The worst troubles have been met with in building banks which shall be firm and stable in places where the cutting runs through oozy, treacherous stretches of country. The work is not altogether perfect yet. At Booston Woods and Pool Hall, on the Eastham section, there have been slips of more or less extent, and it is now thought advis- able to make some alterations in the bank. Some additional land is to be bought, and in the coming months the slopes will be flattened. This will not interfere in the very least degree with the present navigation of the canal, but in view of the passage of boats of larger burden it is a necessary work. With a connection now complete between the Weaver and the Ship Canal, there will in a few days be a great concentration of effort on the Runcorn section, extending from above Runcorn to the Weaver. The engineers have up to the present been prohibited by Act of Parliament from entering on this work. Ingress and egress to the Mersey had to be preserved until the boats on the Weaver Canal were able to pass down the Ship Canal. Now that such passage is secure the Ship Canal Company may carry forward their work. The present entrance will be closed to the Weaver boats and become part of the line of the Ship Canal. Eventually, however, the way will be re-opened. The Ship Canal Company will build another lock, and the salt boats, after crossing the canal, may be lowered into the Mersey to sail by the flood tide to Liverpool. As an alter- native they may of course,by paying toll, make the journey by way ot the Ship Canal. PASSENGER TRAFFIC. It may be of interest to state that ,within a few days not merely will the salt boats pass down the Ship Canal, but that arrangements have also been made for a passenger traffic. A company has been formed called the Ship Canal Passenger Steamer Syndicate Company. One boat, called the St. Mawes, is already on the waterway. Another named the Falmouth Castle, is on its way from Falmouth. When it reaches the canal a daily service between Northwich and Liverpool will be established. Such a service ought to be popular, for the passengers will be carried through a very pretty stretch of country. At the Manchester end of the waterway the work is so far advanced that it would be possible to com- plete it in little more than six months. The most backward parts of the undertaking are to be found between Warrington and the Weaver; but in a general way it may be said that, should no unex- pected obstacles offer themselves, it may be pretty confidently anticipated that the entire thirty-five miles of canal will be completed by the end of next year.

FLOWER SERVICE AT TFIELWALL. A special flower service was held at the Thelwall Ship Canal Mission Hall on Sunday. The preacher was the Hon. and Rev. R. Grimston. There was also a service of song in the afternoon, entitled " Primrose Garth." The Hon. and Rev. R. Grimston was again the preacher at the evening service, at which special hymns were given by the band and choir. A solo was sung by Miss Silver- ton, entitled "Le Angelus." ACCIDENT AT ACTON GRANGE. Mr. Duncan, the head foreman of the men working on the Acton Grange viaduct, now in course of construe- tion, had his head hurt on Tuesday morning by a plank ' falling upon it. He was conveyed to the Ship Canal Hospital at Latchford, where the wound was dressed by the house surgeon.

div.head: DARESBI7RY ADJOURNED BREWSTER
div.p: DARESBI7RY ADJOURNED BREWSTER
SFSSIONS.

The adjourned Brewster Sessions for the Dares- bury Petty Sessional division were held at the Court Rouse, Dare3bury, on Tuesday. The magistrates present were Messrs. J. C. Parr (chairman), and H. Neild.
TRANSFER AND RENEWAL OF LICENSES.

James Jacobson applied for the transfer of the license of the Bridge Inn, Little Legh, to himself from Thomas Bowers, and also for the renewal of the old license till the 10th of October. The application was acceded to.— Wimp Beswick applied for a renewal of the license of the Ship Inn, Walton Superior, and his application was acceded to.—William Whitlow made application far a seven days' full license for the Red Lion Inn, Preston Brook, or the renewal of the present six days' full license, in case the alternative application were not ac- ceded to. He stated that the seven days' license was very much needed. The population was 500, and there was a travelling population equal to 500 per week through the township; and great hardship was suffered by many travellers, especially people from the country, in consequence of their not being able to get refresh- ments. The trade on the canal was principally worked by the tide at the end of the week, and those coming down could not get refreshment. The men came at five minutes past ten on Saturday night and could get no refreshment till six o'clock on Monday morning. Dr. Carruthers complained of the trouble he had to get stimulants for his patients when necessary. It was his (the applicant's) intention not to open the house for drinking generally, but only to supply travellers. He could make up 20 beds and had stabling for 20 horses.—Superintendent Large said he was in- structed by the Chief Constable to oppose the application on the ground that the license was not required.--The Chairman asked Mr. Whitlow why he had previously given up a 7 days' license.—He replied that it was because his children were at school, and he found it very trouble- some and tiring to be confined so muchm the house; and female servants did not like to be kept in on Sundays. Now his children were maturetand able to take an active part in the business.- -Superintendent Large said the license would cause a great nuisance through excursion- ists being drawn to the house.—Mr. Taylor, stationmaster at Preston Brook, said he had frequently heard complaints from passengers coming from the:train on Sundays and especially from people coming from the neighbourhood of Runcorn. It was about a mile to the next fully licensed house.—By Supt. Large The passengers on Sun- days were not mostly excursionists.—Jonathan Austin, of -Runcorn, said he had been in the habit occasionally of turning out with a lot of men and horses on Sunday wken there had been frost and ice on the canal. He had had to go and meet his boats oa different occa- sions, and had to put up at Preston Brook, He could get no refreshment there for his men, and they had to walk home without ft.—Police Sergeant Costello,was called by Superintendent Large. He said he had measured the distance from Mr. Whitlow's house to the Ring-o'-Bells at Daresbury and to the Talbot Arms. It. was 1,565 yards from the former and 1,590yd5. from the latter and LW to the next nearest licensed house. From 20 to 30 bkes and busses came with excutsionists on Sundays' to Preston, and he had much trouble with them. If Mr. Whitlow were granted a license no doubt they would pull up there, and it would be a great nuisance.—Mr. Whit- low : I don't intend to open for them.—Sergeant Costello: There have been as many as 50 and 60 on a Saturday night. —Mr. Whitlow: That is not Sunday.—The magis- trates,after a few minutes' private consideration,,,,aranted the seven days' license ; and on Mr. Whitlow's applica- tion they renewed the old six days' license till the 10th . of October.
•At Wolverhampton, on Tuesday, Thomas Arthur, manager of the Brewery Arms, was fined £2O for allow- ing betting in the house. The landlord, Thomas Harvey, was fined £5.

A disastrous fire occurred on Tuesday night, near Wareham, at the residence of Mr. Featherstonhaugh, Frampton, master of the South Dorset Foxhounds, and seven valuable hunters, which were in the stables, were burnt to death. .

div.head: LIBERAL FEDERATION.
div.p: LIBERAL FEDERATION.
THE CONFERENCE. The 14th annual conference of the National Liberal Federation was commenced on Thursday afternoon in

the Town Hall, at Newcastle-on-Tyne. There was an unusually large number of gentlemen present, about 2,000 delegates having been appointed to attend. Dr. R. Spence Watson,president of the Federation,occupied the

chair, and amongst those who accompanied him upon the platform were the Marquis of Ripon, Lord Brassey, Mr. John Morley, M.P., Sir Wilfred Lawson, M.P., Mr. H. H. Fowler, M.P., Sir C. M. Palmer, M.P., Mr. Henry road hu t , M.P., Sir Horace Davey, Q.C., M.P., Mr. James Craig, M.P., Mr. Sydney Buxton, M.P., Mr. Schnadhorst, secretary of the Federation, Mr. R. A. Hudson, assistant secretary, and many other well-known

gentlemen. Several female delegates attended. The Chairman, in openinc, the proceedings said they all rejoiced that their great leader, Mr. Gladstone, was able to be once more among them. (Cheers.) On many matters they had made progress since the last meeting. They were delighted that free education in a sense had become a fact, but they would agree with the Federation in pointing out that no measure of free education which was not accompanied by popular control could ever be satisfactory. (Cheers.' They would also rejoice that Welsh disestablislament had made decided headway. The fact of the second reading of the Welsh Liquor Bill was one which also gave them gratification. The whole question of dealing with the liquor traffic was a most important one, with which they would have to deal. (Cheers.) In conclusion, he moved the adoption of the report of the council, which has already been published. The Rev. Canon Balstrode (Ipswich), who seconded the resolution, said he felt that its adoption by the meeting meant a great historical event and a great move forward in Liberal progress. This annual meeting derived deep importance from the fact that we were nearing a general election, in allusion to Irish affairs, he expressed the opinion that the Irish party was better organised at the present time and better fit to take its place in Liberal councils, and to represent Ireland, than it was before Mr. Parnell's fall. Ile spoke in favour of the establishment of periodical councils, and said he should like to see the parson, the tithe, and the Church, all thrown into the melting pot. (Cheers.) Mr. John Morley, in supporting, had a reception which must have lost nothing by comparison with the many enthusiastic greetings which he has received in New- castle. Going back to the Sheffield meeting, and the shadow of the Parnell case which lay over it, Mr. Morley used a simile which recalled the sceaes at several previous conference gatherings when his aptly worked phrases have made a sensational impression. No group of leaders had ever, he contended, been in a more embarras- sing position than they were then, "but," he added, in tones of exultation, "we hadon board our ship a captain whose heart never quailed. He was not a man to take in a hurry to the lifeboats." Round after round of cheering swept over the meeting at this fresh view of the exhaust- less subject of Liberal admiration—Mr. Gladstone. A word about Ireland, and then Mr. Morley delighted an audience evidently strong in temperance forces by a bold discussion of the relation of political parties to tem- perance reform. He introduced Mr. T. W. Russell amid a good deal of derisive laughter, which became more general when it was seen that his use of the Ulsterman was to prove by an enemy's voice that the question of temperance reform had been surrendered into the hands of the Gladstonians. The dominant thought of Mr. Morley's speech was tnat the principle of privilege under- lay almost all the subjects on the Federation programme. There was the question of the House of Lords, and the speaker brought out a sympathetic cheer by echoing the prophetic wail " how long ?" Turning to rural affairs, the speaker insisted that the franchise had been given to the rural population because it involved a question of privliege, and for no such mean motive as the catching of votes. Then Mr. Morley approached the question of religion and his voice took a deeper pathos, as it always does when he touches on these great problems addressed to the human mind and heart ; and he demanded absolute equality, without the State smil-

ing upon one set of opinions. Rural questions were again relerred to in passing, and served to bring in Mr. Bright's true saying that a nation lives in its cottages. An earn- est speech, delivered with great animation and force, came to an end with a fervid tribute to Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Morley had supported the report of the Committee, and when he resumed his seat, the President at once put the motion that the report be accepted. Lord Brassey moved " that Dr. Robert Spence Watson be re-elected president; that all members of Parliament willing to serve, and the presidents of all federated asso- ciations, be elected vice-presidents; and that Mr. Alder- man W. H. Hart be re-appointed treasurer for the ensu- ing year." He warmly eulogised the services of Dr. Spence Watson to the Liberal cause and to the Federa- tion. (Cheers.) Mr. Henry Broadhurst, M.P., seconded the resolution, and it was carried with acclamation.

Sir Edward Grey, M.P., moved the following resolu- tion—" That this Council holds that the case for Home Rule in Ireland has been still further confirmed by the steadfastness, sound judgment, and moderation with which the great body of the Irish people havt,during the past year, successfully faced one of the sharpest ordeals in political history,and it looks with unshaken confidence to Mr. Gladstone upon his teturn to power to frame and —in spite of idle menaces from the House of Lords—to pass the measure which shall fully satisfy the just de- mands of Ireland, andleave the Imperial Parliament free to attend to the pressing claims of Great Britain for its own reforms." In supporting the resolution, he said the House of Lords was like a rusty old musket hanging over the Tory chimneyßiece, an old musket of which they might use the butt end as much as they pleased, but from which they never dare fire a full charge. (Laughter and cheers). Mr. Joshua Rowntree, M.P., seconded, and the resolu- tion was adopted. Mr. T. Ellis, M.P., moved the following resolution : " That this council reaffirms its belief that the time has come for the disestablishment and disendowment of the Church of England in Wales, and for the application of the tithes to the public purposes of the Principality, and declares that the question should be dealt with in the next Parliament as soon as Irish Home Rule is attained." Tried by every democratic test, the establishment in Wales was as indefensible as Dublin Castle in Ireland. The Free Churches in Wales had given the people of the Principality spiritual life, popular calture, faithfulness in principle, and progressive action. (Cheers.) Major Evans Jones (Cardiff), in seconding the resolu- tion, described the Established Church in Wales as stifl- ing the language, crushing the spirit, and breaking the heart of the Cymric race. The resolution was then put to the meeting and unanimously adopted. Professor Bryce, M.P., then moved—" That this council declares that the interests of good government urgently demand that the London County Council should without delay be put in possession of full municipal powers including the control of its own gas and water supplies, markets, and police; and should by taxation of ground values and by other financial reforms be enabled to govern and improve the metropolis without undue pressure upon the occupying ratepayers; and that such powers should be enjoyed by all other 7 municipalities." Professor Stuart, M.P., in seconding the refiAliorf, said that the people of London were 50 years behind the rest of the world, and asked urgently for an early com- pletion of their municipal organisation. The resolution was adopted nem. comm. Mr. Sydney Buxton, M.P., moved the following resolu- tion :—"fhat this council expresses satisfaction that the principle of free education, which for five years has been a prominent feature in the resolutions of the Federation, has been embodied in legislation, but regards the Act now in operation as partial and defective, since it fails to recognise the right of public control, and does not secure that the increased grant shall be devoted to greater edu- cational efficiency, and by omitting, at the instance of the House of Lords, the prevision that free accommoda- tion shall be suitable as well as sufficient, disregards the conscientious convictions of many parents. The council again declared that no system of public elementary edu- cation can be regarded as satisfactory or final unless it secures that every family shall haVe within reasonable reach a free school, and that aff schools supported by public money shall be subject to public representative control."—Liberals objected to parsons having a vested interest in the schools, and would insist upon popular re- presentative control. (Cheers.) Mr. C. Fenwick, M.P., in seconding the resolution, expressed his regret that the Education Act made no pro- vision for evening or continuation schools. The resolution was passed, and the conference then ad- ourned until to-day (Friday). ff

A despatch from San Francisco gives particulars of the ghastly discovery of the murder of thirty-four Chinese miners on Snake River, Oregon, in 1887, by " renegades " and cattle thieves. The corpse S were found flOating down the river at th 3 time, but nothing could be ascertained regarding the perpetrators. Alarming intelligence is to hand from the interior of' Russia. Owing to the failure of the harvest,theieasants, are selling their horses and cattle for a were, trifle in, order to obtain food, while in stunk case sf mothers of families are. selling themselves to support their children. div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

General Boulanger has gone the way of that -loather foiled conspirator Bahnaceda—he has shot himself. Out, out, brief candle! Life's but a walking shadow, a poor player That struts and frets his hour upon the stage, And then is heard no more.

As many as five bishops were consecrated at St. - Paul's Cathedral on Tuesday. What would it cost? There has been a good deal said of late of the fees—amounting to hundreds of pounds— which attend the making of a bishop. But when bishops are made at a wholesale rate, should it not be done at wholesale price?

Virtue is again rewarded. The "London Gazette" announces that the Queen has granted the dignity of a baronet of the United Kingdom unto the right Hon. Peter O'Brien, Lord Chief Justice of Ireland. There was a time when Sir Peter, from his little ways with juries, was known in Ireland as Peter the Packer.

The week has been what is known as "self-denial week" in the ranks of the Salvation Army. Last year as much as £33,200 was raised for the Army in this way, £30,000 coming from the poor, and the odd £3,000 from the well-to-do. This is greatly to the credit of the poor; relatively speaking, the less they have the more they give.

On Tuesday another section of the Ship Canal was opened for traffic—that between the Weaver and Ellesmere Port. With eleven miles of water- way open, we have heard the last of that silly cry —" The canal will never be made." Before long there will be passenger steamers on the canal; and we may yet hear somebody shout—" This way for 'Timbuctoo."

The Scottish Home Rule Association have re- ceived an important letter from Mr. Gladstone. In effect, he says that the Scotch are equally entitled with the Irish to say whether they prefer Home Rule. He has said as much with regard to the Welsh movement. It comes to this, that the way is now open for advocating Home Rule all round. It is a matter for the people themselves in each country ;' anl, as we have often urged, it is the best way out of existing difficulties.

The Licensing Justices of St. Helens, at the adjourned sessions on Monday, took the trouble to deal with several cases separately, and warn various licence-holders. One licence was refused on the ground of character, Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. being owners of the house affected. The Bench are to be complimented on the thorough way in which they have done their work. It contrasts favourably with the attitude d the Warrington magistrates, who two years ago prepared a report and failed either to act on it or even make it public.

Mrs. Dobson, lecturing on dressmaking, at the Warrington Technical Institute, on Monday even- ing, mentioned that dress stuffs which came from the mills of Yorkshire and Sornersetshire at is. 6d. per yard were exported to France, Germany, and Switzerland, and afterwards came back to this country as embroidered goods, and sold at three to four guineas. That's how the money goes, for the ladies do like "the latest from abroad." There is a story told of the wife of an English M.P. who was in the silk trade. She fell in love in Paris with a French silk,and besought her husband to purchase a dress-piece. His answer was—" All right, my .dear, you shall have it when we get home. That French silk 'is made at our mills in England."

Warrington and Widnes have been favoured by 'speeches from Mr. T. D. Sullivan M.P., journa- list, orator, and poet. He was born in Bantry, Cork, in May 1827; and has written songs which have attained a world-wide fame. To mention two, he is the author of" God Save Ireland" and 4‘ The Woaring of the Green." The last-named is .said to have brought tears into the eyes of the Queen when she first heard it sung. The following are four lines from the first verse :
I met with Napper Tandy, and he took me by the
hand, And he said," How's poor old Ireland, how does she
stand?" She's the most distressful country that ever yet was
seen; They are hanging men and women for the wearing of the green.

Mr. Slater Lewis has been presented with an address signed by electors from all parts of the Frodsham Division of the Cheshire County Coun- cil. It expresses the highest appreciation of his services; and presses him to present himself as a candidate at the election in March next. Mr. Lewis will give his final answer at a meeting of his constituents which he will address at Frod- sham at an early date. Meantime, he has a fling at the Tories who are about to oppose him on poli- tical lines. If he should again seek the suffrages of the electors—as it is to be hoped he will—he. may count on being returned by a large majority, for he has made an excellent member of the County Council.

Is the Primrose League getting played out? It was supposed that only the Liberals, who have nothing better than the people behind them, found it difficult to raise funds for political purposes ; but here is the official organ of the Primrose League complaining that as many as 611 habitations have not contributed as much as sixpence to the Grand Council. In Warrington, when the party hat was last sent round, Conservatives who were showing themselves too conservative with their money-bags had it made plain to them that something might be done for the party in their last wills and testaments. Perhaps the 611 Habitations mean to die before they yield anything to the Grand Council.

The Liberals want money of course, and especi- ally in Warrington, but they prefer to obtain it from live Liberals rather than "dead uns." It is with that object in view that the three days' Bazaar will be opened by the Countess of Carlisle on Tuesday next. The party have "meant busi- ness " in this matter from the beginning,; the ladies have taken to the task with a will, and it is now absolutely certain that all the stalls will be well laden with useful and ornamental articles. But to ensure success there must be buyers—buyers in abundance.

The humblest can do something in the way of making a purchase—if only a toy or a doll for the little folks at home. Let every Liberal make it a matter of duty to attend as a buyer, in the sssured conviction that, while getting "good value for the money," every shilling expended will be a help to the Liberal cause. Apart from this, the Bazaar will be a sight worth seeing. It is to take the form of an Ice Carnival (which will be a nice carnival) each stall representing a particular country. The scene will be as brilliant as it will be unique, especially after dark when it will be illu- minated by the electric light. And then the music, and the round of entertainments ! It will be simply "glorious O'er the ills of life victorious."
Moral : "Britons be brothers and true to your trust ;" Attend in your thousands, and down with the dust."

Mr. Cotton, an English gentleman, who received in- juries in the Spanish railway accident, died on Wednes- pay morning from pvmmia and exhanstion. The third biennial session of the International Statisti- cal Congress was opened at Vienna on Monday by Sir Rawson Rawson, president of the Statistical Institute.

div.head: CHRIST CHURCH JUBILEE.
div.p: CHRIST CHURCH JUBILEE.

The jubilee of Christ Church, Weston Point, was cele- brated on Sunday, when services were held as follows : Holy Communion. 8 a.m. ; matins, 10 30 a.m. ; and evensong, 6 30. Preacher, Canon Maitland Wood, M.A. On Moaday night the jubilee and harvest services were continued, when a sermon was preached by the Rev. C. M. Woosman. On Wednesday evening the dedication festival will be held, when the Lord Bishop of Chester is announced to preach.
PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, WIDNES.

The harvest thanksgiving services in connection with Princes-street Chapel took place on Sunday, when the Rev. W. rhornley, of Warrington, preached to crowded congregations. In the afternoon a children's service was held and Mr. Samuel Owens delivered an address. On Monday evening, the customary fruit banquet was held and addresses were delivered by several members of the congregation. The interior of the building had been tastefully decorated for the occasion. BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, RUNCORN.

The annual harvest thanksgiving services were held on Sunday in the schoolroom, in consequence of the chapel having recently being partly destroyed by fire. The room was beautifully decorated with fruit, flowers, and cereals. The Rev. John Simpson, the pastor, preached morning and evening. At the evening service, the choir rendered several anthems in good style, being assisted by several stringed instruments. Mr. A. G. Calvert, of York,was at the organ. There was a crowded congregation at the evening service.
SCALDED TO DEATH AT WIDNES.

Mr. S. Brighouse, the county coroner, on Monday, held an inquest at Widnes touching the death of a young boy named Stacher Govlin, whose parents are Austrian Poles residing in Hope-st. It appeared that on the 18th September the mother was boiling same clothes in a bucket, when the boy poked the fire with a stick and knocked the bucket over. He was terribly scalded about the stomach, and died on Saturday from shock to the system. Dr. Hutchinson had been in attendance. A verdict of accidental death was returned. TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION AT FARNWORTH.

On Saturday afternoon a demonstration took place at Farnworth in connection with the local branch of the Church of England Temperance Society. A procession of the members' which was headed by a brass band, marchaTthrough the village to the church, where a special service was held, and a powerful sermon delivered by the Rev. J. T. Madden,vicar of St. Luke's, Liverpool. In the evening a tea and miscellanous entertainment were held in the schoolroom. The chair was occupied by the Rev. J. R. Jones, 8.A., curate-in-charge. LIQUOR LICENSE FOR A WIDNES FOOTBALL GROUND. James Briggs, landlord of the Queen's Arms, Widnes, on Monday applied to the Widnes magistrates for per- mission to sell intoxicating drink on it. Mary's football field to-day (Saturday), from the hours of 3 to 6 p.m.— Superintendent Noblett had no objection to raise, and the Bench said there was only one difficulty—the appli- cant had already a refreshment tent on the Widnes foot- ball ground and it was questionable whether he could look after both places. Mr. Briggs said he had plenty of competent assistants, and he would take care that everything was properly conducted. The license was then granted. The magistrates on the Bench were Messrs. H. Gaskell, junior, and 4. Birchall. LAWN MOWERS.—Garland, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington. and at Earlestown.—Advt. ST. AIIIBROSE CHURCH HARVEST FESTIVAL, WIDNES. The annual harvest thanksgiving services in connec- tion with St. Ambrose Church, Halton View, were commenced last evening week, when the Rev. Dr. Harrison vicar of St. Mary's, Wavertree, preached an impressive and appropriate sermon to a large congrega- tion. The anthem "The Lord is loving unto all men " was admirably rendered by the choir. The services were continued on Sunday. In the morning the Rev. W. S. Jones, curate of St. Mary's Parish Church, Widnes, occu- pied the pulpit, ani in the evening the Rev. John Stowell, M.A., of Liverpool, was the preacher. The sacred edifice was crowded to excess. In the afternoon a children's service took place, and the Vicar, the Rcv. G. A. Le Bert delivered an interesting address. The church was beautifully decorated with cereals, fruit,and flowers. The collections at the four serves 'realised £l5.

div.head: ROUGH VIOLENT FELLOW AT WIDNES.
div.p: A ROUGH VIOLENT FELLOW AT WIDNES.

Edward Haynes, of Charlotte-st., was brought up at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, to answer a charge of being drunk and disorderly, and assaulting P.C. Mc- Ginnis and also with assaulting a labourer named Edwin Clay. On Saturday night Clay was in the Market Hotql. when the prisoner entered and without provocation struck him on the face. He complained to Inspector Keighley, who turned the prisoner out of the hotel, and afterwards on the Market ground, the prisoner again assaulted him. P.C. McGinnis saw the second assault, and apprehended the prisoner who kicked him severely on the knee. The prisoner had been previously cui- victed of assaults,and the magistrates said he was a rough violent fellow. He was fined 10s. and costs for drunken- ness; 20s. and costs for the assault on the policeman, and 10s. and costs for the assault on Clay ; or in default of payment 42 days' hard labour.

div.head: WIDNES STABBING OUTRAGE.
div.p: THE WIDNES STABBING OUTRAGE.

At Widnes Police Court on Monday, Patrick Devereaux of Victoria-st., was again brought up on a charge of wounding Jacquetta Mayne, refreshment housekeeper, Ann-st. West. On the 19th September about 10 o'clock, the prisoner and a companion entered the refreshment rooms and were served with potatoe pie. As they used most insulting language Mrs. Mayne ordered them out, when the prisoner demanded his money back and Mrs. Mayne refused. "Knife her," the prisoner shouted to his companion, and then struck her on the face,causing a punctured wound half an inch below the left eve. Nothing was seen in the prisoner's hands, but Dr. O'Keeffe said the wound could not have been caused by a fall,or a blow from a fist.—Patrick McDermott, Margaret-st., said Mrs. Mayne cut her eye by falling against the door, after the prisoner had pushed her.—The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial, bail being allowed. div.head: run E EXAMINER, SAT URDA Y , OCTOBER 3, 1891.
div.p: run E EXAMINER, SAT URDA Y , OCTOBER 3, 1891.

THEFT FROM A TILL AT RUNCORN. Reuben Mitchell, of no settled residence, was brought up at Runcorn Police Court,on Thursday, charged with stealing is. 2d. from the till of the Bridgewater Arms, Percival-lane, kept by Thos. H. Barton. The prisoner, who had been caught in the act,was remanded until Mon- day. FIRE ON THE RAILWAY NEAR WIDNES.

_ On Monday night a pile of timber weighing several tons became ignited on the London and North-Western Railway betweeu Appleton and Farnworth, it is supposed by a spark from a passing train, but the flames were sabdued before any clamaire was done to an adjoining bridge.
SWIMMING GALA AT WIDNES.

A swimming gala arranged by the notorious Tommy Burns, "The hero of Runcorn Bridge," took place at the Widnes Baths, on Tuesday evening, and was fairly well attended. At the commencement 'a series of swimming contests took place. A match two lengths of the bath for boys under 17 resulted as follows : 1, W. B. More wood, 2, F. Dixon, 3, H. Dixon. A two lengths trades- men's handicap was won by R. Burrows; 2nd, D. O'Keeffe, 3rd, F. Dixon. Afterwards Burns performed a variety of startling feats under the water, not the least being the singing of a song with his head hidden in a bucket. He also showed the best means of saving a drowning man. Professor Burnley assisted.

The 11,y for the working people was coming in England and in other lands too, and throughout the civilised world, the workers, who up te now had not had their rights, would assert their power and get redress. (Applause.) In conclusion, Mr. Sullivan advocated the claim of Mr. Deacon at the next election, and said that any Irishman that did not vote for him would act as though he had plunged a dagger into the heart of his country. (Applause) The motion was carried unanimously.—Votes of thanks were accorded. Subsequently a knife and fork supper was held in the League rooms, and various toasts were proposed and honoured, and responded to.
RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Thursday. Mr. S. Taylor. presided and there were present Messrs. E. W. Humphreys, D. Bisbrown, W. Hankinson, H, Coward, J. W. Lightburn, F. Wis- wall, %V. Fisher, H. White, W. R. Wass, P. Smith, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), M. Barker (surveyor.)
HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The Medical Officer (Dr. McDougall) reported that the number of deaths registered during the past month amount to 37, of which five were due to diarrhea, six to mesenteric disease, three to fever, seven to convulsions, two to cancer, three to heart disease, and one each to inflammation of lungs, phthisis, bronchitis, puerperal fever, peritonitis, croup, erysipelas, hydrocephelas, abcess. aneurism, and natural decay. The 37 deaths showed an average dsath-rate of 22.2 for the 12 months.

div.head: STACK FIRE AT NORTON
div.p: STACK FIRE AT NORTON

_ On Tuesday morning two stacks of hay belonging to Mrs. Haslarn, of Warlord Farm, Norton, were destroyed by fire. The Runcorn Fire Brigade prevented the flames spreading to other stacks. The damage is estimated at £l5O and is covered by insurance in the Alliance Insur- ance Company. • FIRST AID TO THE INJURED.

A Ship Canal navvy fell down in High-st., on Tuesday and broke his leg just above the ankle, and P.C. Crow- der, one of the ambulance corps, coming upon the scene, bandaged tho injured limb, and then had him conveyed to Dr. McDougall's surgery, where the bone was set. The man is progressing favourably.
A FORGIVING WIFE AT RUNCORN,

_ Yesterday at Runcorn Police Court James Collister, of Bentinck-st., was brought up under a warrant charged with assaulting his wife on the 17th September. On that day the prisoner returned home drunk after an absence of 12 weeks, and violently assaulted his wife. The woman did not now wish to proceed with the case, and the prisoner was discharged.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday, Mr. F. H. Parkhurst presiding. Accounts amounting to £34 16s. Bd. were passed for payment. The number of attendances at the reading room during the month was 12,577, an increase of 360. The number of books issued was 4,120, an increase of 23 in the lending department, and 139 in the reference depart- ment. £1 14s. 80. hdd been paid in fines. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W.Purros, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. FARMERS AND LIGHT WEIGHTS AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, A. J. Johnson, farmer, Bold, was summoned for having in his posses- sion a 561 b. weight 2oz. light,a 281 b. loz. 10drachms light, a 281 b. 17drachms light and two 141 b. weights 26 and 8 drachms light respectively.—Mr. Knowles, who defended, said the weights were placed amongst old iron and not intended for use. A fine of 10s. and costf was imposed.— James Warburton, farmer, Bold, was convicted of hav- ing ten weights which were all light, and he was fined 20s. and costs.—A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed upon Catherine Stead, Bold, who had also a number of light weights.
ALLEGED FRAUDS AT WIDNES.

James Holden, Widnes-road, and James Conroy, pitton, were brought, up on remand at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Monday, charged with obtaining by false pretences Bs. 6d. from Ellen Ward, Moor-lane, and a similar amount irom Mrs. Griffiths, Moor-lane. The circumstances of the alleged fraud have been reported, and the prisoners were committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. In a letter we have received from them they deny the statement reported in our columns last weer, to the effect that they had promised a dinner service would be given with pound packets of 3s. tea, and allege that the statement is "false from beginning to end." LENIENT SENTENCI4 ON A RUNCORN RUFFIAN.

Lewis Jones, a ship canal labourer,was brought before Major Hazlehurst and Mr. James Handley at Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, on a charge of assaulting Ann Baker, wife of Alfred Baker, keeper of the Rose and Shamrock Inn. On the previous evening, about seven o'clock, the prisoner engaged two beds at the Inn, and paid one shilling. He then complained that the price was too high, and Mrs. Baker returned him his money and told him he could go elsewhere. Immediately he picked up a tumbler and threw it at her, the missile striking her between the eyes and smashing in pieces. Her face was badly cut. The prisoner was fined 255. in- cluding costs, or 14 days hard labour.

div.head: WIDNES PERFECT BUILDING SOCIETY.
div.p: WIDNES PERFECT BUILDING SOCIETY.

In connection with this Society a public meeting was held on Tuesday night in the Conservative Club Assembly Room, the Rev. R. G. Hughes presiding. The proceed- ings opened with a musical contest. A prize of ss. for the best rendering of a pianoforte solo was won by Master Alfred Barber, of Lacey-st., and the second prize by Miss Lily Burgess, Oakland-st. For the best cornet solo the first prize of 7s. 6d. was awarded to Mr. John Brady, Oakland-st. Mr. Horsley then delivered a lecture on "How to live rent free." In conclusion a ballot was taken resulting in Mr. J. Lewis, of Luton-st., being en- titled to £lOO free of interest for 16i years. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.-3. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington .—Advt.
LECTURE BY CAPTAIN LE COUTEUR AT RUNCORN.

At the weekly meeting of Brunswick Mutual Improve- ment Society on Wednesday evening, Captain Le Couteur delivered a lecture entitled " Reminiscences of life in the Tropics." The lecturer gave a graphic description of his voyages in tropical regions and the wonderful climatic changes there to be witnessed. The heaviest rainfall here was but a gentle shower in comparison with a tropical downpour, and our thunder was but a faint echo of the thunder of that clime, while the vividness and power of the lightning was indescribable. The treacher- ous white squalls were referred to. The tropics were the breeding place of the Cyclones, which finally exhausted their power by causing devastation and ruin on British shores. The lecturer also described the vegetation and animal life of tropical lands. At the close a hearty vote of thanks was accorded Captain Le Couteur for his interesting and instructive lecture.—Mr. T. Simister presided.
PROPERTY SALE AT RUNCORN.

On Monday morning at Wilson's Hotel, Runcorn. Mr. Samuel Yarwood, auctioneer, offered for sale four lots of valuable freehold and leasehold property. Lot 1, two freehold dwelling-houses, Nos. 77, and 79, Greenway-rd. were withdrawn at £6oo,but they were afterwards again put up, when the bidding rose to £620. The reserve, however, Lad not been reached and the lot was with- drawn. Lot 2, two freehold dwelling-houses, 56, Green- way-road, and 52, Albert-street, caused considerable competition, and Mr. J. H. Spender, eventually became the possessor at 11570. For Lot 3, two leasehold dwell- ing-houses 21, and 23, Lowlands-road, and three cottages Nes. 3,5, and 7, Surrey-street (ground rent £4 19s. 7d.), the bidding was very spirited commencing at £4OO and ending at £BO5, when the lot was knocked down to Mr. NV. Gittens. Lot 4, four leasehold cottages, 12, 14, 16, land 18, Loch-street, (ground rent £2125.) was purchased by Mr. James Douglas for £205. Mr. Fred A. Lake was the solicitor in the matter. WIDNES REVISION COURT. Mr. J. T. Foard, revising barrister, on Monday com- menced the revision of the voters' lists for the Parlia- mentary Division of Widnes. Mr. H. B. Shores appeared for the Liberals and Mr.Woodnorth for the Conservatives. The first court was opened at Garston, and was continued until Tuesday morning. On Tuesday the court was opened at Widnes Town Hall, and was continued on Wednesday and Thursday. There were no points of interest raised in regard to registration law, but the barrister had a great number of claims and objections to dispose of. The Conservatives had made wholesale objections, and their agent had to pay no less a sum than £3 to voters who had been objected to but appeared and substantiated their claim to the franchise. The Liberal agent escaped without the payment of a farthing of eosts.—Claims were made by Messrs. E. Carey, E. K. Muspratt, E. F. Gossage, H. S. Timrnis, H. W. Deacon, F. Gaskell, in regard to property owned in the town, snd the barrister plaeed the whole of these gentlemen on the list. —Mr. J. P. Coupe, tailor, ,Vic- toria-road, who resides in Southport, was granted a parliamentary vote for the occupation ot business premises. Mr. Guy, manager for Scales and Sons' boot shop, Victoria-road, claimed a parliament ry vote for Mr. Jonathan Webster and Mr. Scales, partners, in regard to the shop.—Mr. Woodnorth opposed on the ground that they lived at Leeds outside the seven miles radius, but Mr. Shores quoted Acts to show that they were entitled, and the votes were allowed. DRONE OR EXCITED AT WIDNES.

Pritchard Whelan, of Widnes-road, was brought before the Widnes magistrates on Thursday to answer to a charge of having been drank and disorderly in Alfrode- st. on Sunday night at twenty minutes past ten.—P.C. Hall said the defendant was staggering about and cursing and swearing, and refused to go home,saving he had as much right on the King's highv ty as a policeman. —P.C. Almond assisted to take the man to till police station,and he was very drunk.—lnspector Keighley,P.S. McGregor, P.S. Clarkson, and Constables Thompson, Rohinson, Evans, and Balmforth all stated that defend- ant was very drunk at the station.—Dr. Hudson said he saw the man at midnight at the police station. He was then under the influence of drink and unable to walk steadily. He was not sober.—Mr. Knowles contended that the man was excited and not drunk.—Defendant denied that he was drunk or made use of bad language. It was a good test that he was not drunk when he walked ' from Ann-st. and climbed four flights of stairs to the Irish League room ,and if the constables had been put to the same test they would not have been able to do it.— Hugh O'Donnell, grocer, Widnes-rd., said defendant was perfectly sober at seven o'clock when he saw him on the stairs of the League-rooms.—P. Quinn, Luton-st., M. Whelan, Wellington-st., and T. Whelan stated defendant was sober when arrested.—Dr. &Kees said he saw the defendant at the police station on Sunday night. He was not drunk but perfectly sober and able to take care of himself, and answered all his questions in a proper manner. No doubt he was a little excited, as any man would be after beitr, treated as defendant was by the police. He (witness") felt indignant that an innocent man should be put in such a place.—By Superintendent Noblett : He did not see defendant fall against the cell door. Defendant had had some drink but was not drunk. —Other witnesses were about to be called, when Mr. Muspratt said the bench would give the defendant the benefit of the doubt. The case was dismissed. HARVEST THANKSGIVING SERVICES AT WHITLEY.

On Sunday tvro sermons were preached in Whit- ley Chapel by Mr. Brough, of Warrington, in cele- bration of the ingathering of the harvest. The in- terior of the cLapel was very tastefully decorated for the occasion, among which were two mottos. The services were well attended, both morning and evening, and good collections were made. FATAL FALL AT Sr. HELENS.

William John Thomas Dean, of 108, Albion-st., St. Helens,l2 years of age, died on Wednesday night in the Providence Hospital, from the effects of in- juries received on Tuesday morning. Dean was em- ployed at the St. Helens Copper Works, and on Tuesday morning he was working with a man named Henry Bridge, a plumber,on a platform 30ft. from the ground. Bridge sent the boy to a scaffold some 20ft. higher to fetch a wallet. Dean went up and immediately afterwards Bridge heard a thud on the platform behind him, and on looking round he saw the deceased lying on the platform with a bucket of lime on his head. Dr. Challenor attended to the boy, but he died as stated. THE CARBOLIC ACID POISONING AT WHISTON. Last week we reported an inquest held before Mr. S. Brighouse on the body of a boy named Roscoe, son of a collier residing in Carr's Cottages, Whiston, who was accidentally poisoned by drinking from a 'bottle of carbolic acid kept in the house for disin- fecting purposes. The evidence showed that the father had had his children down with scarlet fever and afterwards with typhoid fever, and the coroner remarked that Roscoe seemed to have had his share of this world's troubles. A few days ago the coroner received a postal order for .£1 from Mr. G. H. Lloyd, of Rhayader, North Wales, with a request that it should be forwarded to Roscoe. Mr. Brighouse has accordingly forwarded the order to Mr. John Leatherbarrow, the foreman of the jury, and asked that gentleman to kindly hand it to Roscoe. He added that he himself would contribute to a local fund for the man and his family if the sum of £2O or £25 could be raised. UMBRELLAS RECOvERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Saukey-st., Warrington.—Adv. GOVERNMENT FROSEeiTTION OF Sr. HELENS COLLIERY PROPRIETORS.

At St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, Messrs. Glover, Urmson, and Glover, proprietors of the Phcenix Colliery, St. Helens, and Mr. Richard Marsh, the certificated manager, were summoned on the information of Mr. H. Hall, Government inspector of mines, for a breach of the rules in force under the Coal Nlines Regulation Act.—Mr. Collins, of Liver- pool, who prosecuted, said the proceedings were taken under the 17th general rule, which provided that all travelling roads in the mine should be of sufficient dimensions to allow horses or other arimals to pass along without rubbing against the roof. On the 31st July Mr. Hall, the inspector,was down the mine, and found a white pony which had been rubbing against the bars of one of the roads. The pony's shoulder was quite sore. He then ex- amined the bars along the road and found that the bark on two of the bars had been rubbed off by the pony catching them when walking along the road. —Mr. J. 0. Swift, who appeared for the defence, stated that there was no dispute as to the facts. The road in question had a very bad roof, and it was continually altering the face of the road. The , moment the manager and the employer had their attention drawn to the circumstances they took immediate steps to remedy the cause of complaint., and he submitted that everything had been done which was possible by reasonable men. He added that if a technical offence had been committed it, was of a most trivial character, as there were 2,000 yards of main roads in the mine, and out of the thousands of bars complaint had only been made against two.—The bench thought the Act had been contravened, but that the offence was not of a serious character. A fine of £2 and costs was im- posed. uMB KELL AS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-it., Warrington.--Aevt.

div.head: IRISH NATIONALIST DEMONSTRATION
div.p: IRISH NATIONALIST DEMONSTRATION

AT WIDNES. Under the auspices, of the Widnes branch of the Irish National League a demonstration was held on Thursday evening. The proceedings commenced in the League-rooms in St. Paul's chambers, where Mr. T. 1). Sullivan, M.P. for the College Green Division of Dublin, was presented with an illuminated ad- dress from the Irishmen of Widnes. Dr. O'Keeffe presided, and there were about 50 persons present. Mr. T. E. Delaney formally made the presentation, and Mr. Sullivan in reply said he was glad to see such good feeling amongst them, and the address. should have a place amongst others he had received At 8 o'clock a public meeting was held in the Drill Hall under the presidency of Dr. O'Keeffe, who was supported by Mr. Sullivan, Major Wareing, Dr. McCambridge, Messrs. E. K. Muspratt, J.P., E. Carey, P. Kearney (Liverpool). J. Randle, F. Hartland, J'. Drury, H. O'Donnell, P. Mulholland, and T. E. Delaney. —Mr. H. W. Deacon, J.P., wrote expressing regret at his inability to, be present.—After a brief address by the Chairman, Mr. E. Carey proposed the following resolution :—" That we once more enter on record' our firm conviction that no measure lof Home Rule which does not give full power to the Irish people to manage their own local affairs will be accepted as a 'final or satisfactory measure, and we feel confident that the friendly relations between the Nationalist members of Ireland and the great Liberal party will result in a full measure of Home Rule for Ire- land." That resolution he said expressed the feeling not only of the Irish people but of the great majority of the Liberal party in England. He was convinced the Liberal leaders were thoroughly satisfied that England had muddled whenever she had meddled in Irish affairs, and they were determined that the Irish people should have an opportunity of managingtheirovvn affairs, so that the fruits of their industry would not betaken from them as had been the case in the past. (Applause.) Mr. Mus- pratt seconded the motion, and remarked that the Irish people had spoken out and had convinced the majority of the English people that they were deserving of Home Rule. (Applause.) Mr. T. D. Sullivan supported the motion. He said there were many noble Englishmen at Newcastle that day and at the head of them all was the noblest Englishman that ever breathed the breath of life (cheers) and that assembly would convince them that there was no indifference in the minds of Liberals upon this important question, thus opening for the Irish nation a glorious vista of peace, prosperity, and happiness, and a real union between England and Ire- land for all time to come. (Applause.) The House of Lords was the great stumbling block in the way of the progress of the British people, and of the concession of justice to Ireland ; and it was that old institution, slow- witted and evil-hearted that had kept both the English and the Irish people in the miserable condition in which they had existed for so long. But they would have to yield
