FINANCE.—INCREASE OF RATEABLE VALUE.

The Finance Committee reported that during the past month the Treasurer had received the following sums : General District Rate, £591 16s. 11d. ; market rents and tolls, £3O 19s. 10d. t • slaughter-houses, £5 Os. 11d. ; night soil sales, £27 3s. 3d. ; Fire Brigade charges recovered, £lO 53. 10d. ; total £665 63. 9d. Accounts were recom- mended for payment amounting to £321 12s. 2d., on general fund ; £93 6s. 7d., on loan accounts; and £5 53. 4d., Library Fund, it was recommended that the assessment of Thomas Harrison be reduced from £3O 133. 4d. to £27, and the assessment of Henry Lacey be reduced from £l2 to £4. That the irrecoverable arrears of the first instalment of the general district rate, amounting to £46 19s. 6d. be allowed. That the general district rate made on April 16th last, be amended by raising and reducing certain assessments as set forth in the schedule to be submitted, the net increaso amounting to £766 is. Bd., rateable value.—Mr. Fisher moved and Mr. Wass seconded.—ln reply to Mr. Humphreys, Mr. Fisher said about £3O of the irrecoverable arrears con- sisted of assessments that were now out of use altogether, such as quarries, the smelting works, brickfields, &c., and about £lO was caused through empty property, The increase in the assessment of £766 was equal to about £4O a year on the rate for the half year.

div.head: NEW ACTS.
div.p: NEW ACTS.
The Secretary produced a circular from the Local Government Boaad, drawing the attention of the Board to Acts passed in 1891, affecting Urban Authorities. DEEP DOCKS AT RUNCORN.

Under the head of general business, Mr. Lightburn said,there was amatter which he wished to brisg before the Board, and his excuse was its supreme importance. He referred to the Deep Docks at Runcorn. In less than two years the Ship Canal works would be completed at Runcorn and when that was the case, there would be a depth of the canal opposite the Runcorn tidal basin of something like (he was not speaking of the sill but of the basin), 14 feet below the level of the basin, prob&bly more. Suppose there were a 2 or 3 thousand ton ship coming to Runcorn, it isauld be absurd, and impossible, to think of lifting that vessel from the Ship Canal into the Tidal Basin, and even if it were got there it would not float. That was quite sufficient to show the position in which they would be placed when the Ship Canal was completed. There was no doubt that, as in the Suez Canal, there would be many vessels specially built to trade on the Ship Canal, with masts sufficiently low, or made telescopic, so that they could go under Runcorn Bridge and pass on to Warrington or Manchester. There would still be a large number of vessels whose lower masts would be too high to go under that bridge. This was not mere guess work with him, because ship- owners bad been to Runcorn with a view of ascertain- ing whether their vessels could pass under the bridge by striking their top masts, and he knew one large firm whiz!) found the lower masts of their vessels tan feet to.) high for that purpose. It was quite certain that vessels whose structure made it impossible for them to go under the bridge would not come to Runcorn. What would be the result? Vessels that could pass the bridge would just say " Good day " and pass on to Manchester, and the other vessels which could come to Runcorn would have to go to Liverpool or elsewhere to be discharged because Runcorn had no deep docks, and the trade of the town would suffer in consequence. They talked very much about recreation grounds, about baths and about .a vehicular bridge across the river—and there was no man apprehended more the great advantage those things would be to Runcorn, but at the same time he contended that they all sank into absolute insignificance compared with the 'question of deep docks. It. was a very vital question for the town that there should be some place where large vessel 3 could discharge and load at Runcorn. . He did not know that in the history of Runeorn a point had ever been reached of such vital importance; it was a matter that would not keep, and it must. not he allowed to slumber. On the 9th December, 1889, a Committee of the Board of which he was Chairman had a meeting with representatives of the Ship Canal Company. There was an agreement that the Man- chester Ship Canal Company should make a second lock near the Bridgewater Lock and the Company should ask the Commissioners to relinquish that and in considera- tion of that relinquishment certain concessions were made to the Board. Amongst the things asked for was that the level of the tidal basin should be reduced to the level of the sill which was three or four feet lower. The Company's representatives replied, "Don't press that question upon us because we will go in for a much larger scheme." He thought after the way in which the Board had always dealt with the Company they might , approach them upon the question with all the energy I they were possessed of. To his mind this matter was of such extreme importance that it could not be over- estimated, and he wanted this subject to go to Corn- mittee.with all the momentum that the Board could give it. He did not wish it to be dealt with in a perfunc- tory manner. If the Company met the Board in the spirit they usnally had done, and the Board could assist them by extending their boundaries sd as to give them facilities, he was sure the Board as the representatives of the people of Runcorn would do their best to meet them. He hoped that some active interest would be I taken in the matter, and he proposed that the ques- tion be referred to the Parliamentary and Legal Committee.—Mr. Taylor said he quite agreed with Mr. Lightburn. It was, and would be a still more essential thing that they should have deep docks at Runcorn. There was no doubt that a very large trade could be developed in the district, but if they had not dock accommodation for those large vessels that could not pass under the bridge those vessels would go elsewhere. He trusted the matter woull be taken up with all the energy and power the Board possessed, and that something beneficial would come of it. In their cleanness with the Ship Canal Company in the past, the Board had always been treated with courtesy, and full consideration had been given to any proposal they had made for the benefit of Runcorn, and he felt sure that if they were approached upon this momentous question, they would be met in the same manner.—Mr. Hankinson seconded Mr. Lightburn's motion, remarking that deep docks would be a boon to the locality.—Mr. F. Wiswall said ho might inform the Board that the ques- tion was receiving the serious consideration of the directors of the company. He need not point out that it would cost money to provide all this accommodation,and the directors were considering the question in all its bearings. He was quite sure that the directors would receive with respect and attention any representation from that Board. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Lightburn said he was quite sure of that and no doubt sooner or later deep docks would be made at Runcorn, but they did not want to wait eight or nine years before they got that supreme advantage for Runcorn.—Mr. Bisbrown supported the motion so ably proposed by Mr. Lightburn and remarked that the Ship Canal Company would be studying their own interests if they acceded to the request of the Board. —The motion was carried. MR. SMITE ASSERTS HIS POSITIDIt. Mr. Smith,referring to the appointment of Committees at the last meeting, oblected to them being so small as , they were. He advocated each Committee consisting of , the whole Board. He proposed that he be a member of every Committee, but no one seconded the motion.—Mr. Humphreys said probably some injustice had been done. He did not know on what principle the Committees had been elected but white some members were on ten,eissht, six,and five Committees other members -were only placed on two.—Mr. Wiswall said the reason Mr. Smith was not placed on the Committees was because it was not settled s. whether he had forfeited his seat.---Several members

spoke in favour of small Committees,and Mr. Lightburn said he should be glad of Mr. Smith's services on the Health Committee,and Mr. Humphreys proposed that he be a member.—Mr. Smith declined to sit on the Health Committee. If he were not on every Committee he should attend the Board meetings and put the Chairman to the trouble of saying" Why don't you attend the Committee meetings ?"—The Chairman said he supposed that re- mark was dincted to him. Mr. Smith had the privilege of attesding the Commmittee meetings last year, but there were very few meetings that he attended.—Mr. Smith: lam not promising to attend now, but I wish the privilege.—Although Mr. Smith persisted in declining to act on the Health Committee,he was unanimously elected a member.
THE NIGHTSOIL DEPOT.

Mr. Hankinson drew attention to complaints of the nuisance caused by the nighsoil depot on the Canal bank —Mr. Wiswall : The tip is only a temporary one.—Mr. Lightburn said the Committee had done all in their power to flnd a more suitable place but had failed. They would do all in their power to diminigh the nuisance, as they sympathised very much with the inhabitants of the neighbourhood.
INSUFFICIENT LIGHT.
Mr. Lightburn complained that the whole of the lamps of the town were not lighted, and the subject was referred to the General Purposes Committee.
BATHS COMMITTEE.

On the motion of Mr. Smith, seconded by Mr. Light- burn, the following was constituted a Baths Committee: Messrs. Hankinson, W. Timmins, W. H. Wass, J. W. Lightburn, H. Coward, H. J. Grice, and P. Smith.

div.head: RUNCORN TONIC SOL-FA CHOIR.
div.p: RUNCORN TONIC SOL-FA CHOIR.

The members of this choir gave the first concert of their seventh season in Runcorn Public Hall, on Monday evening. The audience was fairly nume- rous, but it is doubtful if the receipts would equal the heavy expenditure, and it is surprising that so deserving an institution does not meet with more generous support from the townspeople. Perhaps the public celebration of a fortnight previous,when the hall was filled to its utmost capacity, had an adverse influence on the attendance on Monday last. However,musically the concert was a decided success, and the audience showed their appreciation by frequent and enthusiastic applause. The princi- pals engaged were Madame Madge Morgans (soprano), Miss Maude Yates (contralto), Mr. G. H. Lawton (tenor), and Mr. Fred Gordon (bass). In consequence of illness, Miss Yates was unable to appear, and Miss Alice Walker kindly took her place,with a very slight alteration of the programme. The choir, which consisted of about 50 voices was, as usual, distinguished for the excellency of its performances. The various part songs and glees were rendered with tunefulness and har- mony that did the artistes and their new conductor, Mr. John Holford, G.T.S.C., the greatest credit, and the audience were not slow to demonstrate their favourable opinion. The items were "Strike the lyre," " Lovely Star," "Hail blushing goddess," "The voyagers." "The fisherman," and "The lullaby of life." Madame Morgans is the possessor of a soprano voice of good tone and quality, and being • gifted with power of expression, her vocalisation is of a high order. She sang " Flight of ages "and " Carrissima," and for the latter she received an encore but did not respond. Miss Walker has a pleasing contralto voice and she rendered with good effect Noble Signor "(Les Hugenots), and' The Better Land." Mr. Lawton ably sustained his part of the pro- gramme, his light though clear tenor voice being heard ,to much advantage in his rendition of "Mona," "Love's Request," and "My Home, my heart's first home." Mr. Fred Gordon made a most favourable impression by his powers of vocalisation and dramatic expression, and he was enthusiastically encored for his interpretation of Hatton's " Revenge, ' and he responded by a capital ren- dering of "Rocked in the cradle of the deep." His other contribution was "Down in the deep." The duet" The singing lesson," by Madame Morgans and Mr. Gordon caused much amusement,and the vocalists had to repeat it. The National Anthem brought an enjoyable concert to a close. Mrs. W. B. Kay ably officiated as accom- panist.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. E. K. Muspratt, and Mr. A. Stapleton-Bretherton.

MiSCELLANBOUS.—Frederick Lunth, a tramp, was sen- tenced to seven days' hard labour for begging.—Mary Daley, Warrington-road, and Thomas McDonald, Major Cross-st., were each fined ss. and costs for drunkenness. John McCabe and James Cusick, Midwood-st.; Lawrence Mooney, Nelson-st. ; and George Roughley, Victoria-st., were each bound over to be of good behaviour for creat- ing breaches of the peace.—John Staines, Martley-street, was fined is. and costs for allowing the chimney of his dwelling to be on fire.—For being drunk while in charge of a horse and cart, at Ditton, Thomas Cank was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.—Patrick Burke, Catherine-st., was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for allowing his dog at large un- muzzled.

ILLEGAL REMOVAL OF SWlNE.—James Fletcher and Hy. Fletcher, Widnes-road, were summoned for removing swine from Chester to Widnes without the necessary order authorising the same. Mr. Knowles pleaded that the defendants had no intention of breaking the law, but the Bench fined, Tames £2 and costs and Henry 103. and costs.

WITHDRAIVS.—John Proffitt, of Ellis-st., was sum- moned by Mr. J. Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., for causing his horse to be worked in an unfit state, and Joseph Hudson for working the same.—The horse was suffering from an enlargement of the knee, but as the defendant had only had the animal a few weeks, he withdrew the charge on payment of costs.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

REFUSING TO QUlT.—Before Mr. A. Thomas, at Frod- sham Police Court, on Tuesday, Christopher Flannaghan was remanded to Oakmere Petty Sessions, on a charge of refusing to quit the Golden Lion Inn, and also of assaulting the landlord, Thomas Pletcher.

THE LIGHTING OF THE STREETS.-1 he dispute between the Frodsham Gas Inspectors and the Frocisham Gas and Water Company, Limited,has not yet been settled. Tao town presents a most deplorable and neglected appear- ance of an evening, from the non-lighting of the street lamps, and this must necessarily cause great inconven- ience and much disadvantage to the majority of the resi- dents in the locality.

„„..... THE LICENSE OF THE ALBERT INN.—Mr. Arthur Lin- aker, of Runcorn,applied to the magistrates at Oakmere Petty Sessions, on Monday, for the approval of plans of alterations &c., and for the renewal of license of the Albert Inn, Frodsham. It was found necessary to en- lame the house for the convenience of the tenant and his family, as well as the customers. The Bench,ha,ving examined the plans, sanctioned the alterations and re- newed the license. _ .

TRINITY CHAPEL.—The harvest thanksgiving services in connection with the Wesleyan Methodists were held in the above chapel on Sunday, the service in the morn- ing being conducted by the Rev. P. Pizey. circuit minis- ter, and that of the evening by Mr. W, Collier, of War- rington. The usual hymns of thanksgiving were sung by a full choir, and the anthems, "The Mount of Olives" and "The Lord is my Shepherd," the solo in the latter anthem being very beautifully rendered. The congrega- tions were very large. AN INHUMAN FATHER.—On Monday, at Oakmere Potty Sessions, Joseph Allmark, Frodsham, was summoned for assaulting his wife on the 4th September.—Complainant spoke to defendant entering the house and striking her about the breast. He knocked her down and turned the children out, and she had to go out with the babf, which was naked, in her arms. She wished fora separation.— A judicial separation was granted, and tbe defendant was ordered to pay 6s. a week towards theimaintenance of his wife and children. A PROMISING KINGSLEY BOY.—At Oakmere Petty Sessions, on Monday, James Hicks, schoolmaster. King- sley, applied for an industrial school order to be applied to John Edward Griffiths, a boy who had been at King- sley Boy's Home for some time. The applicant stated that he was the master of the home,and, as the guardian of the boy, he could not control him. The lad was sent out to service at Weaverham, but he was soon sent back again, having stolen some whiskey and some money. He exercised a very bad influence over the other boys in the home, and he wished for an order to send him to the Standen Bridge Industrial School.—The necessary order was made.

div.head: TERRIBLE COLLIE RY ACCIDENT IN SOUTH WALES, LOSS OF EIGHT LIVES.
div.p: TERRIBLE COLLIE RY ACCIDENT IN SOUTH WALES, LOSS OF EIGHT LIVES.

Seven men were killed in a new colliery, being sunk at Glyncorwg, South Walev, owing to the overwinding of the pit gear. The accident occurred between ten and eleven on Wednesday night. At the time of the accident the afternoon shift was being drawn up, and the night shift lowered, when, as is alleged, owing to a defective valve in the steam chest, the machinery ran wild and seven men were precipitated down the shaft and must have been instantaneously killed, while another man named Richard Skinner, who was dashed with great violence on the bank, received frightful injuries and died not long afterwards. The name of the man in charge of the engine is David Davies, and the colliery property is owned by Messrs. Perch and Cardiff. The names of the deceased men are:—

James O'Connell ; Humphrey Jenkins, age l 30; Thomas, sinker, 30; Thomas Thomas, 27; Wm. Evans, 46 ; Wm. Carpenter, 30 ; and Thos. Lewis. Medical aid wassoon at hand,the first doctors to arrive being Messrs. Hemming and Grant, of Abergwnf. They were followed by Drs. Jones and Davies. of Ma,esteg, but with the exception of attending to the injured man Skinner,their services were of no avail. Mr.Wm.Thoreas, who had charge of the sinking operations, has arrived st the spot. The new colliery is situated in a district not easy of access,aad there is no telegraphiecommunication ; but by daybreak the news had rapidly spread, and the greatest excitement arose in the surrounding districts, hundreds of colliers leaviii,g their work to visit the scene of the disaster.
WARaiNGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. .

The monthly Zeeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse' yesterday morning. The Rev, G. F. Roberts presided,. and there were also present Afessrs. J. White, W.. Houghton, Heaton, Jelley, Owen, Smith, and Swinton; S. Sutton (Clerk), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), W. Owen (surveyor), and F. Kerfoot (nuisance inspector.) THE ALLEGED NUISANCE AT LONGFORD DEPOT: THREATENED ACTION AGAINST THE CORPORA- TION, The CM. 3RIE reported that he had received the following letter from the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle) with ' regard to the complaint made as to the alleged nuisance caused by Longford depot, viz :—" I am isstructed by the Sanitary Committee to inform yeu that they have carefully codsidered the report of your medical officer, respecting the condition of the depot at Longford. In their opinion the nuisance complained of does not arise on the premises of the Corporation. The Committee would respectfully point out that although they have on several occasions sold crude manure to farmers in the neighbourhood of the depot they can scarcely be held responsible for the way in which it is deposited on the fields about Orford.' The Ceminittee also wish me to point out that they have had reason to complain of the condition of the premises belonging to Mr. James Toole which have been erected in the vicinity of the depot, and they firmly believe that much of the annoyance ef which some of the inhabitants in Orford complain arises from the works referred to. The Committee further wish me to assure you that they are most anxious and are doing everything in their power to conduct the opera- tions at the depot insuch a manner as to avoid the pos- sibility of complaint."—Mr. Owen : That letter is all bosh, gentlemen. He could taste and smell Longford depot at his place atCroft at 11 o'clock at night. The,sys- tem at Longford depot was a rotten one,and was a nuis- ance to the locality. It was a great hindrance to the pros- pects of the landed proprietors of the district in which it was placed, and this could be corroborated by plenty of people at different times. That morning it was simply unbearable. There ought to be something done to stop that stench that arose from the manufacture of that "muck." It was a manufacture which was supposed to alleviate the rates, but it was a question whether it did alleviate the rates or not. He considered that the nuisance they suffered from was due to the "cooking apparatus." The smell arising from the manure on the roadside was simply nothing.—Mr. Heaton said the smell arising from the raw manure at the roadside and that arising from Toole's place was quite different from the smells from Longford. The smell from the works went all over the country.—Mr. Owen said as he passed the works that morning he could not help arguing that the Town Council of Warrington or the burgesses must own land somewhere else, and wanted to stop the owners of land in the neighbourhood of the depot going on with buildings. He could not understand why that Authority did not take steps.—ln answer to a question, the Nuisance Inspector said there was no doubt a bad smell at Toole's place when you got there, but the smell did not travel far.—The Clerk said the Authority were in this difficulty—if the Corporation said the depot was really a manufactory and they proved that they used all available means to pre- vent a nuisance the Authority could not do • anything.— Mr. Owen said he should proceed against the Corpora- tion' to abate the nuisance. He thought anything was bad in principle that could be smelt and tasted three miles off.—Dr. Sephton thought the fault lay in the working of the destructor. If too much material were put on the furnace disagreeable smell passed from the chimney, but if the furnace was properly stoked these smells did not arise. The smells did not ccme from the dry- ing of the material but from the burning of the refuse. —Mr.Owen: Nothing of the sort ; it comes from the excre- ment.—Dr. Sephton said the excreta was dried in closed boilers,and there could be no smell from closed chambers. —Mr. Heaton said there was no doubt the farmers in the neighbourhood of the depot put up with a good deal, but when the machinery went wrong they got presents of crude manure.—Mr. Owen said he must compliment the Town Clerk on the way in which he blamed every- body but the Corporation. He moved that the Authority take steps at once to cause the nuisance from the Long- ford depot to be abated.—This proposal was not seconded.—The Chairman suggested that a better plan would be to delay matters and instruct their officers to again bring the question up if the nuisance continued.— Dr. Sephton said that whenever they had complained before the nuisance was abated for a time.—The sug- gestion of the Chairman was then agreed to. THIN LIGHTING OF DISTRICTS.—A RAFLECTION ON HEX. OFFICIOS."

The Clerk mentioned that there were applications for the public lighting of Croft from Mr. R. Owen, and of Pad gate from Mr. J. Houghton on behalf of th e overseers of Poulton. Mr. Owen moved that Croft should be lighted, and argued that they were as much entitled to have lamps placed on the roads there at the expense of the Authority's district as were Qrappenhall and Latch- ford. There were people living in his locality who had never seen Grappenhall or Latchford, and he did not know whether some of them had ever seen a gas lamp— (laughter)--and therefore the lamps would be appreciated. —ln answer to the Chairman, Mr. Owen said they had no gas mains laid at Croft,but they could be brought from Warrington or somewhere else.—Mr. W. Houghton said he would give notice of a motion for the next meeting to rescind the resolution passed at the last meeting that the charge of lighting Latchford and Grappenhall should be placed on the whole of the Authority's district.—The , Clerk then read a resolution which had been passed at a meeting of ratepayers of Penketh asking the authority to erect lamps at Penketh.—Mr. Jonas Forster, who was present on behalf of the Penketh ratepayers, said they wanted the lighting there, and they were not greatly concerned whether it was made a charge on the township or a general charge on the Authority's district.—lt was moved by Mr. Owen, and seconded by Mr. Smith, that the request be granted, but ultimately it was decided to refer the matter to the Lighting Committee.—ln the course of some further remarks, Mr. Owen commented upon the sup- port which the Warrington members of the Authority had given to the proposal to light Latchford and Grap- penhall, and said that these members wanted to throw a halo round the town for their own purposes; they were decidedly the right men in the wrong place, on the Authority. He also referred to the ex-officio members, who, he said, attended the meeting for specific purposes. —Mr. John White, who spoke rather warmly, said it was only tbe second meeting he had attended, and as he was the only ex-officio member present, he was told that he attended for snecific purposes. He did not: come there for any specific purpose. He did not know that he had been put upon that authority at all till a few months ago, and he had attended the previous meeting because it was about the first he could attend. He did think it was very uncalled for for anyone to tell an ex-officio member on his first attendance that he came for a specific purpose.—Mr. HEATON said Mr. Owea seemed to think there was no other place than Croft. The Warrington members represented more property than any of the other members.—Mr. OwEN said he was not at the last meeting but he knew that Mr. White voted for the lighting of Latchford, thereby taking money out of one township for the benefit of another. He, however, took Mr. White's word for it that he did not attend for any specific purpose. He might say that Croft had no bankers and county magistrates living in it like Latch- ford and Grappenhall.—The CHAIRMAN was glad Mr. Owen had apologised for his remark. As to the consti- tution of that Authority that was a question for the Board of Guardians.—The subject then dropped.

div.head: DEATH-RATE.
div.p: THE DEATH-RATE.

The Medical Officer reported that there had during the past month been 17 deaths and 18 births in the district, the death-rate being 15.9 as compared with 13.2 in the corresponding period of last year.

div.head: NEW BUILDINGS.
div.p: NEW BUILDINGS.

The Surveyor reported that the following plans had been submittod and were in accordance with the bye- laws—Wesleyan school, Sankey Bridges; and Mr. T. Fletcher's addition to house in Grappenhall. During the month certificates of habitation had been issued to Mr. Thomas Antrobus for two houses at Padgate, and to Mr. Massey for one house in Orford Park. This Was all the business.

The British barquentine -§t. Croix and the schooner Charles have been in collision off New London, Connecti- cut, the schooner sinking immediately. The Ramsgate smack Transit was on Wednesday sunk by the Hamburg barque Columbus, three hands being lost. COLLIERY FATALITY AT GARSWOOD.—On Thursday, Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at the Railway Hotel, Garswood, on the body of Edward Kelly, day wagernan, age 45 years, who lodged at New Boston, Haydock, and was killed by a fall or stone and dirt in Messrs. J. and R. Stones colliery, Garswood. Mr. C. H. Higson, certificated manager, represented the colliery company, and Mr. Henry Hall, Government Inspector of Mines, was present The deceased was repairing the roof of the mine and he was told to put up two props, one on the higher side, and the other on the lower side, but he only erected one. The fall occurred shortly afterwards.—Henry Topping, fireman, said he gave instructions for the work. If they had been obeyed the accident would not have taken place, because one prop would have been directly under the stone.—Mr. Hall, Government Inspector, said that the only point that should be impressed was that the men must obey orders.—The jury, after a few minutes' conversation,returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and added that there was no blame attached to the officials.
