div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
THBET ;BY A BOY.

At the Borough Magistrates' -Court, on Wednesday, Andrew Carrington, a boy, son of William Carrington,s, Leonard-st., was charged with stealin; the sum of 2s. from his father's house, some time during the night of September Ist. The lad was sent to jail for 14 days., to be sent thence to a reformatory for five years.

TNESFT OF A JACKET. Andrew McLoughlin was charged with stealing from the model lodging-house, Friar's Green, on the previous day-, a rean's jacket, value 35., the property of William rickersgill, a ledger in the house. He took it to a second- hand clothes dealer's, and pawned it as his own.—He was sent to prison for a month's hard labour. A MAN SEEKS FOE LODGINGS AND FINDS THRM.B Michael Coleburn, who said be had recently come from South Wales., was on Tuesday charged at the Police Court with having been on the premises of the Longford Wire and Iron Company, for an unlawful purpose the previous evening. It appeared that the prisoner had been behav- ing in a very eccentric fashion. One woman, who lives in Kerfoot-street, said she left her house about ten minutes and when she went back she found Coleburn lying across the hearth. When asked what he wanted he said he was seeking lodgings. Another woman, living in the same street, said the prisoner walked into her house and demanded lodgings, but she took him by the shoulders and put him outside. P.C. Smith afterwards found prisoner on the premises of the Longford Iron Company, and when questioned, he still said that he was seeking lodgings. The bench said they would give him lodgings for seven days in Strangeways gaol.

A LIGHT-FINGERED YOUNG ADVENTURER. At the Warrington borough police court Anthony Thomae, a respectably dressed youth, and a stranger to Warrington, was charged with being in Museum-st., on Saturday afternoon,with intent to commit a felony. P.C. Hollingsworth deposed to seeing the prisoner lift up the jacket of a Mrs. Armstrong, and put his hand into her pocket. She had just taken out her purse containing £2 and put it up her sleeve. Corroborative evidence was given by a young man, and Mrs. Armstrong deposed to seeing the prisoner behind her, but she did not feel him do anything, and did not know what he had done till he was taken into custody.—The prisoner denied his guilt, but would give no satisfactory account of himself. He remarked that it was a strange thing he should only have 3s. on him if be was a thief.—The Mayor: You see the pocket was not in the right place.—The prisoner was sent to jail for a month's imprisonment with hard labour.

div.head: ANOTHER CHILD MOLESTER IN THE PARK.
div.p: ANOTHER CHILD MOLESTER IN THE PARK.

Charles Smith, labourer, last from Runcorn, was I charged with behaving in an indecent manner to Sarah Ann Allen, aged 8 years, in Bank Park on Sunday after- noon. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle appeared for the prosecution, and said in consequence of the frequent complaints from parents about children being molested in the park, the park-keeper had been put to considerable anxiety and trouble to detect cases of this kind. The prisoner had been watched in the park for a month and at lengtk de- tected. Evidence having been given proving the case by one of the park-keepers who said he had watched the prisoner because he had been at the same game before, the child was called. Mr. Whittle said he did not know whether the Bench would have the oath adminsstered to a child like that. The magistrates heard the child's statement, which consisted of an answer to but one ques- tion, unsworn. The prisoner was sent to jail for three mouths' hard labour.
STREET RuFFIINS.

At the borough magistrates' court, on Monday, Wm. Lythgoe was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Battersby-lane on Saturday afternoon, and with as- saulting P.C. Leathwood on the same occasion.—P.C. Leathwood said the defendant was drunk and very, disorderly, and fighting his father. On witness inter- fering the man gave him a smack in the mouth. He took him into custody, and he promised to go quietly, but when he had got about 200 yards, said,with an oath, he would shew him the soldier's trick, and " burst out" like a madman, knocking him to the ground and kicking him several times on the head an hitting him repeatedly on the back, saying he might as well have a month for a lot as a little.—The prisoner denied the charge.—The Mayor told the constable that he ought to have been careful to bring to the court those who witnessed the 'prisoner's conduct, as it was desirable to have the evi- dence of constables corroborated if possible. The pri- soner was fined 10s. and costs; in default 14 days' hard labour.—At the same court, on Monday, Michael Quinn was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Hill-st., on Saturday afternoon, and with assaulting Henry Green on the same occasion.—P.C. Brewin deposed to hearing the screams of a woman and finding that defendant had 'knocked a woman to the ground and had hold of Green, who had come to her assistance. Witness had great difficulty in loosing his hold.—Green said he saw the defendant knock the woman down, and went to pull him away as he was about to strike her again. The man got him by the neck,and they both fell together. P.C. Brewin came up and took the prisoner away. He was fined 10s. and costs; in default 14 days' hard labour.
`CHARGE 037 STRALING A HORSE .-A STUPID '
PROSECUTOR.

Charles McCollom, cabinet maker, 32, Gee-st., was Charged at the Warrington Borough Police Court on Thursday, with stealing, some time between August 12th and September 28th, a bay horse value £8 to £lO, the property of Robert Taylor, his father-in-law, of 344, liorth-road,Preston. The prosecutor stated that he left the horse in Mr. Robert Heaton's field on the 12th of Septem- ber, and never saw it after. He immediately afterwards said that he next saw it on Monday last at Mr. Heaton's office. The prisoner had been working for him, but left his employ two months since. The prosecutor could give no further account as to the circumstances under which the horse was alleged to have been stolen ; and in the course .of a close cross-examination by the prisoner he said he did.not know how the horse came into his pos- session. It was his somehow or other. It was his money that paid for it. The prisoner,he said,had exchanged one of his (Taylor's) horses for the bay horse. The prisoner made a lengthy and, to a great extent, irrelevent, state- ment, but denied that the horse ever belonged to the prosecutor, but said he had bought it himself.—ln an- swer to the prisoner, the prosecutor admitted that he had turned over his business in Warrington to him, and he was to have the use of everything about the place. He was not sure whether there were any horses on the pre- mises. He did not think there were. The prosecutor manifested extraordinary stupidity, and the prisoner confused the case considerably, by his manner of stating the circumstances.—But as"the result. the Chairman (Alderman Sutton) remarked that Taylor's evidence was not satisfactory, and he could not show that the horse belonged to him, and the Bench would dismiss the case.

div.head: ANOTHER BRUTAL WIFE BEATER.
div.p: ANOTHER BRUTAL WIFE BEATER.

At the Borough magistrates' court,yesterday morning, ;Joseph Ireland, of 19, Hind-st., was charged with as- saulting his wife,Mary Ireland,on the 12th of September. ISlrs.lretand said the defendant came home when she was in bed and threatened what he would do to her if she did not get up. She got up and put her skirt on, and he threw her from the top of the stairs to the bottom., and then kicked her and when he was tired of doing that took his shoe off and split her head with it. He beat her till she was.black and blue from the top of the head to the sole of the foot. The defendant said the woman had provoked him by coming home drunk the previous ,night.-,-.T.S.C.hantle,r said about a month or five weeks

ago Dr. Jackson came and made complaint to him about the defendant's conduct to his wife. Witness went to his house and found the woman bleeding like a pig. There was a pool of blood on the floor. It was a wonder she was alive now. She said then she did not want to send him to prison. Witness went and saw the defendant at the Ring-o-Bells public-house, and cautioned him, and told him that if she applied for a warrant she would get one and that he was liable to be taken up then. Dr. Jackson also cautioned him, and he promised he would not molest her again.—The defendant : I beg your pardon--Alderman Harrison: Beg fiddlestick. Don't talk to me about beg- lug pardon.—P.S. Chantler : He will be killing her some time, there is no doubt.—The defendant: She has never been sober for five weeks.—P.S.Chantler : She was sober that day.—Alderman Harrison Yes,l dare say. (To the defendant) : You had better look to your misconduct and ,correct your shortooniings.---rhe defendant: There is no man in Warrington behaves better to his wife than I do. (Laughter.) She will be drunk to-night, your Worships.—The Bench sentenced him to six months' im- prisonment with hard labour.—His wife pleaded that they would not send him to prison, saying she only wanted an allowance from him, to live apart from him, and would be ,content with Bs. a week.—The Bench re- duced the sentence by five months, and ordered the de- fendant to atisw her Bs. a week, and not to go near her again.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SlTllnnsy.--Mefore Alderman Burgess (in, the chair)..

Councillor Voisey, and Mr. John Geddes. AITENIL6 MECHFTS. —William Woods, aged nine years; Bennis Creaghan, aged ten; Percy Quinn, aged nine; and Thomas Ireland, nine years, were charged with stealing, on the 25th September, from the shop of Mr. William Lawiess, Market-place, two jars of jam, value Bd.„ and a pair of dumbbells, value 2s. 6d., from Mr. Joseph Garland, Bridge-street, and also two cauliflowers, value 4d., from a stall in th 3 Market-place.—Constable Bell said he went in search of the prisoners, and found them asleep in a cab.—They had in their possession a jar of marmalade, and they pleaded guilty to stealing the other articles.--Inspector Spinks said that the lads were often out at night. 'Woods and Ireland had been previously summoned 'before the magistrates.—They were each ordered to receive twelve strokes of the birch rod.—Alderman Burgesszemarked that if the offenders came before them again they would most certainly be sent to the reformatory for five years.

MONDAT.—Before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Fran- comb) and Aldermen Harrison Wright and Burgess. DRUNK AND DISORDERI.Y.—SamueI and Henry Dagnall, in Buckley-st, on Saturday night, 10s. and costs each.— John Fogg,waszharged with being drunk and disorderly in Rumball-st., the same -night. The prisoner had his head covered with a bandage. He charged one of the constables concerned in the case, P.C. 24, with kicking him in the ribs, but evidence was given that he had made no complaint of this at the police station,where had been locked up.—Detective Sergeant Monaghan said the prisoner had complained to him. Fined ss.—Wm. Roberts was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Academy-st., on Saturday night. Evidence having been given against him by the poEce, the prisoner denied the charge, but said he was annoyed at the police treating him and his wife as suspicious characters when they were talking in thestreet. He.said he did not think it was right to round on any working-man in the way they did in Warrington.—The Mayorsaid he thought perhaps the prisoner had suffered a li.tle injustice, but in Academy. St., the iron bridge, Wilderspent-road, and other places, the police had considerable treuble ; and they were sus- picious as to these places. The defendant would be dis- charged.—Mary Ann Legh, drunk and disorderly at mid- night on Saturday in Church-st, ss. and costs.—James Addison, in Battersby-lane, on Saturday night, ss. and costs.—Wm. Plinston, in Winwick-st.. on the 18th of September ss. and costs.--Wm. Glover, in Winwick-road, on the 19th of September bound over to keep the peace. —Mary Bennett, drunk and disorderly in Pitt-st., on the 21st of September, ss. and costs. DRUNIC—Frank Bueknall, drunk in Wilderspool-road, on Saturday night, ss.—Michael Day and Mary Garrity were charged with being drunk in Bank Park, en Sun- day afternoon. It was stated that•the man acted in an unseemly way in the park.—Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, town clerk, said the park was being used by all sorts of char- acters, and this must be stopped. Day was sent to jail for a month and Garrity was fined ss. and costs. IMPROPER CONDUCT.—Margaret Ann Coleman, a Welshwoman, for this offence in Wilderspool-road, on Saturday night. She was sent to jail for a month's hard labour. BREACHES OF THE PEACH.—William Parker, for being disorderly on the 19th of September in Winwick-road, was bound over to keep the peace.—Martin Fennelly, Bertram Bradbury, James Rowe, and Frederick Garnett were charged with fighting in Tanner's-lane., on the 19th of September.—P.C. 9 proved the case. He said the fighting took place near the Three Pigeons Inn. Fen- nelly was stripped and bleeding and had his shirt sleeves torn off. Rowe was actin.' like a madman, and had one of his shirt sleeves torn o"ff.—William Trino said the defendants were "arguing the point over volunteers and militiamen "in the inn. They went outside and Brad- bury and Fennelly got to fighting. Garnett never struck a blow.—Fennelly and Bradbury were bound over in £lO, and Garnett and Rowe in £5, to keep the peace for 6 months.—Annie Daley, aged 21, Irlam's-yard, a War- rington Woman, 31st appearance, and Annie Daley, of 3, Naylor-street, a native of Liverpool. were charged with fighting in Buttermarket-street, on the 21st of September. The former was bound over in the sum of £lO, and in two sureties for £lO, and the latter in £lO, to keep the peace for six months, the alternatives being imprisonment with hard labour for two months in the case of the first wonaan,and for seven days in that of the other woman. FURIOUS DRli'lNG.—John Kelly and Joseph Lewcock, cabmen, were charged with furiously driving in Cross- ley-street, on September 18th. They had each a fare at the time and were racing each other. Fined ss. includ- ing costs each. THH CARD MANIA.—Adam Cliffs and Samuel nankin- son for playing with cards for money in Factory-lane, on Saturday morning, were fined is. and costs each. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett (in the chair), E. • J. Guest, and Alderman Greenall. As INCORRIGIBLB TRUANT.—A lad, named Bate, was again before the Bench on account of his non-attendance at school. It was stated by Mr. G. Riley that the lad was under the guardianship of his brothers and sisters but they really could not control him. Councillor Shaw Green, a member of the School Attendance Committee,

was present, and asked the Bench to send the lad to the " Clio "if they possibly: could, though, he understood, there was a difficulty in the way because he had been convicted of a felony. The Bench decided to adjourn the ' case for a week in order that inquiries might be made as to whether he would be accepted on the" Clio." DRUNKENNESS AND ASSAULT.—Patrick Farrell was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Hill- st., and with assaulting his sister, Kate Farrell. He was fined ss. and costs for the drunkenness, and 10s. and costs for the assault, or three weeks' imprisonment. SOLDIERS IN TROUBLE.—Francis Roberts and Patrick McTighe, two soldiers, were charged, with having been drunk and disorderly in Sankey-st., the previous day, and Roberts was charged with having assaulted P.C. s Hollingsworth and Smith. It appeared that the defen- dants had had a quarrel with a civilian about billiards in the Nag's Head, and they had to be ejected by the policemen. Roberts, it was stated, had been particularly violent. A non-commissioned officer said the men had been in the army five years, and both had a good charac- ter. Roberts was fined 10s., and McTighe ss. DRUNKENNESS, &c.—Michael Brodrick and Martin Moore were charged with having been drunk and dis- orderly, in Dial-st., on the previous night, and also with having assaulted Elizabeth Beswick, Agnes Cloynes, and George Walsh. It appeared that Brodrick had assaulted the women named, after very little provocation, and, p when Walsh interfered, he too was struck. Brodrick was sent to gaol for a month, and Moore was fined 10s. and costs, ,or 14 days.—John Saunders and Harriet Saunders, man and wife, who sometimes sing ballads in p the streets, were sent to gaol for seven days for having been drunk and disorderly the previous night. SCHOOL CAsss.—The following person:. were summoned ler neglecting to send their children regularly to school: —Leah Briars, School-brow, three children, fined 7s. 6c1.; James Bibby, Hamilton-st., fined 2s. 6d. ; John Allen, Bewsey-road, lined 55.; James Bibby, Dannett-st., fined '2s. 6d.; Alfred Birchall, Silver-st., fined 55.; John Edwards, Dial-st., fined is.; James Gleave, two children, Cropper's-brow, fined 25.; Henry Howell, ' Bewsey-road, fined 2s. Bd.; Patrick Leonardy, Warbur- ton-st., warrant granted; John McCone, Friars'-green, fined ss. ; Mary Owen, Fennell-st., boy was sent to Father Nugent's Industrial School, Liverpool; Henry Palmer, Latchford, fined is. ; Thomas Ryder, Bewsey- road, fined2s. 6d.; Aaron Tasker, Rowe-st., fined 2s. 6d.; and Seth Travis, School-brow, fined ss. Wannssner.—Before Alderman Holmes and Councillor John Fairclough. _ _

CHARGES OF FlGHTlNG.—Sergeants Wm. Blisland and , Wilkes, of the barracks, and David Walsh,of Kerfoot-st., were charged with fighting in the Market Place, the previous night. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, Town Clerk, ap- peared for the prosecution. Mr. Browne defended Walsh, and Mr. Forshaw the sergeants. Mr. Whittle asked that Walsh, who pleaded guilty might be bound over, and that the sergeants might be handed over to the military authorities, who would deal with them.—Mr. Browne said this was an unfortunate affair arising out of a case heard there four or five months ago, which lasted seven or eight hours. it was better to let byegones be bye- gones, and he had advised his client to plead guilty, and he would ask their worships to bind him over in his own surety, he paying the eosts.—Mr. Forshaw pointed out that if his clients were handed over to the military authorities the case against them must be dismissed by that court. The three defendants were dealt with in the way suggested by the solicitors. PATINE AND Disonnipmv.:—Ann Smith alias O'Dowd, drus)r and disorderly in Bridge-street, on Tuesday after- noon, was fined ss. and costs. WIFE PESIBETION.—James Scully, 9, Lilford-street, was charged by Mr. B. Shearer, on behalf of the Board of thaar.diam with leaving his wife and four children

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 3, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 3, 1891.

chargeable to the common fund of the Union. He was sent to prison for a month's hard labour. TIIIESDAL—Bsfore Alderman Sutton (chairman), Councillor James Fairclough, and Captain Ridgway. NON-MATIMINANCIL—Thomas Healy, labourer and pen- sioner was charged by Mr. B. Shearer, on behalf of the i Guardians, with deserting his wife and seven children, on the 13th of September, and leaving them chargeable ' to the Union. Mr. Shearer said this was the third or fourth time the defendant had been prosecuted for a ' similar offence, and he always got cif through pleading , that his wife was a bad•character, which was true to a certain extent.—He offered now to allow Bs. a weak,and said the uncertainty of his work prevented him from af- fording more.—The Chairman (Alderman Sutton) : It is a strange thing when everybody is complaining that they cannot get any men to work and if they do they have to pay twice as much as usual.—Mr.Shearer said Bs. a weekonly allowed is. 2d. a day for each of his family. , —The case was adjourned to allow the defendant an op- portunity of making payment of the amount required. , ' STAMPING OUT.—lsaac Friars was charged with sleep- ing in apipe kiln at the works of Messrs. Kenyon and (Co., that morning.—The Chairman: This is your 16th appearance for almost similar offences.—Fourteen days' hard latour. Am OBJECTIONABLE Waxam.—Rosanna Finley, for im- moral conduct, the previous night, in the Market Place. This was her fifth appearance since July.—Seven days' imprisonment.—The Prisoner: That's nothing. WIFE ASSATILT.—AIfred James Brown was charged under a.warrant, with assaulting his wife Mary Ann Brown,on the 29th of September. • She said he kept her without money and food and constantly beat her. He stated that she had given him provocation by scandalis- ing him.—lnspector Spinks said that on his apprehend- ing the prisoner that morning he said "She's a good wife:; I don't know why I did it."—The prisoner: I .acknowiedge all that.—Mrs. Price-gave evidence of the ill-usage, and said the woman was a good wife to the fnan.—He now said he was very sorry, and it would never occur again ; he would become a teetotaller.—The com- plainant asked for an allowance that she might live with her children separately.—lle was anxious to make peace . with her, but she objected to live •with him again.—He agreed-to a separation, and to allow her 12s. a week ; and he was discharged on this understanding, but bound over in the sum of £2O in case of his • tact carrying out the agreement. Fame-Ir.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Alder- man Wright, and Dr.,Gornall. AN Amer Aussyraa.—William ,Falmer, was charged with deserting the Royal Artillery at Dover, on Septem- ber 26th. He was remanded to Strangoways jail to await an,eacort. DatTNI AND DISORDBRLY.—Patrick Tivnan was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street, on Thursday night, also with assaulting P.C. Smith on the same occasion. Smith in proving the charges said the prisoner threw him down by getting his head between his legs, and kicked him. He had to chase the prisoner some distance.—Fined 10s. and costs; 14s. 6d. in all ; in default 14 days. NOE-MAINTENANCE OP SONS.—Michael Connor was charged by-Inspector James, with non-contribution for the maintenance of his son in St. Anne's industrial school. He was ordered to contribute is. a week. A similar order was madcagainst Moses Williams as to each of two boys Jacob and John Williams in the same school. CRUELTY TO a HORS.—George Dodd was charged by Inspector Dowty, S.P.C.A., with cruelty to a horseby working it while in an unfit state on the 18th of Septem- ber, in Chester-road, Latchford.—lnspector Dowty and Mr. Smith, veterinary surgeon, proved the case. The horse was attached to a spring cart and lame and suffer- ing from ringbone and strained tendons. He was fined 103. and costs, Ll lls, in all.—Job Wardle, 48 Sharpe-st., was similarly charged as to a horse which lie had worked in aa unfit state in Wilson Patten-et., on the 26th of September.—lnspector Dowty proved that the horse was lame. 10s. and costs, 16s. in all.
DIRESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.?
TIIIISDAY.—Before Messrs. J. C. Parr (chairman) and H. Neild.

JunT LISTS.—The assistant overseers presented the lists, of persons qualified to serve on special juries ; and these were accepted with the striking out of a one or two names on account of disqualification. DRUNK.—John Dobson, at Appleton on the 30th of August ; ss. including costs.—John Bennett, at Lower Walton, on the 13th of September, 103. including costs. —Darby Mee and James Keadinan at Moore, On the 13th September, ss. each including ,costs.—Samuel Littler, at Seven Oaks, on the 28th of July,ss. including Costs. DRUNK AID DISORDERLY.—John Wilkinson, at Little Leigh, on the 23rd of August, 103. including costa.— Thos. Hart, at Appleton,on the 30th of August, 103. and costs.—James Hamblett, at Appleton, on the 15th of September, 53. including costs.—Benjamin Whittaker, at Preston-o'-th'-Hill, on the 15th of August, 53. includ- ing costs. Does AT LARGII.—Eaton Bretherton, at Newton, on August 26th, and Jacob Millington, on the 2nd of Sept., at Seven Oaks, to pay 3s. ed. costs each. • OFFIINCHS BY DRIVERS.—John Smith, asleep in charge of a dray and two horses at Moore, on the 22nd of Aug., 53. and costs.—James Toole,ll,Foundry-st.,Warrington, was charged with using a cart, at Seven Oaks, on Sept. , 3rd,without having his name painted thereon. The con- stable proving the case said the defendant told him the cart had passed at Warrington and at Nnrthwich, and surely would pass a country bloke like him. ss. and costs.—John Egan, labourer, Latchford, and Hy. Hayes, for driving without reins,the former on the 13th of Sept., at Grappenhall, and the latter at Daresbury, on the 19th , of September, were each fined 55., including costs. NIGHT CYCLING WITFIOI7T LAMPLIGHT.—WiIfred Whit- ley was charged with riding a bicycle at Walton, at mid- night,on September 12th,without having a lighted lamp. , The defence was that he lit the lamp, but there was a fault in it and the oil can fell out. The Bench accepted this excuse, and discharged the defendant. CnueLTT To A Houss.—Joseph Marshall, of Runcorn, was charged with cruelly torturing a horse at Walton Superior, on September 10th, by working it while in an unfit state. He pleaded not guilty. Inspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., proved the case. He said the horse was drawing a barge along the canal, loaded with 49 tons of timber. The animal was in poor condition and had two wounds the size of a shilling on the back and one the size of a two-shilling piece on the shoulder. The harness was rubbing on the wounds. 10s., including costs. Several cases were adjourned in consequence of two constables who have to appear in them having been seriously assaulted by poachers.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. James Handley. THS JURY LISTS for the various townships in the Petty Sessional division were submitted and signed. DRUNKENNIISS.—For this offence a fine of ss. was im- posed upon Henry Jones and John Sefton Ball. MAINTRNANCH OF A. FATHRIL—John Massey, a boatman, was summoned to show cause why he should not con- tribute towards the support of his father, Robert Massey, who was a poor person unable to work, and chargeable to the common fund of Runcorn Union. Mr. Frocisham, collector to the Guardians, said the old man received 3s. per week from the union. He had four sons, three of whom contributed to his support, and the Guardians asked for Bd.per week,which he was willing to pay. An order was made accordingly, together with 133., 6d. the costs of the order. FIRRWORKII IN MR STRERT.—Arthur Wilkinson, Law- rence Peacock, Walter Leyland, Roland Hughes,and Wm. Whitby, boys, pleaded guilty to discharging fireworks in the streets, and were each ordered to pay a fine of 55., and cautioned. SHOP DOOR ROBRERY.—A boatman named Thomas Richards, of Manchester, was brought up on remand, charged with having on the 18th September, stolen from the shop door of Messrs. Robertson and Son, Bridge-st., a coat, worth 20s. The circumstances were reported last week. The police had made full inquiries into his pre- vious character, and had found nothing previously re- corded against him. He was fined 205.0 r 14 days' impri- sonment. SCHOOL BOARD PROSIICUTIONS.—The School Board had summoned 36 parents for not sending their children re- gularly to school. Four summonses had not been served; the remainder of the defendants were each fined 55., in- cluding costs. Mr. Bowyer, attendance officer, proved the whole of cases, and said nearly the whole of the chil- dren in question received free schooling, but they had attended very much worse than formerly since they had had free education.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

*** Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

div.head: RUGBY.
div.p: RUGBY.

WARRINGTON 2ND WIDNES RINGHRS.—This match was played at Widnes, and resulted in a win for the visitors. For the winners Warburton played a very good game, as he dropped the goal and scored the try. Result :-2nd, 2 goals, 2 minors; Rangers, 2 tries, 1 minor. WARRINGTON ST. MART'S T. RUNCORN TRIM BLUES. Played at Runcorn on Saturday. The home team started against the wind and up hill, and the visitors soon had a lead of two goals, Longraore and Woods scoring, Hels- by placing the goals. In the second half the homesters had slightly the best of it., Forster and Spencer crossing the line, but Darlington only landed one goal. Final score .:—St. Mary's, 2 goals, 4 minors; Runcorn 'True Blues, 1 gool, 1 try, 2 minors. Weness v.SALFORD " Tessms.—This match was I played on Saturday on the Widnes ground, before a very poor number of spectators. It proved a very one-sided game all through, the home team being unable to score a single point. If the Widnesians had combined a little more, and played a better passing game, they would have fared better, but as it was, it was decidedly poor play thrcraghout. At the end of the game the visitors were declared victors by 1 goal, 3 tries, and 2 minors to nil. Reseconie " A." T. STOCKPORT " A".—This match was played at Runcorn on Saturday. Burrows started the game, the kick being charged. Play located in the centae, May being prominent in some tall punting. Play was keen in the Stockport half, when Webbe passed to Antrabus, who scored, and afterwards kicked the goal. Soon after the re-start Webbe very smartly dropped a fine goal. Play for a time was extremely fast. Ashton made a run let° the home quarters, May, by huge kick- ing causing play in the Stockport half. \With a strong effort by Stockport, Gibson scored. Score at half-time:: Runcorn "A," 2 goals; Stockport, 1 try. After the interval, Webbe scored easily. Final result—Runcern, 2 goals, 1 try ; Stockport "A," 1 try. FRODSHAIE v. Rurecome RECRICATION.—This match was played at Frodsham, on Saturday. The home team won the toss, and elected to play up the slope. Runcorn kieked off, Darlington making a good return. From a pack in midfield Johnson got hold and passed wide to Speakman, who ran and kicked well into the home quarters. By some good forvard play, in which W. Rogers, T. Brown, and F. Darlington were conspicuous, the danger was removed. Play continued even till half time, neither side having scored. On the re-start, after some wood kicking on the part of Parker and Johnson, F. Darlington secured, and, making a good run, scored try. T. Darlington just failing at the place. T. Rogers then dropped a goal. Frodshana was having much the best of the play, the Recreation not being able to stay, and after some loose play near the visitors' line,T. Rogers scored a try, the same player landing a goal from the place. At the call ef time the score stood—Frodsham, 2 goals (1 dropped) 1 try to nothing. Parker, Peacock, T. Darlington, T. Rogers, and F. Darlington, played a good game for the home side, as did Speakman, Williamson, Johnson, and Carr for the Recreation. STOCKTON HEATH •. ASPULL ALBION.—The Blue and Whites opened their season on Saturday with the Albion. The Aspullites arrived late, and it was quite 5 o'cloek when Bullen effected a start for the visitors. Glover smartly returning to the half-way flag, where play re- mained for a while until the visitors broke away to the home line, Cross just saving in time. From a scrimm- age, however, however. Dickenson got possession and passed to Shepherd, who dropped a neat goal. On re- starting the home team looked up, and Broady, after a good run, took play to the visitors' lines, where from some fine passing between the home backs Glover almost scored, missing a very easy chance. Sheppard,however, relieved by a timely punt, but Lawless obtained posses- sion, and after dodging several opponents took a drop, which nearly had the effect, a minor resulting. At half- time the score stood—Aspull 1 dropped goal. Stocktow Reath 2 minors. In the second half the home team soon began to press. From aome'neat passing Grounds scored under the posts, no goal resulting. Play now settled at half way, but Rathbone again got possession, and after a splendid run transferred the ball to Lawless, who raced over the line in grand style, Hallows making a good bid for goal. Soon after the drop-out Grounds took a drop at goal, but without success. The home team had now hard fines, but could not score the winning _point, and the game ended in a draw of 4 points each. WARRINGTON A v. BROUGHTON RANGERS A.—The usual crowd bad assembled on Saturday to see these oppon- ents, when the Ranges commenced hostilities against a strong wind which prevailed. Notwithstanding this drawback, the Ranges' forwards early demonstrated their dribbling abilities, and taking advantage of the slipshod attempts of the home team, Farnell crossed the line. This early reverse somewhat aroused the lethargy of the Warrington men, Knowles, Bailey, Russell, and Warburton transferring the game to more desirable quarters. Lawless improved the situation, and succeed- ing a combined rush of the forwards, Barnes equalized tram a line-out. Following the drop-out, Warburton almost dropped a goal. a•minor accruing. After Russell, Molyneaux, Rowlands, and Davies had been prominent, the visiting forwards, headed by Newell and Shore, came away with a good cross dribble right into Warrington , quarters' but were quickly repulsed by Heesom's fine kick. A series of fine kicks were made by the backs on both sides, and ended in Lawless flooring Robinson under the posts, a minor being the result. The ensuing play was not of a very exhilarating nature, and one of the visiting forwards was hurt, and had to retire. Proceed- ing in the same uninteresting fashion, a bad mistake found the Broughton team maintaining a strong and vigorous attack, the play of the homesters being weak, and the result was that Clayton passing quickly to Kennedy, the last-named dropped a very smart goal. Immediately after the kick-out the visitors were penalized, and the situation was ominous from a Rangers' point of view. After some pretty passing between Antrobus, Lawless,and Heesom, like most other attempts, the finishing touch was bungled, the conse- quence being that Shaughnessy and Dalton, taking full advantage of it, caused the defence of the homesters to be heavily taxed. Sampson and Plinston came to the rescue by some kicking, but the usual minors followed. Then Bailey, Molyneaux, and Barnes indulged in a bit of passing, but a splendid bout of a similar nature by Lawless, Antrobus, Heesom, and Plinston found the latter making a good bid for a try, only to be pushed touch in goal. Another foolish pass again found Brough- ton in the ascendant, and although penalized for off-side, Dalton, in double quick time, dribbled back. Heesom's smartness was here noticeable, but nothing of note was obtained before half-time. The brief rest had an inspiring influence for good on the home team, ' for they began to attack with such resolute vigour, a vast contrast to the initial halff that it was ultimately rewarded with success. Once Samp- son was called upon, and replied splendidly, and Law- less's pass to Heesom nearly resulted in a try. There were a tight five minutes on the visitors' lines, and the result of a series of passes by Lawless, Antrobus, and Plinston, was the addition of another try. Still War. rington, by the aid of Teare and Davies, kept up the pressure, and Molyneaux obtaining possession ran to the line, and passed to Teare, who also scored. Like the other attempts, the place failed. Succeeding the drop out, Heesom obliged with a fine bit of play, and the strenuous exertions of Davies and Barnes forced the ball in dangerous proximity to their antagonists' goal where a grand display of passing between Lawless,Antro- bus, and Heesom gave Plinston a chance of distinguish- ing himself; and a second try to his credit was recorded. Then the Rangers dashed away to half way, but Knowles, Teare, and Russell retaliated. A wild pass lost any advantage gained, untilßowlands came through and passed. Barnes, who was playing splendidly, was con- spicuous, as was Rowlands, by a strong rush. Any im- pending danger was averted, and while play was wag- ing in neutral territory, Plinston seized the leather, and ran capitally to the line. A minute later, Antrobus got possession, and, outwitting his opponents obtained a splendid try, Sampson placing a goal. Warrington took matters easily after this, and nothing of any consequence was scored. Warrington 1-4-7 to 1.1-2. SALFORD v. WIDNES. -

_ Played on the ground of the former. In spite of the counter-attraction at the racecourse, fully 3,000 assembled round the rails. A stiff breeze was blowing across the field. Barrett, for the Salford men kicked off Hartles returning into touch at the half-way flag. From the throw in a scrimmage followed, and the Widnes men with a rush neared the home line and forcedMainwaring to touch down. The Reds now worked their way up the field, but Hartles returned with a good kick to centre. Several packs were' now formed. Finally play was carried close to the line, but the home forwards came away with a fast dribble, with Knowles and Roberts tak- ing the leal. Hartles, however, again returned with a capital kick after a short run. Kent was next conspicu- ous, and with the ball at his toes made a capital dribble down centre, and carried play close to the Widnes line, but failed to get over. The game was now veryexciting, and Sudlow made a capital run, and then passed to Roberts, who gained a try amidst loud cheering. Walsh took the place kick, but failed. Nicholas had hard lines shortly after, being brought down on the line. Half- time score :—Salford, one try, one minor (or two points) ; Widnes, one minor. On changing ends the visitors started, and immediately after Barber gained a try. The same player took the chance of goal, but the kick was charged down. This reverse roused the Reds, who carried play within their opponents' 25, but a fast dribble by the Widnes for- wards soon transferred matters. The game at this point had to be delayed for a short time, Walsh receiving an ugly knock on the head. On restarting Peters broke away, and, after beating Sudlow, grounded a second try for the visitors, Barber taking a difficult position for the conversion, and failing. Farmer was next on the list for scoring, and after a neat run, grounded the leather over the line, Barber failing at goal. After a well-fought game, Widnes proved the winners. Final score: Widnes three tries one minor ; Salford, one try one minor. Teams: —Salford: Mainwaring, back ; Miles, Barrett, and Sud- low, three-quarter backs; Walsh and Franee, half backs Eagles. Kent, Robert's, King,Casey, Makin, Knowles, and Nicholas, forwards. Whines: Hartles, back ; Brennan
(captain), Peters, and Barber, three-quarter backs; Mullinger and Drummond, half backs ; Whelan, Holmes, Parmer,Emery, Johnson, Gordon, Hardman, Lyons, and Ridgeway, forwards.

div.head: CONSECRATION OF BISHOPS.
div.p: CONSECRATION OF BISHOPS.

The following Bishops were consecrated at St. Paul's Cathedral, on Tuesday :—Dr. Gott, Dean of Worcester, as Bishop of Truro; Rev. and Hon. Augustus Legge, as Bishop of Lichfield; Rev. H. B. Boulby, as Bishop Suf- fragan of Coventry; Rev. H. W. Yeatman as Bishop Suffragan of Southwark; and Rev. W. M. Carter, as Bishop of Zululand. The procession of Bishops elect was headed by the Archbishop of Canterbury, who conducted the service. The cathedral was crowded.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE IN SCOTLAND.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE IN SCOTLAND.

Mr. Gladstone attended communion in the chapel of Trinity College, Glenalmand, on Thursday morning, and afterwards breakfasted with Lord Lothian and other distinguished guests. The right hon. gentleman looks well, having been very much braced up by the highland air. A large number of visitors from Perth and the neighbourhood arrived to witness the laying of the foundation stone of the new wing of the college. About noon, a company gathered in front of the new wing of the college, where Mr. Gladstone laid the found- ation stone, at the same time repeating a prayer that the true faith might flourish there, and that the place might be set apart for instruction in the doctrine of Christ. Anode was then sung, and luncheon followed.
The Liverpool steamer City of Lincoln reached Dun- de on Tuesday with cattle, having lost over a hundred of the animals during a series of heavy gales in the Atlantic.

div.head: WIGAN Y. RUNCORN.
div.p: WIGAN Y. RUNCORN.

- - The fact of two champions being in the field together was sufficient inducement for a crowd above ordinary dimensions assembling at the Wigan ground on Saturday afternoon. The match has been awaited with interest since the opening of the present campaign, and there would be over 6,000 present when Faulkner kicked off against a stiff breeze. The Wiganers had the assistance of Roberts, of Aspull, and though this player was fore- most in bringing relief to the Wigan lines from the start, the useful combination of Crompton., Davies, Evans, and Abrams frustrated all the efforts of the burly Wigan forwards to invade. Eventually the homesters got the better of a series of hotly-contested scrimmages, and Runcorn experienced an anxious time of it. Davies however, relieved splendidly, and although Anderton soon regained the lost ground, Houghton's reputation as being the best back in Cheshire remained untarnished when he snapped up the oval from the feet of his oppon- ents, and piloted it well beyond the half way flag. Roberts frustrated an attack for a moment, but, not to be denied, the visiting backs got the oval working in a skilful manner. Abrams was the first away, and after passing to Faulkner, the latter transferred to Hampson, who in turn handed over to Davies,and the latter, being soon in his stride, eluded Anderton and Halliwell, wind- ing up a brilliant effort by scoring the first major. Faulkner failed at tl e place. Wigan now adopted the !Runcorn men's system of play, at least for a time, and a neat display of passing by Hatton, Mitchinson, Wardle and Seddon was the means of Runcorn defending. A "thence was presented to Anderton, who ran and passed to Halliwell, for the last-named to throw wide to Roberts the Aspull captain finishing up by making the scores equal. Wigan, aided by the elements, had a trifle the best of it; but Houghton, Crompton, and Davies were in fine form, and repeatedly staved off many attempts to score. A minor fell to Wigan's credit near the inter- val, and the scores read at half time as Wigan, 0-1-1 ; Ruacorn, 0-1-0. Resuming, the Cheshire men soon at- tacked, but the Wigan forwards, using their strength to .advantage, confined the game to the forward depart- ment. The tackling was a trifle vigorous, but what 'Runcorn lacked in strength was made up by the skilful movements of their backs. Seddon was finely tackled .by Hughes, when bent on scoring, and from this point Wigan were played out. Crompton effected a fine run and pass to Davies, and this smart three-quarter was equal to the task imposed on him, scoring in a favourable position for Crompton to kick a goal. This was the last interesting item of a fine game, and when the teams re- tired the scores read as Runcorn one goal and a try (seven points) to Wigan a try (two points). It was certainly no runaway game, and the comparison of the two teams was indeed remarkable. On the one hand Runcorn relied on those skilful tactics which have long been associated with their name, whilst on behalf of Wigan, they used their strength to no small purpose. Evidently it was Wigan's intention to break up the Run- corn combination by sheer strength, but the result serves to prove that science will always prevail in the end. Evans and Abrams were very energetic behind the scrim- mage, whilst Crompton still plays that fine clear game which has long been his forte. Davies further enhanced his reputation as being one of Cheshire's best three- quarters by playing a wonderful game,both his tries being brilliant efforts. Houghton got through a vast amount of work in creditable style, his kicking being one of the features of the match. Faulkner, Hampson, and Riley were the pick of a capital set of forwards. Teams : Wigan; J. Halliwell, back; J. Anderton, R. Seddon, and 3. Roberts, three-quarters; W. Halliwell aqd J. Mitchin- son, half-backs.; W. Atkinson, E. Bullough, J. Lowe, J. Dannelly, J. Hatton, R. Seddon, E. F. Wardle, E. Demp- sey, and M. Macnamara, forwards. Runcorn : S. Houghton, back ;T. H. Davies, J. H. Crompton, and G. Pendlebury, three-quarters; W. Evans, and S. Abrams, half backs; W. Faulkner, P. Riley, R. Dolan, A. Hamp- son, W. Shaw, H. Williams, 0. Hughes, D. Massey, and R. Reece, forwards; referee, Mr. Cattell, Sheffield.

div.head: WARRINGTON Y. LEIGH.
div.p: WARRINGTON Y. LEIGH.

The keen rivalrr:which exists between the above clubs was fully manifested on Monday evening, when the teams met at the Wilderspool enclosure. There would be fully four thousand present when the game was com- menced. Leigh lacked the services of Coop, their full back, but had drafted into the team Cross (Lancashire County), Anderton (Aspull). Bell (Kendal Hornets), and Bancroft (Tottington). Nevins started towards the pavi lion goal, and the game opened in vigorous style. Evans- prompt return was spoiled by the off-side play of Gra- ham, and Leigh at the onset were compelled to defend. A series of passes between Smith and Anderton took play to neutral ground, but Boscow with a judicious kick drove the Leighites back. Sharp passing by the home forwards was loudly applauded, and Turner and Jolley were prominent in an effort near the line. A wild pass to Lawless served as relief, and the visitors gained further ground by short forward rushes. Another com- bined movement, in which the two Bates were the shin- ing lights, again saw the homesters attacking vigor- ously, and a free kick by Lawless was well met by Smith. Severe tackling was the order, and several I.nintfrlsngb'emthent".te Barilteal'eerlSefeWrleree t r leedd Croup .fo,r, athnids knocked unluckily on when all opposition had been cleared, and although :Anderton got the oval away to Boscow, the home custodian, aided by some smart tactics by Evans, Lawless Nevins, and Bate, , again pressed Leigh back on the line. The play was generally confined to this quarter, and a fine exhibition , in the art of passing by both sides was duly applauded. Buckley dribbled well, and J. Bate again cleared the , opposing half backs, passing to Donohue, who was held ' a yard from the line. No sooner had the ball been scrimmaged, than Evans received possession,and passing to Lawless, the latter dropped a clever goal amidst a hurricane of applause. The cheers had hardly subsided before Warrington were penalized on the Leigh lines,and Smith taking the kick in judiciously punted to Evans, who coolly awaited the oval, with a result that a well judged drop registered a second goal. The second half was all in favour of the homesters, for after Cross had dribbled to the home lines,the Warringtonians completely routed the Leigh defence. The Warrington half backs played a wonderful game, and certainly were the nseans of their side having so much the best of it. Jolley led off with an unimproved try whilst Turner landed a penalty goal. Near the close the play was of a rough description, and the only item worth recording was a clever try by Lawless, which Webster failed to im- prove. Final score—Warrington 3-2--1 (15 points) to nil.

div.head: WARRINGTON V, BROUGHTON RANGERS.
div.p: WARRINGTON V, BROUGHTON RANGERS.

_ The Warringtonians were again in fine form on Satur- day, when they journeyed te Broughton, and adminis- tered defeat to the Rangers of that district. The smart display of the Manchester team against Wigan the week previous lent additional interest to the match, and the Broughton supporters were sanguine that their team had at last reached a level whereby they could administer to Warrington their first defeat. True it is that Warring ton have been a bit too clever for the Broughton men in the list of their engagements, which extends over a period of six years, but the chance of the result being r eversed were certainly not remote when it was found that Barnes, James Bate, and Nevins were absent from the visiting side. . .

The oval was set in motion by Ashton, against a strong wind, and play opened of a fast nature. Lally, a mini- ature half back, was the first to become prominent, Buck staying his progress when he reached the quarter flag. Evans and Turner assisted Warrington in their aggressive tactics, and although Boscow was called upon to respond to a kick by Wardley, the visitors still con- tinued to press. Daniels foiled a movement of Fleet and Deakin, but eventually Wardley and Jackson cleared the danger' and play was now at half way. A couple ot free kicks fell to the credit of Lawless, but the War rington forwards packed in a half-hearted sort of man nor, and Broughton utilizing this advantage, repeatedly" cleared their lines with ease. Jackson and Medley dribbled well, and Wall passing finely to Fleet, the home- sters now pressed vigorously. Daniels and Ashton headed the visitors in taking the oval to the half way, and eventually Fleet dropped at goal, Boscow saving immediately after, from a free kick, taken by Jackson. Chapman met the drop out in fine style, but Jolley was more than a match for several of his opponents and got clear at last, being pulled up when he had taken the ball beyond the halt way flag. Bate and Lally passed pret- tily across the pack, the latter's essay to Lawless being a trifle forward. Boscow and Evans in turn exchanged kicks with Fleet and Wardley, and then Holmes, Turner, Donohue, and Buckley were foremost in a long dribble, which had the result of the Rangers defending. Their forwards were equal to the task set them,and more than counterbalanced the last effort, for Hamilton and Storer rushed down the field at a rapid pace,the former exper- iencing hard lines in not having a major point placed to his credit. Chapman had a shot at goal,which recorded a second minor. Evans and Randles now joined in a combined movement, the latter kicking and tack ling Fleet in smart style. Boscow was applauded for a couple of judicious kicks, and although Jackson had an opening presented him, he was soon floored by Jolley. Some fine passing, initiated by Thornley, was followed by Evans and Lally passing well, Buckley almost scoring. With the aid of a strong rush, War- rington forced a minor, and the interval arrived with the score two minors to one. After the usual breathing space, Jackson re-started, and although Lally and Evans dribbled through l the opposing backs, the home forwards upset calculations, when they rushed down the field, compelling the visitors to adopt the de- fensive. For fully ten minutes was the attack kept up, Boscow, Evans, and Lawless having all their work cut out to prevei* their goal froni being lowered. Eventually Daniels tackled Deakin near the home quarter flag, and Warrington were within easy reach of the Rangers' goal. Wardley came to the rescue, and a kick and tackle by Evans eased the pressure. Lally, Bate, and Evans passed well, but it was to no purpose, little headway being made. A similar result awaited Lawless on his receiving

the oval from Turner, Chapman tackling the three- r quarter in fine style. The Warrington forwards were playing better together now, and some fine passing by Bate, Evans, and Lawless saw the latter being pushed Into touch at the corner flag. Daniels was pulled up the next minute under the posts, whilst Jolley had an ap- parently fair try disallowed a moment later. The attack I was still kept up, and Turner had a shot at goal from a penalty kick, a minor resulting. About five minutes from the call of time, Warrington assorted their superiority in a marked manner, and the oval was kept continually on the home lines. Turner had at last a chance, and making every use ot it, he pushed aside Fleet, struggling over the line with two players clinging to him. Ashton took the place, the oval going outside. Soon after" no-side" was called, the final result being Warrington, 0-1-2 ; Broughton Rangers 0-0-2. Teams :—Warrington Boscow, full-back; Lawless, Evans, and Daniels, three-quarter backs; J. T. Bate and Lally, half-backs: H. Ashton (captain), Fair Turner, Randles, Jolley, Dillon. Buckley, Holmes, Thornley, Donohue, forwards. Broughton Rangers Wardley, back; Chapman, Fleet, and Deakin, three-quarter backs; Wall and Buck, half-backs: J. Jackson, Fitton, M'Growan, Medley, Wheeler, Oman, Hamilton, Thomas, and Storer, forwards.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

WLERINGTON ASSOCEATION v. PRESCOT SWIFTS.—These teams met at Warrington in very windy weather. The home captain wen the toss, and Prescot started uphill and against the wind. Ball and Norman, getting posses- sion, made a pretty run down the right, and from the centre Warrington had hard lines, the ball striking the post and rebounding into play; and for the whole of this half Warrington experienced hard lines, as several shots hit and skimmed the posts and bar, and were very un- lucky not to score on three or four occasions. Half-time arrived with no goals scored. Warrington started the second half. The visitors soon got the ball, and Scott gave Jones a warm handful to deal with, and he cleared splendidly, and Phillip gave the ball to Norman, who passed to Ball, and he screwed across the goal mouth. The shot from the left wing struck the post and saved Prescot all further anxiety from this to the end of the game. Prescot had the best of the play, but were a long time before they could get the ball past Jones, who was playing splendidly. At last they scored from a well- placed corner, and a second followed from a penalty kick. Final score : Prescot Swifts 3 goals to nil. The Warrington backs played a good game, and Jones saved his charge in a marvellous manner on many occa- sions.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
THIIRSDAY.—Before_ his Honour, Judge Ffoulkes.
THE CAUSE LIST included 10 default summonses, 266 original plaints, and 59 original judgment sum- monses.

A DISPITTHD CONTRACT. —Thomas Waring, a house decorator, living at Earlestown, sued Jacob Lane, Park- road, Newton, for £3 11s. for work done at some cot- tages owned by the defendant. Plaintiff stated that he was engaged by the defendant to paint, paper and plas- ter a cottage in Crew-lane, Earlestown. The work was done by a man, in the employ of a Mr. Hardman, who had been temporarily engaged by the plaintiff. After the work had been finished the man went to two other cottages the interiors of which he renovated. Mr. P. Davies, of Warrington, who appeared for the defendant, said that his client never ordered the plaintiff to do any- thing except paint and paper cne cottage. The defend- ant had paid £1 lls, into court which,it was submitted, fully covered his liability. His Honour said that the whole question was one as to the contract between the parties. So far as the evidence went it showed that £1 11s. was the amount agreed upon for the first cottage, and with regard to the other two the plaintiff appeared to have nothing to do with them. The amount paid into Court seemed to be sufficient, and he therefore gave a verdict for the defendant. CLAIM BY FURNITURB DICALERS.—Messrs. A. and D. Cohen, furniture dealers Rylands-st., Warrington, sued Mrs. Elizabeth Gleave, of Scotland-road, for £7 the price of goods supplied. Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the plaintiffs, and Mr. A. Browne defended. It appeared that, along with other goods, the plaintiffs had supplied Mrs. Gleave with a bedstead value £6 45.. and for this bedstead the defendant objected to pay on the ground that it had not been ordered. It had, however, been ' sent by the plaintiffs and was taken into the house by , the defendant's daughter when defendant was away at St. Helens. She admitted that the bed was slept on the first night that it was in the house,and she added that it , broke down the first time it was used. It was also admit- ted that a balance of 16s. 6d. was owing to plaintiff for other articles and this sum had been paid into court. 'His Honour Observed that the bed was sent to the defen- dant, she had an opportunity of judging it, and it was used and broken when used. That being so defendant most pay for it. He, therefore, gave a verdict for the plaintiffs, but deducted Bs. from the £7, this being a sum for which the defendant had got a receipt but for which it appeared the piaintiffs had not allowed in their claim.

.... A BAD SYSTEM.—Mr. Gough, furniture dealer, Win- wick-road, sued George Ballingsley, labourer for £1 16s. money owing under a hiring agreement for furniture. Defendant, it appeared, purchased some goods from Mr. Gough in 1889, the cost of which was £3 Bs. As it was UgFeed. to pay-, under the hire system, is. 6d. a week,the price, it was alleged, had been raised considerably. £1 12s. had been paid, and Mr. Gough said he was willing to accept the balance of the £3 Bs. His Honour said that system of getting more money than the goods were worth was a contemptible one, and he had condemned the system in that and other courts. It was a system that deserved to be exposed. Judgment was given against the defendant for £1 16s.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

Ibis stated that the smallpox epidemic in Leeds, so far from abating, shows signs of increasing. A railway collision has occurred at Kent, Ohio, re- sulting in five deaths, and the injury of thirty persons. A rich old lady named Bourdilleau has been murdered presumably by robbers, at Chasseigne, seven kilometres from Loudun.
A persistent rumour prevails in Bombay that Captain Younghusband has been killed by Russians in the Pamir country. _ _
- -Mr. John Morley, M.P., has promised to visit tho Manchester Reform Club on the 26th October, and deliver an address to the members.
A telegram from Deland, Florida, describes the lynch- ing of a negro named Lee Bailey, who has been arrested for perpetrating an outrage on the wife of a leading white citizen. _

The fire which broke out on the Peninsular and Oriental steamer Rome, at Greenock, on Sunday,burned till Monday afternoon, and the damage is estimated at £20,000. At West Houghton, near Bolton, on Tuesday, a boy, four years old, set fire to a haystack, and before the flames could be subdued, six stacks and a barn were destroyed. A special telegram to the "New York World " from Dakota is responsible for the statement that "John S. Sinclair, heir to the earldom of Caithness, has been found in that district." M. Medina, minister representing Guatemala in Paris. says he believes the reported riot and the killing of five hundred people to be pure invention on the part of unscrupulous American newspapers. , The Welsh Theological College at Bala, which has been enlarged and extended, was opened on Tuesday morning lunder the principalship of the Rev. T. C. Edwards, late principal of the University College of Wales. ' A terific gas explosion on Monday evening in the pro- vision stores of Mr. J. W. Schofield, Bridge-st., Bolton. Three assistants who were in the shop at the time es- caped injury, although extensive damage was done to the premises. Corporal Macdonald, of the Chatham garrison police, committed suicide on Monday by shooting himself, and almost simultaneously a recruiting sergeant named Ryan , cut his throat at Chatham Casualty lioipital and lies in a critical condition. A Hallandale, Mississippi, telegram to the "New York World " describes the murder of a barkeeper named Charles S. Davies, on Sunday night, by a coloured man and woman, who were shortly afterwards lynched by the infuriated populace. Owing to the strong public feeling in Berlin against the new Russian loan, the Berlin bankers, Messrs. Mendelssohn and Warschauer, have withdrawn from all participation in it. In Paris the enthusiasm on behalf of the loan continues unbonnded. Intelligence has been received in Derby of the alleged suicide in New Zealand of Edward Whalley Prestman, the successful claimant to £60,000 in the famous Whalley will case, after squandering the entire fortune on the turf and in Stock Exchange gambling. On Thursday morning, Richard Baxter, engine driver, found the body of a man lying on the railway under the Vicars-bridge, Preston Station. The body was lying in the four-foot and the head in the six-foot. The deceased has been identified as Christopher Alston, of Grimsargh, and it is supposed he wandered down the line on return- ing from the Blackpool Bowling Sweepstakes. The " Times " understands that Mr. James William Lowther, M.P. for Mid-Cumberland, will be Sir James Fergusson's successor as Parliamentary Under l Secretary for Foreign Affairs. Mr.Lowther is the eldest son of the Hon. Wm. Low ther, who is also a member of Parliament, representing Westmorland, Appleby division, and who has been in the diplomatic service. He entered Parliament in 1883, sitting for Rutland from August in that year to November, 1885.

div.head: ATHLETICS.
div.p: ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

The Rugby clubs in Yorkshire are already in full prac- tice. Bradford appear to be formidable as usual, but Wakefield Trinity are doing badly. They were com- pletely slaughtered by Batley, who ran up n 4 fewer tha.n. 20 points to nothing, Some of the Yorkshire players are anything but gentle on the field, despite the fact that at almost every sitting of the Union there are suspen- sions for foul play. In the game between Hull and Huddersfield one of the latter was ordered off the ground for fighting.

Of the Alliance members none stand such a chance of the championship as Notts Forest. They have now a. splendid team, as is evident from their record of four victories in which they scored 19 goals to two. Titer were at Glasgow on Saturday, where they defeated Queen's Park by three goals to one. The Lancashin- League honours appear to lie between Blackpool and Bury, both of who.n are playing smart football.

It is sometimes said that without Valentine the Swin— ton club is not much to speak of, and judging from the match with Oldham on Saturday there seems to be something in this, Oldham beating the SwintonianB on their own ground by a try to nothing. But, it slAuld be. noted that besides Valentine, Swinton had two or three other best players away. Oldham are particularly strong in their back division, and on Saturday their forwards held their own mum better than they usually do, hence- the result.

Widnes men seem to boa in high form this season, and on Saturday they humiliated the crack, or perhaps it would be better to say the once-upon-a-time crack, Sal- ford team. Widnes forwards were always famous for- vigorous scrimmaging, and not over gentle tackling, but this season it is said they go in for fine open play, in fact just such as spectators like. Warringtonians will have a chance this afternoon of seeing the" chemicals" perform on the Wilderspool ground, and there is one thing it is safe tor.predict--tbere will be a big crowd.

Warrington have added two more victories to their list. On Saturday Broughton Rangers gave them a tough game on the Broughton ground, and the winning point was only registered near the close of time. The- " wirepullers" seemed to take things rather easy at first, and it was only by a spell of hard play that they preuented a draw. On Monday they made up for any lukewarnmess at Broughton by rubbing it into Leigh. The Leigh team, helped as they were by powerful auxi- lihries from St. Helens and Dukinfield, appeared deter- mined to win, and they seemed seriously crestfallen when Lawless and Evans smartly dropped a couple of goals within two or three minutes of each other. This was enough to take the exuberance out of any team, but it is only fair to Leigh to say that they played pluckily to the finish. But it was all to no purpose. for the homesters added point to point without allowing a single mark to be scored against them.

After quite a model colonial tour in South Africa, the Rugby Football Team have returned to England; they landed on Monday at Plymouth from the Garth Castle. The team left this country in July last, and during the cool season in the southern clime they have played nine- teen matches, witnessed by no fewer than 75,000 per- sons. If there be one drawback to their tour, it is to be found in the monotony of success: for they won every one of the nineteen matches in which they•were engaged, having scored a total of 22's points, while the sole point credited to the Colonials was a solitary "try." In all some £7,500 was taken as gate money. Everywhere the Rugby players were received with enthusiasm, and at Kimberley the day of the match was observed as a general holiday. Before the men sailed for England a grand ball was given in their honour at Cape Town, and on the morning of departure a luncheon on board the Garth Castle was attended by the Hon. Cecil Rhodes, the Hon. ,T. F. Hofmeyer, Sir Thomas Upington, and other distinguished personages. Specially careful precautions were taken to prevent the tour becoming in any shaps or form a professional one, and all its expenses were guaran- teed by the Hon. Cecil Rhodes.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

A Russian athlete, M. Valowsk, having made a bet that he would cover the distance between Bordeaux city and AngouMme, there and back on foot, a total distance of 145 miles, in 24 hours, started on Sunday morning from Bordeaux. He returned, having accomplished the double jnurney in 40 mins. less than the stipulated time. thus winning a wager of 2,000 f.

div.head: SUICIDE OF GENERAL BOULANGER.
div.p: SUICIDE OF GENERAL BOULANGER.

BRUSSELS, WEDNESDAY NIGHT.---Greneral Boulanger committed suicide this morning at half-past eleven up- on Madame de Bonnemain's tomb at the cemetery of Ixelles,: a suburb of Brussels. He drove out from his house in the Rue Montoyer straight to the cemetery. after staying for a short time at the tomb, he took from his pocket a pistol, and shot himself through the temple_ Death was immediate. The superintendent of the ceme- tery and a police magistrate was called in haste, and the body of the deceased General, which was covered with blood, was removed. Beneath his waistcoat, over his heart, was found a lock of white hair woven into the shape of a heart, with a photograph of Madame de Bonnemain. _ _ _

He had arranged everything for his death, and had prepared telegrams to be sent to different persons. 'Po his mother he had written a letter announcing his de- parture on a long voyage, and asking her not to be un- easy. He got up at seven this morning, and said, in the presence of his valet, " Although I am abandoned by everybody, 41 still know what to do." It is said that General Boulanger visited Mdme de I3onnemain's tomb daily, and frequently wept there. The stone bore the inscription" A Marguerite," and to this last week he had added, A Bientot." The funeral will take place on Saturday. To-night the General is lying on his bed in evening dress, and wearing the cross of the Legion of Honour. It is difficult to recognise the features of the deceased, as they are covered with blood. General Boulanger has left two will., a political will addressed to his secretary, M. Mouton Defraiste, and a private will, which is depo- sited at a notary's office. An intimate friend of the General tells me that the deceased long ago made up his mind to commit suicide, and was many times prevented from accomplishing his determination. It is rumoured that the Archbishop of Malines has refused to give the necessary authorization for the solemnisation of a reli- gious funeral. PARIS, WEDNESDAY NIGHT.—The suicide of General Boulanger on Madame de Bonnemaine's grave has come with great suddenness on the general public, but does not surprise the few friends that remained to him. Since her death he often said that life was too heavy a burden to bear and that the stagnation of Brussels was killing him. A short time ago he showed symptoms of tuberculosis, the malady of which she died. In addition to this his wounded vanity made him suffer constantly and cruelly. Nobody ever loved the approbation of others more than he did, and he found himself disgraced by the indictments read out before the High Court. He was utterly stranded at Brussels, forgotten by the poli- ticans who gathered round him during his boom, and by the Russian agents here who more than any other class helped to boom him. Madame de Bonnemain's fortune was left away from him, and the !prospect of poverty stared him in the face. All the above causes for mental depression were too much for a brain whose balance was easily overturned ,and which had the taint of hereditary insanity.

FTM9II Ain AND HOT Ant CRANKS.—I am not alluding to machinery, but to "folks." What should w do if the word " crank " had not been invented I What other name should we give those two indiv. .uals, usually found in every large family, the fresh air crank and the warm air crank The former is generally fat and comfortable well fed and full-blooded; the latter, thin and delicate, with no appetite, and an aversion to exercise. Between these two the people who do not go to extremes, but know that there are times when doors and windows should be shut, and times when they should be open, have a very hard time of it. The fresh air crank—usually a lady—gets up on a winter morning, spreads her bedding upon the window-sill, thiows all the windows up, sets the door back, and is heard ejaculating, "What a lovely, fresh morning V' by the 'people who have dashed out of their warm rooms into the cool draught she has created on the stairs and in the entries, and who enter the dining-room shivering. Ten to one she has pulled the window half down there. Tropical fashions go with her into the frozen regions. She enjoys riding in a coach with both windows open, sitting in the crack of an outer door after dancing, welcoming wild winas that blow away the hearth rugs and cause the pictures on the walls to rook to and fro. She is responsible for all the bad colds in the family, and for heaven knows what lung complaints and influenzas amongst those who have the misfortune to be her fellow passengers on public conveyances. For if there is a window, up it goes; if there is a door, it must fly open, regardless of blast or tempest. Nevertheless, she is always boasting of her love of ',fresh air, and uttering her belief that if people would only do as she does they would be as well, as happy and as wise. Even if she herself becomes a victim of pneumonia, she loudly declares, after her miraculous recovery, that it was the most astonishing dispensation of Providence ever known that 8/se should take cold 1 The warm air crank is usually a man. His room is kept at the temperature of a firing furnace at ja china-maker's. He has a register from the heater, a little coal-stove and a gas-stove in it, and often they are all in full blast at once. He stops the window crevices with cotton, and has weather strips on all the doors, and a sand bag where a door opens. He has been known to stuff up a key-hole to keep off a draught and to get hot water bottles sent up from the kitchen while the perspiration was pouring down the backs of his companions. If any one enters he cries out: "Pray don't keep the door open an instant longer than you can help I There's the most dreadful draught 1 We shall all perish 1" If ay one goes out he utters the same caution. As for looking out of the window of that room it is not permitted. The fresh air crank is always at sword's point with the hot air crank, of course, and he with her. They mask their hatred under a guise of superior wisdom; but one can see it when, in the parlours or other common rooms, she sits gasping and fanning herself, while he turns his coat collar up behind his ears, chafes his hands, and utters predictions of quick consumption for everybody. And at times she will remark: "No wonder your Uncle William is so unhealthy. He will not allow himself to breathe. He is really a little off on that subject. Quite mad, indeed 1" Or he says, solemnly: "tour Cousin Sally may be a good woman in other respects, but as to fresh air, and all that, she is simply too crazy to be allowed her

How TO EAT WISELY. —As a universal rule in health, and with very rare exceptions in disease, that is best to be eaten which the appetite caves or the taste relishes. Persons rarely err in the quality of food eaten; Nature's instincts are the wisest regulators in this respect. Ihe great sourres of mischief from eating are three—quantity, frequency, and rapidity, and from these come the horrible dyspepsias which make human life a burden, a torture, a living death. By eating fast, the stomach, like a bottle being filled through a funnel, is full and overflowing before we know it. But the most important reason is, the food is swallowed before time has been allowed to divido It in sufficiently small pieces with the teeth; for, like ice in a tumbler of water, the smaller the bits are, the sooner they are dissolved. It has been seen with the naked eye that if solid food is cut up in pieces small as half a pea, it digests almost as soon, without being chewed at all, as if it had been well masticated. The best plan, therefore, is for all persons to thus comminute their food; for, even if it is well chewed, the comminution is no injury, while it is of very great importance in case of hurry, forgetfulness, or bad teeth. It re- quires five hours for a common meal to dissolve and pass out of the stomach; hence persons should not eat within less than a five-hours' interval. Always breakfast before work or exercise. No labourers nor active persons should eat an atom later than sun-down, and then it should not be over half the mid-day meal. Persons of sedentary habits, or who are at all ailing, should take abso- lutely nothing for supper beyond a single piece of cold, stale bread and butter, or a ship biscuit, with a single cup of warm drink. Such a supper will always give better sleep and prepare for a heartier breakfast, with the advantage of having the exer- cise of the whole day to grind it up and extract its nutriment. —Hall's Journal of Health.

IN folk-lore the crow always appears as a bird of the worst and most sinister character, representing either death, or night, or winter. In German Switzerland it is believed that a crow perching on the roof of a house in which lies a corpse is a sign that the soul of the dead is irrevocably damned. And in Sussex its cry thrice repeated is considered a sure token of death. The raven lives to so great an age that the ancients believed the time allotted to it was 27 times that of a man. Jewish authors tell strange stories of this bird—that it was orgin- ally white, and was turned black for its deceitful conduct; also that it flies crooked because it was cursed by Noah. There is a widespread belief that the appearance of the raven prognosticates death. In Denmark, its appearance in a village is Con- sidered an indication that the parish priest will soon die. In Andalusia, if it is heard croaking over a house, an unlucky day is expected; repeated thrice it is a fatal presage; if, perching high turn- ing and croaking, a corpse will soon come froth that direction. In many parts of Germany they are believed to hold the souls of the damned, some- times to be the Evil One himself. LONGEVITY OF PUBLIC MEN. —The longevit of famous statesmen is remarkable. Imagine rd Palmerston acting vigorously as Prime Minister of England when over 80, governing the vast British Empire with steady hand, making speeches three hours long in the House of Commons, and rising next day fresh as a man of 40. Think of the venerable Guizot, the French statesman, who at the age of 67, was still writing histories, presiding over religious conventions, and carrying on lively disoessions in the French Academy. The late Lord Lyndhurst made able speeches in the House of Lords when he had passed his 90th year; and his long-time rival, Lord Brougham, wrote his autobiography, in three goodly volumes, when he had nearly reached 90 years. The Marquis of Lansdowne, who, as Lord Henry Petty, was a leatling member of the "All the Talents " Cabinet of which Charles James Fox was the chief, in 1806, was still an active member of the House of Lords nearly 60 years later, in 1863, and died in that year at the age of 83. The Duke of Wellington took part in public affairs until his death in 1852, in his 8311 year. In former generations energetic statesmen of advanced years are found thickly scattered through the pages of history. There was the old Marquis of Winchester, who could remember Edward IV., the first York Sovereign, and who, when he died in 1572, at the age of 97, was holding offioe under Queen Elizabeth. As to the Presideaats of the United States, it is a familiar fact that John Adams and Thomas Jek:erson, the second and third Presidents, both died the 4th July, 1826, Just half a century from the day on which both signed the Declaration of Independence, Adams being ninety-one, and Jefforson eighty-three. President Andrew Jackson lived to be eighty-two, John Quincy Adams to be eighty-one, and Madison eighty-five.
