INCOME TAX APPEALS 1891-2.

Sir,—With reference to the "Notices of First Asscgs- meat " for the current year now being issued by the Local Commissioners of Taxes, may I point out to your readers that if it is their intention to appeal against the charge, it will be advisable when giving notice also to give notice for the repayment of any overcharge for the past year ending sth April last, as the statement required in support of such appeal is applicable to both years. It should be clearly understood that notice must be given before a reduction or repayment of an overcharge can be obtained. The insertion of the above information will I think be of great interest to your readers.—Yours obediently,
JOHN J. HITCHINGS. Head Offices: 10. Serjeant's Inn, Flest-st., London, E.C., 29th September, 1891.
THE TEACHINGS OF THEOSOPHY.

Sir,—Your correspondent Mr. Kenyon, in his remarks on Theosopby says that it is based on natural and not on supernatural phenomena; and in accordance with this view, he maintains it should be judged by the former. But,if I mistake not, Theosophists claim to be in possession of powers unexplainable upon any scientific or materialistic principle or theory ; and hence their claim comes into direct conflict with Mr. Kenyon's statement. It is curious to find that while Mr. Kenyon maintains that Theosophy can be explained on scientific principles, he puts forward in its behalf no reasoning, either scien- tific or logical, but indulges in the quotation of poetic effusions (which are consistent with any Pantheistic theory). Would Mr. Kenyon commit the proof of the law of gravitation to poetic effusions? If so his scien- tific attainments stand in great need of regeneration. Mr. Kenyon also urges that scientists should treat the claims of Theosophy " with unprejudiced consideration and justice." But Theosophy is an importation from the East where science is almost unknown, and where theories regarding the creation of the world are as crude as those of any crazed lunatic. Before claiming for Theosophy the support of scientists, Mr. Kenyon should make sure that the founders of the system were scientists in every sense of the term. Mr. Kenyon also says "the teachings of Christ have been perverted and made to sanction almost every evil." Now, whatever conclusion can be deduced from this statement might equally well be drawn from a similar statement regarding science. The teachings of science have been perverted and made to sanction almost every evil. Would Mr. Kenyon on that account extirpate science? If so his ideas again stand in great need of regeneration. lam &c.,
AN INQUIRER.
METEOROLOGICAL SUPPLICATION.
Sir,—l hope your correspondent referred to by" H. J. w. 2, as undervaluing the efficacy of prayer for the Prince of Wales will not be offended by my dipping into the controversy.

As an old correspondent upon the subject of train pro- duction and rain retardation of prayer, I am still seek- ing information upon which sound opinions upon this subject may be founded. For this lam willing to accept H. J. W." as my Garnaliel, and to sit at his feet disciple-like. But to clear the ground, I should like to ask what logic has to do with this matter? Surely 'H. .3. W." must have introduced this word by a slip of the pea! No logic with which I am acquainted counten- ances any connection between Prayer land Meteorology. Has" H. J. W." reflected what a serious matter it would be were the linked concatenation of nature's laws to be thus rudely broken, and what undue disturbance might, nay undoubtedly would, accrue to our foreign neighbours in the matter of their weather. They might behaving weather which suited them, and would have just cause for complaint were it changed for the worse at the instigation of any busybodies, lay or cleric. Does " 13. if. W." think our weather is cut up into slices and handed round " promiscus like ?" Assuredly the school- master must have been very much abroad to have allowed the idea of a modern Jupiter Pluvius to exist who arbitrarily dispenses atmospheric conditions in ans- wer to the supplication of his devotees. "H. J. W." would seem to have forgotten that the reign of Jupiter hasgivsn place to the reign of Law. But the richest bit comes in his last paragraph, where he asks "if the Prince's conduct and 'character might not ham keea worse had no prayers ever been offered in his behalf:" A whole congress of Philadelphia lawyers would be,required to decide what possible influence the opening of these innumerable wind-bags might or might not have upon " H.R.H." One great loss would, how- ever, have occurred to the Prince had these silly suppli- cants but sought Divine interference in their own affairs. In that case H.R.H. would undoubtedly have lost abund- ant food for laughter. To one whose training and education, however deficient in some respects, has been on a higher standard than that of the conventicle it must have been amusing, albeit annoying, to be thus the sub- ject of prayer by these self-elected intercessors. But Avotld it not be anore pertinent to the occasion to ask if the conduct and character of H.R.H. might not Lave been better had he not been treated so like a demi-god, and teen less exposed to influences calculated to impair or prevent the developernent of much of the best that is in a man, while on the contrary the want of the stimulus of a natural and healthy occupation induces the craving for the vicious stimulus of gambling. But with regard to the power of prayer to break the sequence of natural law, let me offer " H.J.W." a final AoA.C.ltaskre lest, 14 ttw daud all of his way of,
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

In my peregrinations the other day I came across the following lines written by one longfellow a long way after another : I stood on the Bridge at midnight As the " Parish " was striking the hour, And the pale moon shone o'er Runcorn, Behind the Old Soapery Tower. I saw her calm reflection In the waters down below, And a flood of thoughts came o'er me That caused my tears to flow. I thought of the brave Commissioners In times, Oh! how far removed ; Who gallantly decided That the Bridge should be improved. Far back in the distant ages The work was resolved upon : Ever since it has been progressing— And still it is going on! I thought how at some future time The Bridge must become complete, In times, perchance, to be toddled on By our great-grandchildren's feet.

Although the scheme for providing a Cottage Hospital for the town has not been mentioned for some time, and appears to have sunk into oblivion, I am in a position to state that this is not the case. The holiday season has prevented things progres- sing as fast as they otherwise might have done, be- cause several members of the committee have been away from the town, but the public may expect to shortly hear of something definite being accom- plished. I believe the committee have decided upon building a hospital,and several suggested sites have been inspected, but a site has not yet been chosen. WA1:2114 An interesting dispute is at present taking place between the Frodsham Inspectors and the Frod- sham Gas and Water Company. The former have fixed several lamps in streets where the Company have no mains, and where they contend that the Inspectors should lay the mains. The Company have, however, made a "concession " to the extent of becoming willing to bear half the cost. The Gas Inspectors decline to bear any portion, and fairly argue that, as the Company will be well paid for their gas and make all the profit, they should pro- vide the means of supplying it where it is wanted. The Gas Inspectors have given the Company notice that they will discontinue using the gas altogether, and in the night time the streets of Frodsham are not even illuminated by the faint glimmer of one small light, and darkness reigns supreme. Much inconvenience is the result, but the ratepayers' re- presentatives are determined to maintain their position. If a settlement is not arrived at quickly it is probable an effort will be made to obtain the necessary light from oil lamps. The subject brought before Runcorn Board of Commissioners on Thursday by Mr. Lightburn is one of vital importance to the town and port of Runcorn. If there are no deep docks at Runcorn capable of accommodating large ships, we shall as Mr. Lightburn pointed out, have the chagrin of see- ing all the vessels that can pass under the bridge sail on to Manchester, and those that cannot do so will seek another port.—Liverpool or our rival Ellesmere Port. Mr. Wiswall's assurance that the Ship Canal Company are seriously considering the matter is gratifying and satisfactory, but the Com- missioners should not on that account relax th sir exertions; rather should 'they redouble them and by every argument at their command, cause the Ship Canal directorate to come to a speedy and favourable decision.

The evening schools of the Runcorn School Board are progressing. The number of pupils has con- siderably increased during the present week, and Mr. Moulton, .the headmaster, has now over 70 youths under his care anxious for self-improvement. The science and art classes commenced on Monday, and a gratifying start was made.

The visit of the provincial grand lodge of Free- masons to Runcorn, on Wednesday, created quite an interest in this secret order, and the procession from the Public Hall to the Parish Church was wit- nessed by hundreds of spectators. One of the members of the Runcorn lodge, Bro. T. H. Annett, P.M., was paid a high compliment by his masonic brethren. By an almost unanimous vote he was elected Provincial Grand Treasurer, and he came in for hearty congratulations on all hands.

JOHN PEERS. The Haws, Penketh, 27th Sept., 1891.

WORK AND WAGES: HOW DO PEOPLE LIVE? Sir,—ln these days we hear a great deal about social reform and the elevation and general betterment of the working classes. Many schemes have been mooted with these objects in view, and mnch has been heard of Trade Unionism—particularly of that latest phase of it which is known by the name of the New Unionism, and which has been at work amongst the very lowest classes of unskilled labourers, such as dock labourers, chemical labourers, &c. Reflecting on some of the things that I have heard, I have asked myself the question, `, How do some of these people live ? " We have heard again and again of the low wages earned by some of these men ; and how any of them manage to exist on such pittances as 145., 165., and 18s. a week, lam quite unable to comprehend. It is my good fortune to number amongst my personal friends several respectable and intelligent working-men, and in conversation ith one of them the other evening I asked him if he could explain the difficulty. I explained to my friend that I had a wife and six children, and that three of my lads were working and that the total in- come of myself and three lads would probably be about £2OO per year, or say £4 a week, and that out of this sum it was scarcely possible for me to save anything; indeed, I found it required my best efforts to keep every- thing straight with such an income. Now,you will under- stand, sir, that my wife and I are both teetotallers, and that my wife does her own housework—since she keeps no servant, and that my own personal expenses are al- most nil. My tastes and habits of life are of the simplest possible character. I not only don't drink, but I don't smoke, and a walk in the country, or the company of a good book, and a little music occasionally, supply all the relaxation I ask or desire. Five pounds a year will pay my tailor's bill, but this of course, does not include the cost of my lads' clothes, which will perhaps be about the same as my own. I have four sons, and the tailor's bill for the lot will be about £25 a year, or say 10s. per week.

Well, my friend and I compared notes. He earns 355. per week, but is subject to broken weeks, consequently his income is at times liable to be interrupted. It work is slack he has to go on short time; sometimes he may be stopped for a week or two together. If he should be sick his wages are stopped, and in various ways his earnings are to some little extent uncertain. My friend is a total abstainer, but smokes. He has a family of four children, which with himself and wife makes six. Now, he and his family all make a respectable appearance, and I asked him how he does it. He puts a shilling a week by in a Building Society which is all the money he can possibly save after paying the subscription to his club. "Well," I said, "how do you live—what kind of food do you have ?" He replied that they usually had tea and bread and butter or toast for breakfast; often the same for dinner, with the addition, perhaps, of a bit of bacon or an egg ; sometimes potatoes and a little meat; for tea, bread and butter, and occasionally a little jam or a herring. He said nothing about supper. On Satur- days they bought a piece of beef or mutton, the cost of which never exceeded four shillings. This was for Sun- day's dinner, which was usually a good one. The same piece of meat was served] up -old on Monday and Tuesday. Well, I thought, this was very plain living in all conscience, and if a man earning 355. per week could not afford a more generous diet than this how must the labourers fare who were employed at the same works and whose wages only reached the sum of 18 or 19 shillings per week, and were even more uncertain than his? Suppose such a labourer to have a small family like my friend, of four children. He will have to pay 4s. per week for a small cottage with two bedrooms, is. 6d. per week for coal, and 6d. per week for candles or lamp oil ; then there will be wear and tear in the house, soap, Ikc., and until recently, school fees. And what about shoes or clogs, and stock- ing? (My wife says it takes at least 10s. a week for shoes for my lads. She constantly complains of the heavy expense in this one item alone). And then the clothes and bedding. These are all absolute necessaries that cannot be dispensed with. And suppose our labourer spends two or three shillings a week in beer and tobacco, as many do, how much is there left for food? How they exist at all is an unfathomable mystery to me, and yet what splendid physiques many of them possess ! I shall be glad if some of your working-men readers will enlighten me on these matters. A few letters on the subject would prove very interesting and suggestive reading.—Yours truly, SOCIAL REFORMER.

THE WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

The brickwork, &c., in connection with the Wesleyan Chapel is now practically completed. The woodwork, decorating, &c., inside the chapel is be- ing rapidly pushed forward, and the work should ba completed early next month. Preparations are being made for the opening services.

There's fairly a bonny lot o' werpheyds i' th' world!

Aw couldn'd help quotin' to mysel' for aw dorn'd know which theawsandth time Carlyle's wed-known remerk abeawt th' population bein' so mony million, " mooastly foo's," when aw read i' th'papper Vother day heaw a simpleton perted wi' his watch an' cheean for a bird as were painted. It seems as a chap coom up to this werpheyd in a London street. an' axed him to buy a bullfinch ascould sing "Ilooam Sweet hooam," an' " Th' Blue Bells o' Scotland " ; id wor a bobby-dazzler, an' i' th way' o' colour nayther a paycock nor Joseph s coat o' mony colours were owt to come up to id. Afoore th' werpheyd could say owt at o' another mon caom up an' axt th' owner nod to chuck it away, but to save id for him at four peawnds ; he couldn'd pay for it then, becose he'd left his poss "on th' peeano aside ov his clogs." This were enough for th' werpheyd, for beawt hearin' th' brid sing he swapt his watch an' cheean for id, an' sailed off after t' other chap, an' arranged to let him hey id at th' price he'd offered, an' meet him at a certain place at a certain time. Oy coorse th' chap ne'er torned up, an' ov coorse eawr werpheyd fun eawt as th' brid were nobbut a painted chaffinch, an' as it could no moore sing nor—nor—well, say a comic opera tenor. Th' two chaps is i' custody, but aw shouldn'd think as any magistrate would punish 'em for doin' a chap o' thad soort, th' temptation were too gret for a honest tradesmen to resist, ne'er mind Vother soort.
An' yet we laugh neawadays at th' buzzes abeawt th' wise men o' Gotham, an' th' Autswick caries; yigh, an' they're fiction, but this bits t' truth !

A dread di.'s'easei—in its most chronic form, I poetized upon the small event - In manner following (that is to say):
He clasped his sweetheart in his arms, And whispered in her e3r ; " Cheer up my lass, the time will pass, 'Tis barely half a year; 'Tis only five short months, my love,
, . ~ And then I roam no more, But with my wife shall pass my life In the cot upon the shore." * * *

And he is on the deep, dark sea On his last long voyage bound, For the gallant ship in the tempest's grip A resting place hath found ; And o'er his grave a requiem Is sung in the ocean's roar, While the hot tears start from the mother's heart, In the cot upon the shore And thou discoloured piece of bronze, Would hear his hurried prayer, As he grasped for breath in the throes of death In the channel over there; His brief and earnest prayer for those He would see on earth no more, For the lass so fair and the mother there In the cot upon the shore. Thus did I moralize, with more to come, When cries of youthful anguish smote ray ear. And looking up before me I beheld

The daily tripper, with his buxom wife, And crowd of boys and girls; their day's provisions In a vermilion kerchief, and the sire Said to me: " Mestur, han yo' fun a penny? 'Cose iv yo' han my little lass lies lost id.'

Aw think th' halladays are welly o'er wi' till next summer. At leeast till next June, July, August, an' September; we ged no summer neaw, nobbut a bit at Kesmas. Th' Isle o' Man hed 1057 moore visitors last August nor they hed i' August 1890, an' there'd ha' bin 1061 iv there'd ha' bin a under- greawnd tunnel, or a brig across: but me an' th' wife an' two childer isn'd gooin' till they ged a air tram, or submarine booat, or a balloon on th' job. An' there's theawsands moore said th' same thing. an' they'll stick to id, for say wod yo' will it's nooan so nice bein' seea-sick, an' throwin' up everything except.yc'r sittiwation.

TaWkin' o' halladays aw'll bet as Blackpool's the shop for th' next year or two, just on ackeawnt o' th' new Eiffel teawer ; fooak as corn'd affoord to go to Paris 'll go theere—except they hear as th' price o' lodgin's an' eytables are .Eiffel too. Mind thad, yo' Blackpoolers! Fooak doesn'd mind givin' two bob a peawnd for Kiel butther labelled "New," or a bob for seven new laid crate eggs,but draw th' line at thad, an' dorn'd come id too :strong, then yoll hey a seeason as'll be th' best on record, nod even exceptin' th' seventies.

Aw see Mrs. Besanti doesn'd intend to shew th' precipitated letters hoo hes, but hoo gi's a varra poor reeason for nod doin' sooa, an thad is as fooak wodn'd believe in 'em. Hoe doesn'd seem to know as fooak 'll swallow ony mortal thing neawadays, providin' id doesn'd give 'em indigestion, physical or spiritual. Believe in 'em ? Ov coourse they wod —at leeast theawsands on us wod, even iv one linefl were written i' Greek wi' a black lead, another line ' in shorthand wi' pen an' ink, an' th' next line i' La.nkisher dialect wi' a lump o' chalk or a bit o' red I riddle. Bless yo' , Missis, we'll believe as th' moon's med o' green cheese, churned eawt o' milk fro' th' milky way—iv cheese is med bi churning; an' we'll nod ax for a sample, noather. Yo' know we believed th' Chatterton forgeries, an' th' Ossian forgeries, an' o' thad stuff abeawt Formosa, an' why nod Koot Hoomi an' his letters? There is odd uns as wod swear they worn'd written bi Koot Homni at o' an they'd proove id in a big book,, just as easy as they'd proove as somebody else wrooat Shakespeare, an' as a tooathri somebody elses dudn'd write Junius's letters. An' happen as eesay as somebody 'll proove some o' these days as aw ne'er mixt this Brimstooam an' Tracycle every week, but as id were Gladstoone's werk. Ne'er gawn 'em, Missis ; tek 'em to yo'r bankers for safety. It's quite eneugh for us to know wod th' owd chap says: but there is one thing as some on yo' could do, an' thad is to precipitate a lot o nte fleawers o' th' hospitals every mornin' ; mention this to th' colonels, an' Owd Koot when yo' write.

There's nowt nobbut leckshuns an' rumours o' leckshuns knockin' reawnd just neaw ; whether yo're at th' theayter, or cherch, or a footbot match it's o' th' same. Yo' may ax th' chap next to yo' wod he thinks o' th' play, an' yo' find he's ne'er sin id, becose he's bin readin' a political speech in his evenin papper ; th' same wi' th' chap next to yo' a.; cherch—" th' sermon isn'd bad, but id isn'd in id wi' John Morley's speech at Cambridge " ; yo'r next door nayber at th' footbo' will torn o' th' dodgin',an' t an' off-side play, an' foul chergin into poli- tics, an' it's generally yo'r side as gooas in for th' rough play, an' his side as plays th' gentlemanly game. Id olez happens this woad wi' me; aw ne'er dud come across a chap bi accident as hed th' same views as mysel' ; an' they olez lookt at me in a pityin' sooart o' way an' towd me to go hooam an' read. Aw should ha' blusht for seemin' so igner- ant, iv aw hedn'd ha' known as id were nobbut a dodge to ged eawt o' arggin' on a subject they knew nowt abeawt. It's a dodge as aw've used mony a time mysel', an' it's a good un, an' olez wo'th a hencore fro' a-audience as hesn'd heeard id afore; but it's varra okard iv yo'r opponent kes read, an' nod only his own side but yo'rs too, an' axes yo' wod he mon read, an' why, an, then tackles yo', on th' subject, an' meks a laughin'- stock on yo'.

An' accidents o' that soort will happen to th' best politician gooin', as wed l as to th' wost, an' aw may ncd be believed when aw say there's ignerant chaps on booath sides, but there raly is. Aw know this for a fact.
It is reported in New York that the North Germa n Lloyd Steamship Company have decided to build six whaleback steamers. _ -

Mr. Parnell has announced that his new papers will be published five weeks hence under the names of the "Irish Independent" and "Evening Star" respectively. DOG RACE.—A dog race was decided at the West End Grounds, Wigan, on Saturday, before 200 spectators, the competing dogs being Parke's Marvel, Blackrod, and Smith's Pit Legs, Golborne. Marvel received three yards inside 200 yards for £3O. At the start Pit Legs was favourite at six to four on, but after a good race he failed to reach Marvel, and was defeated by three yards and a half.

DEATH or OLD LOWTONIANS.—On Saturday afternoon the death of Mr. John Pearcey took place at his resi- dence, in Lowton, at the age of 73, after a long illness. Deceased, who was a churchwarden at St. Mary's Church was well known, and was a Liberal in politics. On Saturday morning, the death took place, at Leigh, of Mr. Roger Wood, formerly of Lowton, he being 82 years of age, and was interred in St. Mary's Churchyard on Tuesday afternoon. On Saturday morning Mrs. Mary Fearnley, wife.of Mr. Isaac Fearnley, took place at her residence, Firs-lane, she having attained her 50th year. Deceased was formerly a resident of Lowton, and had been in ill health for over two years.
ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
Sir George Stokes, M.P. for Cambridge University, has announced that he will not seek election to the next Parliament.
NORTH-EAST MANCHESTER.

The writ for the election of a member of Parliament for North-east Manchester was received on Wednesday by the Mayor (Mr. Alderman Mark), who, as returning officer, fixed Monday, the sth inst. as the day for re- ceiving nominations,and the fcllowing Thursday(the Bth) for the polling. Meetings in support of the candidates were held on Wednesday evening. Mr. Scott (Liberal) addressed a densely crowded meeting in the Congrega- tional. Schoolroom, Every-st., and a resolution in his favour was carried unanimously. He was supported amongst others by Mr. A. H. D. Acland, M.P., and Mr.H. J. Roby, M.P. Sir James Fergusson(Tory)in continuation of his candidature, addressed a meeting of the electors of Newton Heath in All Saints' School,Church-rcad,Newton Heath. He was supported by Mr. J. W. Maclure, M.P., and Mr. J. M. Maclean, M.P., and a resolution in favour of his candidature was adopted.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. T. OWEN.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. T. OWEN.

Much regret will be felt at the death of Mr. T. Owen, grocer, of the Pollards, Penketh, and Sankey st.,Warrington. Mr. Owen who was taken ill about a month ago, has been attended by Drs. Murray and Gornall, but despite their constant often lions he gradually sank, and died at 12.30 a.m. on Tues 'ay, The cause of death was typhoid fe er. A widow and nine children are left to mourn his loss. Mr. Owen had attained the age of 47 years. He took an active interest in everything relating to the Church, and held the office of sidesman at St. Mary's, Great Sankey. He was also a Sunday School teacher at St. Mary's Mission Church Sunday School, Pen- keth. Seven years since Mr. Owen performed the duties of vicar's warden, in connection with St. Mary's Church, in a most satisfactory manner. His death has made a gap in the Church circle which will not easily be filled, as his kind genial manner had endeared him to everyone.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

The funeral of the late Mr. Thomas Owen took place on Thursday, at the Cemetery, Great Sankey. The procession left The Pollards at 11.45 a.m., and the Cemetery was reached about 12.15. A large number of private carriages belonging to various friends followed, and a considerable number of the members of the congregation of St. Mary's Church united to pay a last token of respect to the memory of the deceased by walking. A number of friends from Warrington were also present. All along the route to the Cemetery, the blinds of the houses were drawn as the procession passed. The funeral ceremony was performed by the Rev. T. E. VI inder. Whilst in the mortuary!" Rock of:Ages," the well-known hymn, was sung. A large number of beautiful wreaths were sent by sympathising relatives and friends. The coffin was of oak, and the whole of the arrangements were carried out by Messrs. R. Garnett & Sons.

div.head: RATEPAYERS' MEETING.
div.p: RATEPAYERS' MEETING.

The half-yearly meeting of the ratepayers for the township of Penketh was held on Thursday evening, in the Wesleyan School-room. There were present Messrs. A. Thorpe, J. C. Routledge, C. E. Parker (overseers) ; Tetlow, R. Boardman, Hobson, Bell, G. Randall, J. Randall, Cross, White, Moores, R. Garnett, King, D. Garnett, and the assistant over- seer, Mr.J. Foster. Mr. Thorpe presided. The no- tice convening the meeting was read by Mr. Thorpe. The minutes of the previeus meeting were read by Mr. Foster and confirmed. The past half year's accounts were pre- sented. The total amount of the rate was £367 Os. 3d., and this had all been collected. The balance in the over- seers' hands is £los.—Mr. R. Garnett proposed and Mr. Cross seconded the passing of the accounts, which was done.—Mr. Thorpe proposed a rate of is. 2d. in the £ for the ensuing half year.—Mr. Routledge seconded, and the resolution was carried.—The amount of the volun- tary rate in the overseers' hands is £3 19s. aid. The question of the salary paid for collecting the voluntary rate was discussed, but ultimately left over to the March meeting. The walking of the boundary is left in the hands of the committee previously appointed to arrange. With reference to the recreation ground Mr. Thorpe said as a result of the interview between the Committee and Captain Hughes, Mr. Foster had received a letter from Captain Hughes in which, en his mother's behalf, he agreed to let the recreation ground to the overseers for the annual rental of £6. Captain Hughes and Mrs. Hughes would return of this by gifts of £2 each. After some discussion, Mr. Thorpe proposed, and Mr. Routledge seconded, the following resolution, which was carried :—" That Mrs. Hughes be thanked for her offer, but owing to the existence of certain difficulties, she be asked to allow the matter to stand over to the March meeting." A discussion arose with regard to the unsatisfactory condition of the road leading from Hal- ton's Bridge, and as a result Mr. Garnett proposed, "That the Highway Board be asked to take into con- sideration the road leading from Halton's Bridge, the sharp curve on the rising ground being exceedingly dangerous both to vehicular and pedestrian traffic, and they suggest that a strip of land might be easily obtained whereby the road might be straightened." Mr. Rout- ledge seconded. and the resolution was carried. The question of the lighting of the township was mentioned by Mr. Thorpe. He understood they were in the hangs of the Rural Sanitary Authority. It was ultimately de- cided, after considerable discussion, that the following resolution, proposed by Mr. Hobson, and seconded by Mr. R. Garnett,be sent to the Rural Sanitary Authority: —" This meeting requests the Rural Sanitary Authority to apply their powers under the Public Lighting Act to this township." This was all the business. The meeting concluded after according' a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Thorpe for his services in the chair.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

DEPUTY MEDICAL OFFICE/L—Dr. W. W. Williamson submitted the name of Dr. Smth, of Knutsford, to the Board of Guardians on Wednesday, as his deputy. The appointment was made. REVISION COURT.—The Revision for Lymm took place in the Sessions House, Lymm, before Mr. W. Trevor Parkins, revising barrister. The Conservatives were re- presented by Mr. F. R. B. Lindsell, Mr. Gamble, Mr. Callender, and Mr. Ardern ; the Liberals were represen- ted by Mr. A. E. Paterson, Mr. E. L. Kenyon, Mr. Win. Skilling, and Mr. D. Daniels. The Liberals had to pay ss. and the Toriei lls. expenses. CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH —The anniversary services of this church were held on Sunday, the preacher being the Rev. W. Riley, of Hyde. A service was also held in the afternoon, at which Mr. Riley gave an address. Col- lections were made at each service on behalf of the funds of the school, A series of what are termed " bright Sun- day afternoons "are to be inaugurated by the Lymm Congregationalists. The'meetings will be for men only, and the solos will be given by Mrs. R. H. Pearson, of Warrington. The organist will be Mr. W. H. Payton, also of Warrington.

I- WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.—The parents of the mem- bers of the Wesleyan Band of Hope were invited to tea on Monday night. After tea there was an entertainment Mr. Thorpe presiding. The Rev. Thomas Ross, of War- rington, addressed the meeting. Miss M. Thorpe and Miss Brown sang, and Mr. F. 0. Moston recited and spoke. Mr. H. 0. Briggs also gave a reading. As this meeting practically commenced the session, a report was read as to the work of the coming session, and the Secretary- asked forjthe help of the parents in carrying it out. Re- freshments were served at the conclusion. There was a very fair attendance, but not as large as was expected. A very pleasant evening was passed. GOOD TEMPLAR DEMONSTRATION.—A demonstration in connection with the Tower of Refuge Lodge of Good Templars, Lymm, took place on Satuaday, under the management of Brother Hy. Thomas, D.G.C.T., and secretary of the Lymtn branch. A large company assem- bled at tke Cross,including a good contingent from War- rington. Mr. McGill of the Manchester City Mission gave an encouraging address, after which a procession was formed, headed by the Lymm United Brass Band, under the leadership of Mr. Frost,and marched through Statham, where a short address was given by Bro. Potts, of Northwich. At other points addresses were given by Bro. C. Newman, of Heatley,•Bro. J. Edwards, P.C.T., Bro. J. Price, Mr. Waddington, and Mr. Parker. NIGHT POACHING.—At the Altrincham Petty Sessions, on Monday, a labouring man, named James Robinson, belonging to Warrington, was charged, under a magis- trate's warrant, with night poaching at Lymm, on the night of the 14th August, on land in the occupation of John Longshaw.—John Leigh, woodman, in the employ of Mr. Colin Maclver, said that on the night of the 14th August, he went with other men to watch for poachers. At ten o'clock they concealed themselves in a wood, on land belonging to Mr. Longshaw. They waited until about twelve o'clock, when five men appeared. They ran some nets across the field. He and his companions waited until the men had run the nets out, when they advanced towards them. When they got to within six or eight yards off one of the men cried, " Roll up, chaps, and let them have it." The poachers lined out opposite to his party. The prisoner Robinson was in front of wit-, ness, and as he was making a grab at him, within three yards,another of the poachers struck him on the shoulder. He turned and secured the man who struck him. The prisoner then made off. He searched for several days in Warrington without finding any trace of him. On the following Tuesday night he was on Warrington bridge with P.C. Bell, of the Warrington Police. When they had been there abcut a quarter of an hour he saw Robinson coming across the bridge. They stopped him, and wit- ness identified him as one of the gang of poachers. The night was not o dark one, and he could plainly identify him.—ln cross-examination, the witness admitted that after he examined the prisoner, he turned to P.C. Bell and said "this is not the man I want."—The prisoner: What did you say that for ?—Witness : I knew that I had no warrant for you, and I thought if I told you I was going to take out a warrant you would be missing. —Defendant: You-could have taken me without a war- rant. It is ail false, but you want to make up the gang, and must have somebody.—Charles Chinnock, a game- keeper, said the prisoner was very like the man who ran away.—The prisoner: That will not do. You must say that lam the man.—Mr. Harris: Why do you say that he is very like the man ?—Witness: lie is the man. —Mr. Harris: Is there any witness who absolutely identifies him ?—Leigh I identify him.—The prisoner denisd that he was the man wanted, and called a man named Wm. Healey, who corroborated prisoner's state- ment that Leigh told P.C. Bell he was not the man.— The Chairman said tile maelstrates did no think the

div.head: FREEMASONRY IN CHESHIRE.
div.p: FREEMASONRY IN CHESHIRE.
PROVINCIAL GRAND LODGE AT RUNCORN.

The annual meeting of the Provincial Grand Lodge of Cheshire was held at the Public Hall, Run- corn, on Wednesday. Lord Egerton of Tatton, the Right Worshipful Provincial Grand Master,presided, and he was supported by Bro. the Rev. C. W. Spencer-Stanhope, P.G. Chaplain of England, acting as Deputy Provincial Grand Master, in the absence of Bro. Sir Horatio Lloyd; Bro. Terry, P.G.S.B. of England ; Bro. McLeod, secretary, Royal Masonic Institute for Boys; and a largq number of P.G. officers and others. After formal business had been transacted the R. W. Prov. Grand Master then addressed P.G. Lodge. He thanked the brethren for their attendance that day. Considering that Runcorn was not, perhaps, the most convenient town in the Province to get at, the attendance was very large. It was very satisfactory to find that Masonry had increased, and larger support had been given to it since they last visited Runcorn, eleven years ago. Three lodges had been consecrated in the province during the past year. and he was glad to see that those new lodges were so well and numerously represented that day. (Applause.) It showed that they were not only new, but vigorous„ and gave every hope that Masonry would flourish at Middlewich, Hoylake, and Chester. (Applause.) There was also an increase of members in the whole Province, the numbers on the roll now being 1,836, as against 1,737 in the preceding year. This showed also that the principles of masonry were steadily and gradually gaining ground in the Province. He was sure that the best way to ensure that steady and gradual increase was that the practical work of masonry should be increased and improved and consolidated in every way. He was pleased to notice that the recommendation made at Stockport last year, that charity representatives on the Committee of Benevolence should be elected by ballot every year, had been carried out successfully, and he thought that the work that the Committee had done during the past year had given an addi- tional stimulus to all the charities in the province. It was a matter for congratulation that at the annual festival of the Royal Masonic Institution for Boys in London, the stewards from the Province of Cheshire represented donations, amounting to over a thousand guineas, and thereby gained 240 votes, which increased the voting strength of the Province at each election of candidates for the school to nearly 1,000. (Applause.) During the ensuing year would be celebrated the jubilee of the Royal Benevolent Institution. They had from time to time received help from that institution for masons in that Province, but their voting power was not sufficient always to obtain the success of their candidates. Special advantages were offered to doners during the jubilee year. A donor of five guineas was offered three votes instead of two, for ten guineas eight votes would be received instead of four, donors of 50 guineas got 80 votes instead of 20, and so on. He trusted that an effort would be made to secure to the Province the 240 votes which are given to subscribers of 1,000 guineas. He should himself be happy to head the list with 50 guineas. (Applause.) Mention was made in the report of the Committee of Benevolence of the desirability of starting an additional fund in the Province in order to provide assistance for the aged masons and the widows of masons. in cases where they were unable to obtain the advantages and benefits of the London Institution. It was suggested that a local fund of .£l,OOO be raised to enable an annuity of ..£2O and £l6 to be given respectively to an old mason and the widow of a reason until they were elected on the central institution in London. If the brethren in the Province would endeavour to raise a fund of that kind, he would, in addition to the sum he had already mentioned, contribute 50 guineas towards it. (Applause.) Bro. Herbert Finch proposed the re-election of Bro. J. Cockson, P.M. of Unanimity Lodge, 287, as Provincial Grand Treasurer. Bro. McClellan seconded. Bro. Mellor proposed the election of Bro. T. H. Annett, P.M. of the Ellesmere Lodge, Runcorn. This was seconded by Bro. James Littler, W.M. of , the Ellesmere Lodge. On a vote being taken, Bro. Annett was declared elected by a large majority—a result which was re- ceived with loud applause. Bro. Annett briefly acknowledged the compliment that had been paid him. Bros. Gilbody, Ramsden, Gibson, Wildgoose, and Preston were re-appointed auditors. The R. W. Prov. Grand Master appointed and in- vested his officers for the ensuing year as follows : His Honor Sir Horatio Lloyd, R.W.D.P.G.M. ; Bros William Robinson, ; Frederick A. B. Lind- sell, P.G.J.W. ; Rev. R. Hodgson, P.G. chaplain; Rev. Thomas William Sturgess, P.G. chaplain ; T. H. Annett, P.G. treasurer; Herbert Finch, P.G. registrar ; R. Newhouse, P.G. secretary ; M. Long- ridge, P.G.A. secretary; Henry Jackson, P.G.S.D. ; William Henry Finchett, P.G.S.D. • James Gamlin, P.G.J.D. ; John Stainforth, ; Henry Mat- thews, P.G., superintendent of works; a H. Brown, P.G.D.C. ; John Lewis, P.G.D.D. of C.; Arthur C. Muir, P.G. assistant D.D. of C.; John Morris, P.G., sword bearer; W. F. Norman, P.G. standard bearer; Charles Edmund Brooke, P.G. standard bearer; Alexander J. Phipps, P.G. organist; W. H. Collier, P.G. pursuivant ; Seth Flitcroft, P.G. assistant pur- suivant ; Thomas Litherland, T. W. Markland, Jas. S. Jolley, Thomas Haddon, C. W. Phillips, and Thos. S. Burgess. _ .

Charity medals were presented to the following brethren :—H. Brett, P.P.G.D.D.C., P.M., Sincerity,. 428; J. T. Appleby, P.M., De Tabley, 941; G. T. Kertin, Bari of Chester, 1,565; 11. G. Small, S. W., Alan, 2,368; W. Ramsden, P.P.G.J.D. Bars were presented to Bros. J. Ulayton,P.P.G.J. W.; James Cookson, P.P.G. treasurer; Rev. C. W. Spencer Stanhope, P.G. chaplain of England; James Salmon, P.P.G.S.W., ; R. Newhouse, P.G. Sec.; and T. C. Thorburn, P.P.G.S. of W. _
Bro. Lieut.-Colonel Wilkinson proposed that the salary of the P.G.Secretary (Bro.Newhouse) be ad- vanced from £BO to £lOO.

Bro. the Rev. C. W. Spencer Stanhope seconded the proposition, which was carried unanimously. The R. W. Provincial Grand Master announced that the next annual meeting of P.G. Lodge would be held at Congleton. Bro. Benson, Shropshire and North Wales, was appointed as representative of the Province on the Board of Management of the Boys' School in London. On the motion of Bro. Hodgson, seconded by Bro. Stanhope, a vote of thanks was given to the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, vicar of Runcorn, for the use of the Parish Church, in which a service was about to be held.
This concluded the business, and P.G. Lodge was enclosed.

The brethren then formed into procession and walked to the Parish Church, where divine service was held. The lewises who carried the Volume of the Sacred Law were Masters Marcus Mellor, Thos. Mellor, J. W. Coxhill, and M. Upton, all sons of members of the Ellesmere Lodge. In the absence, through indisposition, of Bro. A. J. Phipps. the P.G-.0., the musical arrangements were under the direction of Bro. W. H. Maxfield, P.P.G.0., of Hazle Grove. The service was fully choral, the choir of the Parish Church being assisted by several Masonic visitors. The sermon was preached by the Rev. Mr. Sturgess, and a collection was made in aid of the Pro- vincial Fund of Benevolence. At the close of the service,the brethren proceeded to the Parish Schools, where a sumptuous • banquet was served by Mr. Speakman,of the Saracen's Head,Wilderspool,whose catering gave general satisfaction. The R. W. Pro- vincial Grand Master presided, and the usual loyal, masonic, and complimentary toasts were duly honoured, the proceedings being enlivened by some excellent singing.
Alderman Evans was, on Tuesday, unanimously elected Lord Mayor of London.
The Blackpool licensing magistrates have refused a pro- visional license to the Eiffel Tower Company, and it is understood that the decision will place the directors in some difficulty.

div.head: ST. HELENS AND SCIENTIFIC EDUCATION.
div.p: ST. HELENS AND SCIENTIFIC EDUCATION.

The arrangements for the science and art classes, formed by the Corporation Technical Education Com- mittee and the local committee for the encouragement of science and art have been completed, and the first series of the classes have been held this week. Students and intending students have been informed that Govern- ment certificates will be awarded to all who pass the examinations, in addition to which Queen's prizes and and local prizes may also be obtained. The fees, which have been'fixed at a fairly nominal amount, are payable in advance, and those students who do not attend at least 20 lessons and sit at the examinations will be charged 10s, 6d. extra for each subject. The technical education committee of the Council will, however, re- turn half the fees to those who attend 29 lamas and also the examinations.

div.head: BUTESFIIRE.
div.p: BUTESFIIRE.

Mr. Gladstone has written a commendatory letter to Mr. M'Cullock, the Gladstenian candidate for Bute, where the polling is fixed to take place on the 9th inst. The voice of Scotland, he says, has from the first been unequivocally given on behalf of that reasonable settle- ment of the Irish qnestion without which there can be no effectual prosecution of British reforms in general and no adequate attention to the claims of Scotland in particular. It can hardly be that the electors of Bute can desire the continuation of a state of things under which the known wishes of Scotland in its local matters are constantly overridden by the votes of the English members. It is this state of things, so unjust to Scot- land, that his opponents seek to prolong, and it is only by returning Mr. M'Culloch victoriously to Parliament that the constituency of Bute can, as a portion of the Scottish people, contribute their share to amend it.

THE TEMPERANCE CRUSADE AT ST. HELENS.

At the St. Helens Police Court, on Wednesday, the Rev. R. J. Ward,Congregational minister.applied to the magistrates (Dr. Gaskell, Mr. A. Sinclair, and Mr. A. Walmsley-Cottam) for a summons against Mr. John Marsh, landlord of the Sefton Arms, Hotel, Ormskirk-st. Mr. Ward stated that on Tuesday morning he was passing along Church-st.,when his attention was arrested by two men, one of whom was reeling from side to side, and was manifestly under the influence of drink. A few minutes afterwards he saw them coming out of the Globe Hotel, and he asked the man who was sober, "Have you been served with drink in this place ? " The man replied " No,they would not serve him," meaning his companion. He (Mr. Ward) said they had better not do so. He afterwards saw the men going up the street, and he followed them. He observed that they went into the Sefton Arms, and two or three minutes later he went in also. He saw the two men sitting in a room clse to the door, with two newly- filled glasses before them. The man who was not drunk had a glass of whiskey, and a man who was drunk had a glass of beer before him. He asked a girl who came in- to the room if Mr. Marsh was in, and she replied "No." He then asked, " who is the head barman ?" and she said," I am." He asked, "Did you serve these men ?" and she said " Yes." He then said, " Cannot you per- ceive that one of them is drunk ?" and she said she could not. Another man at that moment took up the glass of beer and said" He has not touched it." Mr. Marsh came forward in his shirt sleeves and at once ordered the drunken man out. He (Mr. Ward) immediately followed He asked for a summons against Marsh for supplying drink to a drunken man. —ln answer to the Clerk, Mr. Ward said he did not know the name of the man who was drunk.—The Chairman: The summons will be granted. At the St. Helens Police Court, on Thursday. the Rev. R. J. Ward, applied for a summons to compel John Littler, of Billinge, to appear as a witness in the case. The summons was granted.

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY OF CHESTER will be holden at the COURT HOUSE, NETHER KNUTSFORD, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 19th day of October next, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Bucklow, Macclesfield, and Northwich, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners com- mitted from such Hundreds, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Knutsford District must be in attendance at the Court House, Knutsford, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 19th day of October, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE Court will be Adjourned to the Castle of Chester, on THURSDA, the 22nd day of October next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon, when another Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within tha Hundreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-mentioned Hundreds will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on THURSDAY, the 22nd day of October next, at Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerleof the Peace for the County of Chester. Chester, 29th September, 1891.

Q UMMER COACHING TOURS. U J During the Summer months we have decided to organise and conduct a series of COACHING TRIPS to the various pleasure resorts surrounding Warrington. THE NEW UNDER-SECRETARY. Mr. Lowther's appointment to post of Under-Secretary for foreign affairs was officially announced last evening. THE GREAT BICYCLE RIDE. The Press Association Wick correspondent telegraphs that Mr. Mills, the bicyclist, arrived at John o'Groat's this morning, having accomplished the journey from Land's End in 4 days, 4 hours, 15. minutes. beating his previous record by over 21 hours. POACHING AFFRAY IN CHESHIRE. Yesterday morning James Whittaker, Wm. Yarwood, Richard Weedall, and Edward Evans were charged with maliciously wounding with intent Constables Richardson and William Gibbons, and assaulting Ser- geant Dalton, at Cogshall, on September 26th. The offi- cers met the wen soon after midnight, and, suspecting them to be poachers, spoke to them, and were then set upon and severely ill-treated. Colonel Hamersley asked for a remand for another week, which was granted. NATIONAL LIBERAL FEDERATION. YESTERDAY'S' PROCEEDINGS. The National Liberal Federation resumed its proceed- ings at Newcastle yesterday. Sir George Trevelyan moved a resolution calling for an amendment of the registration laws, shortening of Parliaments, and the payment of members. This was seconded by Mr. Storey, M.P., and was carried unanimously. The Marquis of Ripon moved a resolution that Parlia- ment should give immediate attention to the condition of the rural population, establish district and parish councils, give compulsory powers to local authorities to acquire land for public purposes, and reform the Allot- ments Acts. Sir Charles Foster seconded, and Mr. Stevenson, Mr. Spencer Balfour, and others supported the resolution, Which was passed unanimously. After speeches by Sir Wilfrid Lawson, Mr. H. Fowler, and Mr. Creig, the Conference re-affirmed its declara- don's in favour of land law reform, the popular veto on the liquor traffic, disestablishment in Scotland, equaliza- tion of the death duties, a just division of rates between owner and occupier, a free breakfast table, the Factory Act Extension, and the mending or ending of the House of Lords. The Women's Federation also held a sitting and dis- cussed several topics, but without committing itself to resolutions thereon. FRFNCHMEN AND ITALIANS.—EXCITEMENT IN ROME. ROME FRIDAY EYEING.—This afterneon a party of French pilgrims grossly insultecT the tomb of Victor Emanuel. The populace at once attacked the pilgrims and wounded several of them. Thousands are now flocking to the tomb shouting " Death to Frenchmen." Enormous excitement prevails.

A RUNCOR,N FLAT CAPTAIN DROWNED. Information reached the Liverpool Lawling- stage early yesterday morning that Thomas Shell- cross, residing in Penketh-st., Runcorn, master of the flat William, fell overboard from his vessel about a quarter to one o'clock, and that his body disappeared almost at once. The flat was at anchor off the Toxteth Dock.
